            best = Math.max(best, p - minPrice);
        }
        return best;
    }

    static int maxProfitUnlimited(int[] prices) {   // as many transactions as you like
        int profit = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) {
            if (prices[i] > prices[i - 1]) profit += prices[i] - prices[i - 1];
        }
        return profit;
    }

    static int maxProduct(int[] a) {                // Maximum Product Subarray
        int max = a[0], min = a[0], best = a[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (a[i] < 0) { int t = max; max = min; min = t; }   // negative flips order
            max = Math.max(a[i], max * a[i]);
            min = Math.min(a[i], min * a[i]);
            best = Math.max(best, max);
        }
        return best;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(maxProfit(new int[]{7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4}) + " "
            + maxProfitUnlimited(new int[]{7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4}) + " "
            + maxProduct(new int[]{2, 3, -2, 4}));
    }
}
5 7 6

All three run in O(n) time and O(1) space. For prices [7,1,5,3,6,4]: min price 1, best sale at 6 gives 5; for unlimited, (5−1) + (6−3) = 7.

How to recognise the pattern

Look for "largest (or smallest) sum or product of a contiguous part" and a hint that the answer depends only on the best run ending at the previous index. The state is tiny: one number, "the best value of a run that ends here". Whenever a problem lets you build the answer at i from the answer at i−1 plus a[i], you can compress a DP table to one or two variables. That is exactly what Kadane does.

A second view: prefix sums

Using the prefix sums from the previous article, the sum of a[j..i] is prefix[i+1] - prefix[j]. For a fixed end i you want the smallest earlier prefix. So the answer is the maximum over i of (current prefix − the minimum prefix seen so far). It is the same algorithm in other words, and it is the same trick as the stock problem: "sell price minus the lowest buy price so far". That is why the stock problem is Kadane in disguise.

static int maxSubarrayViaPrefix(int[] a) {
    long prefix = 0, minPrefix = 0;            // minPrefix starts with the empty prefix
    long best = Long.MIN_VALUE;
    for (int x : a) {
        prefix += x;
        best = Math.max(best, prefix - minPrefix);
        minPrefix = Math.min(minPrefix, prefix);   // update AFTER using it: subarray not empty
    }
    return (int) best;
}

Maximum Sum Circular Subarray in code

In a circular array the best subarray is either a normal one, or it wraps around the end. A wrapping subarray equals the total minus a normal subarray in the middle that is as small as possible. So run Kadane twice (once for the maximum, once for the minimum) in the same loop.

static int maxSubarraySumCircular(int[] a) {
    int total = 0, curMax = 0, curMin = 0, best = a[0], worst = a[0];
    for (int x : a) {
        curMax = Math.max(x, curMax + x);
        best = Math.max(best, curMax);
        curMin = Math.min(x, curMin + x);
        worst = Math.min(worst, curMin);
        total += x;
    }
    if (best < 0) return best;                  // all negative: wrapping would mean "empty"
    return Math.max(best, total - worst);
}
// [5, -3, 5]: best = 7, total = 7, worst = -3 -> max(7, 10) = 10 (the two 5s wrap)

When every element is negative, total - worst would be 0, an empty subarray, which is not allowed; that is why the early return exists.

Dry runs for the stock and product problems

Stock, prices [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]. The minimum so far goes 7, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. The profit if you sell that day is 0, 0, 4, 2, 5, 3. The best is 5 (buy at 1, sell at 6).

Max product, [2, 3, −2, 4]. Keep the largest and the smallest product that end at i, because a negative number swaps their roles.

ia[i]max ending heremin ending herebest
02222
13636
2−2−2−126
344−486

At i = 2 the code first swaps max and min (3 and 6 become 6 and 3 in the roles), then takes max(−2, 3 × −2) = −2 and min(−2, 6 × −2) = −12. The answer is 6 (the subarray [2, 3]). A zero resets both values to 0 through the Math.max(a[i], ...) and Math.min(a[i], ...) calls.

Variants side by side

ProblemState keptAnswer
Maximum Subarraybest sum ending heremax over all i
Maximum Product Subarraymax and min product ending heremax of the max
Circular maximumKadane max and Kadane min, plus totalmax(best, total − worst)
Stock, one tradelowest price so farmax of price − lowest
Stock, many tradesnone (add each rise)sum of positive differences

Edge cases

  • Single element: the loop from index 1 does not run and a[0] is returned, which is correct.
  • All negative: the answer is the largest (least negative) element, never 0.
  • Prices only falling: the stock profit is 0 (do not trade), not negative. That is why best starts at 0 there, but not in Maximum Subarray.
  • Overflow: for very long arrays of large numbers use long. Product problems overflow quickly; LeetCode promises the answer fits in 32 bits.

Divide and conquer also works

You can split the array in half and combine (best in the left, best in the right, best crossing the middle) in O(n log n). Interviewers sometimes ask for it as a follow-up. Kadane is simpler and faster, so mention the idea but code Kadane.

Interview angle

Start with brute force O(n²), then explain Kadane with the "extend or restart" sentence. Be ready for: "return the subarray itself", "what if all numbers are negative", "what if the array is circular". Mention it is DP with O(1) space. A weak answer says "reset to zero when the sum goes negative" without handling the all-negative case.

Arrays: rotation, two pointers and in-place tricks

Many array problems ask for O(1) extra space; the tools are reversal, the read/write two-pointer technique, the three-pointer Dutch flag partition and Boyer–Moore voting.

The read/write pointer pattern

To filter an array in place, keep a read pointer that scans every element and a write pointer marking where the next kept element goes. Everything before write is the finished answer. This single idea solves move zeroes, remove element and remove duplicates.

import java.util.*;

public class ReadWrite {
    // Move Zeroes (283): keep order of non-zeros, push zeros to the end
    static void moveZeroes(int[] a) {
        int write = 0;
        for (int read = 0; read < a.length; read++) {
            if (a[read] != 0) a[write++] = a[read];
        }
        while (write < a.length) a[write++] = 0;
    }

    // Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (26): return new length
    static int removeDuplicates(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 0) return 0;
        int write = 1;
        for (int read = 1; read < a.length; read++) {
            if (a[read] != a[write - 1]) a[write++] = a[read];
        }
        return write;
    }

    // Remove Element (27): remove all occurrences of val
    static int removeElement(int[] a, int val) {
        int write = 0;
        for (int x : a) if (x != val) a[write++] = x;
        return write;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] z = {0, 1, 0, 3, 12};
        moveZeroes(z);
        int[] d = {0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3};
        int len = removeDuplicates(d);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(z) + " " + len + " "
            + Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOf(d, len)));
    }
}
[1, 3, 12, 0, 0] 4 [0, 1, 2, 3]

All are O(n) time, O(1) space. Dry run, Remove Duplicates on [0,0,1,1,1,2]: write = 1; read 1 (0 equals a[0]) skip; read 2 (1 differs from a[0] = 0) → a[1] = 1, write 2; reads 3 and 4 (1 equals a[1]) skip; read 5 (2 differs) → a[2] = 2, write 3. Length 3: [0,1,2].

Rotation by reversal

Rotate Array (189): move each element k places to the right (cyclically). Making a copy is O(n) space. The in-place trick uses three reversals:

import java.util.*;

public class Rotate {
    static void rotateRight(int[] a, int k) {
        int n = a.length;
        k %= n;                                   // k can exceed n; n = 0 would divide by 0
        reverse(a, 0, n - 1);
        reverse(a, 0, k - 1);
        reverse(a, k, n - 1);
    }

    static void reverse(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        while (i < j) {
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;
            i++; j--;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7};
        rotateRight(a, 10);                        // 10 % 7 = 3
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]

O(n) time, O(1) space. Rotating left by k is the same as rotating right by n − k. Guard against an empty array before k %= n.

Dutch national flag (Sort Colors)

Sort Colors (75): the array has only 0, 1 and 2; sort it in one pass without a counting sort. Keep three zones: [0, low) are 0s, [low, mid) are 1s, (high, n-1] are 2s, and [mid, high] is unexplored.

import java.util.*;

public class SortColors {
    static void sortColors(int[] a) {
        int low = 0, mid = 0, high = a.length - 1;
        while (mid <= high) {
            if (a[mid] == 0) {
                swap(a, low++, mid++);              // 0 goes left; the swapped-in value is a 1
            } else if (a[mid] == 1) {
                mid++;
            } else {
                swap(a, mid, high--);               // 2 goes right; do NOT advance mid
            }
        }
    }

    static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) { int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0};
        sortColors(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]

O(n) time, one pass, O(1) space. After swapping with high you do not know what arrived at mid, so you must look at it again. The same three-way partition is used in quicksort with many duplicates.

Majority element: Boyer–Moore voting

Majority Element (169): find the value that appears more than n/2 times (it is guaranteed to exist). Keep a candidate and a counter: equal element → counter++, different element → counter--, counter 0 → take a new candidate. Each non-majority element cancels one majority element, and the majority is more than half, so it survives.

public class Majority {
    static int majorityElement(int[] a) {
        int candidate = 0, count = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            if (count == 0) candidate = x;
            count += (x == candidate) ? 1 : -1;
        }
        return candidate;        // correct only if a majority is guaranteed
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(majorityElement(new int[]{2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2}));
    }
}
2

O(n) time, O(1) space (the HashMap version is O(n) space; sorting and taking the middle element is O(n log n)). If a majority is not guaranteed, make a second pass to verify the count.

Merge Sorted Array (88)

Merge nums2 into nums1, which has room at the end. Merging from the front would overwrite values, so fill from the back with three pointers.

import java.util.*;

public class MergeSorted {
    static void merge(int[] nums1, int m, int[] nums2, int n) {
        int i = m - 1, j = n - 1, k = m + n - 1;
        while (j >= 0) {                           // leftover nums1 is already in place
            if (i >= 0 && nums1[i] > nums2[j]) nums1[k--] = nums1[i--];
            else nums1[k--] = nums2[j--];
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0};
        merge(a, 3, new int[]{2, 5, 6}, 3);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]

Rule: when in-place work overwrites data you still need, change the direction

Merging from the back, and rotating by reversals, both exist because going forward would destroy values. Ask "what do I overwrite, and do I still need it?" before writing the loop.

How to recognise an in-place problem

The words are "in place", "O(1) extra space", "do not allocate another array", or "modify the input array". A quick way to choose a technique is to ask what the final array looks like:

If the result is...UseExample
the same elements, filtered, order keptread/write pointersMove Zeroes, Remove Element
the same elements, shifted cyclicallythree reversalsRotate Array
a few categories grouped togetherthree-way partitionSort Colors
one value that dominatesvotingMajority Element
two sorted lists in one bufferfill from the backMerge Sorted Array

Remove Duplicates II: allow each value twice

The read/write idea extends by changing what you compare. To keep at most two copies of each value in a sorted array, a new element is kept unless it equals the element two places behind the write pointer. That element is the last one you are allowed to keep twice.

static int removeDuplicatesII(int[] a) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        if (write < 2 || x != a[write - 2]) a[write++] = x;
    }
    return write;                              // O(n) time, O(1) space
}

Dry run on [1,1,1,2,2,3]: the first two 1s are kept; the third 1 equals a[0] so it is skipped; 2 differs from a[0] = 1 and is kept (write is now 3); the next 2 differs from a[1] = 1 and is kept (write 4); 3 differs from a[2] = 2 and is kept. The array starts with [1,1,2,2,3] and the return value is 5. Replace 2 by k to allow k copies.

Squares of a sorted array: two pointers from both ends

The input is sorted and may have negatives. Squares make the biggest values appear at either end, never in the middle. So compare the absolute values at the two ends, place the larger square at the back of the result, and move that pointer inward.

static int[] sortedSquares(int[] a) {
    int n = a.length;
    int[] res = new int[n];
    int l = 0, r = n - 1;
    for (int k = n - 1; k >= 0; k--) {         // fill the result from the largest
        if (Math.abs(a[l]) > Math.abs(a[r])) {
            res[k] = a[l] * a[l];
            l++;
        } else {
            res[k] = a[r] * a[r];
            r--;
        }
    }
    return res;                                // O(n) time, O(n) for the output
}

For [-4,-1,0,3,10] the steps place 100, 16, 9, 1, 0 from the back, giving [0,1,9,16,100]. Sorting the squares would be O(n log n); the two-pointer idea uses the sorted order that is already there. The same two-ends idea is the heart of two pointers in Module 2.

Why Boyer–Moore voting works, with a trace

Pair every element that differs from the candidate with a candidate copy and cancel the pair. A true majority appears more than n/2 times, so even if every other element cancels one copy of it, at least one copy is left. The counter never says what the majority is for sure; it only guarantees that the survivor is the only possible one. Trace on [2,2,1,1,1,2,2]:

x2211122
candidate2222112
count after1210101

The final candidate is 2, which is correct. The same idea extends to elements appearing more than n/3 times (Majority Element II): keep two candidates and two counters, because at most two values can exceed n/3.

Edge cases

  • Empty array: k %= n throws ArithmeticException ("/ by zero") when n = 0. Return early for a.length < 2.
  • Negative k: in Java -1 % 7 is -1, not 6. Normalise with k = ((k % n) + n) % n if k can be negative.
  • k = 0 or a multiple of n: after the modulo k is 0 and reverse(a, 0, -1) does nothing, because the loop guard i < j is false. It works, but check it by hand.
  • All zeros or no zeros in Move Zeroes; all equal values in Remove Duplicates (result length 1).
  • No guaranteed majority: verify the candidate with a second pass.

Mistake: using a second array for an "in place" problem

Wrong: extra array breaks the O(1) space rule

int[] tmp = new int[a.length];            // O(n) extra space
int w = 0;
for (int x : a) if (x != 0) tmp[w++] = x;
System.arraycopy(tmp, 0, a, 0, a.length);

Right: read and write inside the same array

int w = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++)
    if (a[r] != 0) a[w++] = a[r];
while (w < a.length) a[w++] = 0;          // O(1) extra space

Interview angle

Interviewers often say "do it in O(1) extra space". Name the technique: read/write pointers, reversal, three-way partition, voting. Explain the invariant (what is true about the prefix at each step) — that is what shows you understand rather than memorised.

Arrays: product except self, next permutation, leaders, missing numbers

These five classics all use a pass from each side, a swap-and-reverse, or the array's own indices as a marker — each is a short idea once you have seen it.

Product of Array Except Self (238)

For each index, the product of all other elements — without division and in O(n). The answer at i is (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i). Build the left products in the result array in one pass, then multiply the right products in a second pass using one variable.

import java.util.*;

public class ProductExceptSelf {
    static int[] productExceptSelf(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] res = new int[n];
        res[0] = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) res[i] = res[i - 1] * a[i - 1];   // left products
        int right = 1;
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            res[i] *= right;                                           // times right products
            right *= a[i];
        }
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(productExceptSelf(new int[]{1, 2, 3, 4})));
    }
}
[24, 12, 8, 6]

Dry run: after pass 1 res = [1, 1, 2, 6] (left products). Pass 2 from the right with right = 1: i = 3 → 6 × 1 = 6, right = 4; i = 2 → 2 × 4 = 8, right = 12; i = 1 → 1 × 12 = 12, right = 24; i = 0 → 1 × 24 = 24. Time O(n), extra space O(1) beyond the output. Why no division? Zeros make division impossible.

Next Permutation (31)

Rearrange the numbers into the next larger permutation in dictionary order (or the smallest if none exists), in place. Example: 1 2 3 → 1 3 2; 3 2 1 → 1 2 3; 1 5 8 4 7 6 5 3 1 → 1 5 8 5 1 3 4 6 7.

  1. From the right, find the first index i where a[i] < a[i+1] (the "pivot"). The suffix after i is in decreasing order — already the largest arrangement of those numbers.
  2. If no such i exists, the array is the last permutation: reverse it all and stop.
  3. From the right, find the first j with a[j] > a[i] (the smallest bigger number in the suffix). Swap a[i] and a[j].
  4. Reverse the suffix after i, to make it the smallest (increasing) arrangement.
import java.util.*;

public class NextPermutation {
    static void nextPermutation(int[] a) {
        int i = a.length - 2;
        while (i >= 0 && a[i] >= a[i + 1]) i--;       // find the pivot
        if (i >= 0) {
            int j = a.length - 1;
            while (a[j] <= a[i]) j--;                  // smallest bigger value from the right
            swap(a, i, j);
        }
        reverse(a, i + 1, a.length - 1);               // i = -1 reverses the whole array
    }

    static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) { int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; }

    static void reverse(int[] a, int l, int r) {
        while (l < r) swap(a, l++, r--);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {1, 5, 8, 4, 7, 6, 5, 3, 1};
        nextPermutation(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[1, 5, 8, 5, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7]

O(n) time, O(1) space. Pivot is 4 (index 3); swap with 5 → 1 5 8 5 7 6 4 3 1; reverse the suffix 7 6 4 3 1 → 1 3 4 6 7. Note: the pivot loop uses >=, so duplicate values are handled correctly.

Leaders in an Array

A leader is an element greater than (or equal to, depending on the statement) everything to its right. Scan from the right, keeping the maximum so far; an element beating it is a leader. The last element is always a leader. O(n) time.

import java.util.*;

public class Leaders {
    static List<Integer> leaders(int[] a) {
        List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        int max = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int i = a.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            if (a[i] > max) {
                result.add(a[i]);
                max = a[i];
            }
        }
        Collections.reverse(result);                // restore left-to-right order
        return result;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(leaders(new int[]{16, 17, 4, 3, 5, 2}));
    }
}
[17, 5, 2]

Missing and repeating numbers: use the array as its own map

When the array holds numbers from 1 to n, the values themselves are valid indices. Three tools, from simplest to leanest:

  • Sum formula: the missing number in 0..n is n(n+1)/2 - sum(a) (Missing Number, 268). Use long if n is large. XOR does the same without overflow (see the bit manipulation article).
  • Index marking: for each value v, negate a[|v|-1]. A value whose slot is already negative is a duplicate; a slot still positive at the end means its index+1 is missing.
  • Cycle sort / swap into place: put each v at index v−1.
import java.util.*;

public class MissingRepeating {
    // Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array (448); values are in 1..n
    static List<Integer> disappeared(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            int idx = Math.abs(a[i]) - 1;
            if (a[idx] > 0) a[idx] = -a[idx];          // mark value idx+1 as seen
        }
        List<Integer> missing = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] > 0) missing.add(i + 1);
        return missing;
    }

    // Find the Duplicate Number (287) when the array may be modified: marking
    static int findDuplicate(int[] a) {
        for (int x : a) {
            int idx = Math.abs(x) - 1;
            if (a[idx] < 0) return Math.abs(x);        // slot already marked
            a[idx] = -a[idx];
        }
        return -1;
    }

    // Missing Number (268): values are 0..n with one missing
    static int missingNumber(int[] a) {
        long n = a.length;
        long expected = n * (n + 1) / 2, actual = 0;
        for (int x : a) actual += x;
        return (int) (expected - actual);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(disappeared(new int[]{4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1}));
        System.out.println(findDuplicate(new int[]{1, 3, 4, 2, 2}));
        System.out.println(missingNumber(new int[]{3, 0, 1}));
    }
}
[5, 6]
2
2

All are O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The marking trick modifies the input; if that is forbidden, use a boolean[] (O(n) space) or, for Find the Duplicate Number with a read-only array, Floyd's cycle detection (Module 2, linked lists).

Edge case: duplicates and negatives break the tricks

The index-marking idea needs every value to be a valid index (1..n). If values can be 0, negative or larger than n, first check the constraints, or use a hash set. Always ask: "can the array be modified?"

Tip: how to think about array problems

  1. Write 2–3 small examples and solve by hand; notice what you do with your eyes.
  2. Ask what must be known at position i: something from the left, from the right, or both? (Two passes or prefix/suffix arrays.)
  3. Ask if sorting or a hash set removes the difficulty (and what it costs).
  4. Try to cut space: can the output array or the input itself hold the state?
  5. Test: length 1, all equal, already sorted, reverse sorted, negatives, zeros.

Interview angle

For "product except self" interviewers want the left/right pass idea and the reason division fails (zeros). For "next permutation" they want the four steps spoken in order and the reason the suffix is reversed rather than sorted: it is already in decreasing order, so reversing it sorts it in O(n).

Strings: the Java API, StringBuilder and palindromes

A Java String is an immutable sequence of chars, so every "change" creates a new string; build results with StringBuilder or a char[], and check palindromes with two pointers moving inward.

Substring, subsequence, subarray

Three words that interviewers use precisely:

TermMeaningExample from "abcde"How many
Substring / subarrayContiguous characters"bcd"n(n+1)/2 non-empty
SubsequenceKeeps order, may skip characters"ace"2n (including empty)
SubsetAny selection, order ignored{"c", "a"}2n

Substring problems often use a sliding window (Module 2); subsequence problems often use two pointers or dynamic programming (Module 3).

The String API you need

MethodPurposeCost
length(), charAt(i)Size and character at indexO(1)
substring(i, j)Characters i..j-1 (end exclusive)O(j − i)
indexOf(x), contains(x)Find a character or substringO(n × m) worst case
equals, equalsIgnoreCase, compareToCompare content (never use ==)O(length)
toCharArray()Copy into a mutable char[]O(n)
split(regex), String.joinBreak and glueO(n)
trim(), strip(), toLowerCase()Clean upO(n)
String.valueOf(char[]), new String(char[])Back from a char arrayO(n)
chars()IntStream of the charactersO(n)

Mistake: building a string with += in a loop

Strings are immutable. s += c allocates a new string and copies all of s each time, so n appends cost 1 + 2 + … + n = O(n²). For n = 105 this is a time-limit failure. Use StringBuilder (O(n) total).

public class Building {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'e'; c++) sb.append(c).append(',');
        sb.setLength(sb.length() - 1);               // drop the trailing comma
        System.out.println(sb);
        sb.reverse();                                 // in place; returns the same object
        System.out.println(sb);

        char[] chars = "hello".toCharArray();         // mutable copy
        chars[0] = 'j';
        System.out.println(new String(chars) + " " + String.valueOf(chars, 1, 3));

        String a = "abc", b = new String("abc");
        System.out.println((a == b) + " " + a.equals(b));
    }
}
a,b,c,d,e
e,d,c,b,a
jello ell
false true

reverse(), append() and insert() change the builder itself and return it, which is why calls can be chained.

Palindromes with two pointers

A palindrome reads the same both ways. Put one pointer at each end and move inward while characters match. O(n) time, O(1) space.

public class Palindromes {
    static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        int i = 0, j = s.length() - 1;
        while (i < j) {
            if (s.charAt(i++) != s.charAt(j--)) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    // Valid Palindrome (125): ignore non-alphanumerics and case
    static boolean isPalindromeClean(String s) {
        int i = 0, j = s.length() - 1;
        while (i < j) {
            while (i < j && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(i))) i++;
            while (i < j && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(j))) j--;
            if (Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(i)) != Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(j)))
                return false;
            i++; j--;
        }
        return true;
    }

    // Valid Palindrome II (680): may delete at most one character
    static boolean validPalindromeII(String s) {
        int i = 0, j = s.length() - 1;
        while (i < j) {
            if (s.charAt(i) != s.charAt(j)) {
                return isRange(s, i + 1, j) || isRange(s, i, j - 1);
            }
            i++; j--;
        }
        return true;
    }

    static boolean isRange(String s, int i, int j) {
        while (i < j) if (s.charAt(i++) != s.charAt(j--)) return false;
        return true;
    }

    // Longest Palindromic Substring (5): expand around each centre, O(n^2)
    static String longestPalindrome(String s) {
        int start = 0, end = 0;
        for (int c = 0; c < s.length(); c++) {
            int len = Math.max(expand(s, c, c), expand(s, c, c + 1));   // odd, even
            if (len > end - start) {
                start = c - (len - 1) / 2;
                end = c + len / 2;
            }
        }
        return s.substring(start, end + 1);
    }

    static int expand(String s, int l, int r) {
        while (l >= 0 && r < s.length() && s.charAt(l) == s.charAt(r)) { l--; r++; }
        return r - l - 1;                                    // length of the palindrome
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(isPalindromeClean("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"));
        System.out.println(validPalindromeII("abca") + " " + longestPalindrome("babad"));
    }
}
true
true bab

Dry run, Valid Palindrome II on "abca": i = 0, j = 3 match ('a'); i = 1, j = 2: 'b' vs 'c' differ → try skipping i (range 2..2 = "c", palindrome) → true. Longest palindromic substring: O(n²) time, O(1) space (2n − 1 centres, each expands up to n). Manacher's algorithm makes it O(n) but is rarely expected.

Edge cases for strings

Empty string, single character, all identical characters, case differences, spaces and punctuation, and — if the statement allows — Unicode. charAt with a bad index throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. null input: ask whether it can occur.

Interview angle

"Why are Java strings immutable?" Safety (hash keys, class loading, security), caching of hash codes, string pool sharing, thread safety — see Core Java · Module 1. For DSA, the practical answer is: so every modification costs O(n), and you reach for StringBuilder or char[].

Strings: anagrams, frequency counting and classic problems

Most string problems reduce to counting characters in an int[26] or HashMap, comparing sorted forms, or walking the string with one or two indices.

Frequency counting

Two strings are anagrams when they use the same characters the same number of times, in any order ("listen", "silent"). There are two standard checks:

  • Sort both and compare: O(n log n) time.
  • Count characters with an int[26]: add for one string, subtract for the other; all zeros means anagram. O(n) time, O(1) space (26 is a constant).
import java.util.*;

public class Anagrams {
    // Valid Anagram (242)
    static boolean isAnagram(String s, String t) {
        if (s.length() != t.length()) return false;
        int[] count = new int[26];
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            count[s.charAt(i) - 'a']++;
            count[t.charAt(i) - 'a']--;
        }
        for (int c : count) if (c != 0) return false;
        return true;
    }

    // Group Anagrams (49): key = the 26 counts, O(n * k) for n words of length k
    static List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] words) {
        Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
        for (String w : words) {
            int[] count = new int[26];
            for (char c : w.toCharArray()) count[c - 'a']++;
            String key = Arrays.toString(count);          // e.g. "[1, 0, 0, ..., 1]"
            groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(groups.values());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(isAnagram("listen", "silent") + " " + isAnagram("rat", "car"));
        String[] words = {"eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"};
        System.out.println(groupAnagrams(words).size());
    }
}
true false
3

For Group Anagrams, the key can also be the sorted word (new String(sortedChars)) — O(n × k log k), simpler to write. Pick the sorted key in a hurry; use the count key when asked to optimise.

Edge case: the alphabet

int[26] is correct only for lowercase English letters. If the problem allows uppercase, digits or Unicode, use int[128]/int[256] or a HashMap<Character, Integer> — otherwise you get ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

First Unique Character in a String (387)

Count all characters in one pass; scan again to find the first with count 1. Two passes, O(n) time, O(1) space.

public class FirstUnique {
    static int firstUniqChar(String s) {
        int[] count = new int[26];
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) count[c - 'a']++;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            if (count[s.charAt(i) - 'a'] == 1) return i;
        }
        return -1;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(firstUniqChar("leetcode") + " " + firstUniqChar("aabb"));
    }
}
0 -1

Longest Common Prefix (14)

Take the first word as the candidate prefix and shorten it until every other word starts with it. O(total characters), O(1) extra space.

public class CommonPrefix {
    static String longestCommonPrefix(String[] strs) {
        if (strs.length == 0) return "";
        String prefix = strs[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < strs.length; i++) {
            while (!strs[i].startsWith(prefix)) {
                prefix = prefix.substring(0, prefix.length() - 1);
                if (prefix.isEmpty()) return "";
            }
        }
        return prefix;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(longestCommonPrefix(new String[]{"flower", "flow", "flight"}));
    }
}
fl

Dry run: prefix "flower" → "flow" matches "flow" → vs "flight": "flow", "flo", "fl" — now matches. Answer "fl".

Reverse Words in a String (151)

Split on whitespace (ignoring extra spaces), reverse the word order, join with one space.

import java.util.*;

public class ReverseWords {
    static String reverseWords(String s) {
        String[] parts = s.trim().split("\\s+");        // one or more whitespace chars
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = parts.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            sb.append(parts[i]);
            if (i > 0) sb.append(' ');
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("[" + reverseWords("  the sky   is blue ") + "]");
    }
}
[blue is sky the]

O(n) time and space. To do it in O(1) extra space on a char[]: reverse the whole array, then reverse each word — the same reversal trick as array rotation.

String Compression (443) and run-length encoding

Replace runs like "aaabb" by "a3b2" (a count of 1 is omitted in LeetCode's version). Walk with a read pointer that finds each run, and write the character and the digits of the count.

public class Compress {
    // in place on a char array; returns the new length (LeetCode 443 style)
    static int compress(char[] chars) {
        int write = 0, read = 0;
        while (read < chars.length) {
            char c = chars[read];
            int start = read;
            while (read < chars.length && chars[read] == c) read++;
            chars[write++] = c;
            int run = read - start;
            if (run > 1) {
                for (char d : String.valueOf(run).toCharArray()) chars[write++] = d;
            }
        }
        return write;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        char[] c = "aabbbccccccccccccc".toCharArray();
        int n = compress(c);
        System.out.println(new String(c, 0, n));
    }
}
a2b3c13

O(n) time, O(1) space. The count 13 takes two characters — that is why you convert the number to a string rather than writing one digit.

Other classics to practise

  • Reverse String (344) — two pointers swap, O(n), O(1).
  • Isomorphic Strings (205) / Word Pattern (290) — two maps for a one-to-one mapping.
  • Roman to Integer (13) — add each value, subtract it if the next symbol is larger.
  • Valid Parentheses (20) — a stack (Module 2).
  • Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (3) — sliding window (Module 2).
  • Implement strStr (28) — brute force O(n × m); KMP for O(n + m) in Module 3.

Tip: how to think about string problems

  1. Is order important (palindrome, subsequence) or only counts (anagram, frequency)? Counts → array or map.
  2. Do I need to look both ways → two pointers; do I need a window → sliding window.
  3. Am I modifying a lot → char[] or StringBuilder, not String.
  4. State the alphabet size out loud: it decides between int[26] and a map.

Anagram checks compared

There is more than one right way to compare two strings by their letters. Choose by the alphabet and by what you must do next.

MethodTimeSpaceUse when
Sort both, compareO(n log n)O(n) for the char arraysQuick to write; any alphabet
int[26] countsO(n)O(1)Only lowercase a–z
HashMap<Character, Integer>O(n)O(k) distinct charactersUnicode or mixed input
Count key (Group Anagrams)O(n·k)O(n·k)Many words, long words

The count-array idea is the most reusable tool in string problems: one pass fills it, and the "state" of a window or a prefix is just 26 numbers that you can compare with Arrays.equals.

Find All Anagrams in a String (a fixed window of counts)

Given a text s and a pattern p, return every start index where a substring of s is an anagram of p. Every such substring has length p.length(), so slide a window of that size: add the new character on the right, remove the old one on the left, and compare the two count arrays. This is the fixed-size window from sliding window, applied to counts.

import java.util.*;

public class FindAnagrams {
    static List<Integer> findAnagrams(String s, String p) {
        List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
        int m = p.length();
        if (s.length() < m) return res;
        int[] need = new int[26], win = new int[26];
        for (char c : p.toCharArray()) need[c - 'a']++;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            win[s.charAt(i) - 'a']++;                      // character enters on the right
            if (i >= m) win[s.charAt(i - m) - 'a']--;      // character leaves on the left
            if (Arrays.equals(need, win)) res.add(i - m + 1);
        }
        return res;                                        // O(26 * n) time, O(1) space
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(findAnagrams("cbaebabacd", "abc"));
    }
}
[0, 6]

Dry run: at i = 2 the window is "cba", whose counts equal those of "abc", so index 0 is added. Windows "bae", "aeb", "eba", "bab" and "aba" fail. At i = 8 the window is s[6..8] = "bac", which matches, so index 6 is added. The last window "acd" fails.

Ransom Note and Roman to Integer

Ransom Note (383): can the note be built from the letters of a magazine, using each letter once? Count the magazine, then subtract for each note letter; a count that goes below zero means failure. It is the anagram check with "at least" instead of "exactly". O(n + m) time, O(1) space.

Roman to Integer (13): read left to right. A symbol smaller than the one after it is subtracted (as in IV or CM); otherwise it is added.

static int romanToInt(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> v = Map.of('I', 1, 'V', 5, 'X', 10, 'L', 50,
                                       'C', 100, 'D', 500, 'M', 1000);
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        int cur = v.get(s.charAt(i));
        if (i + 1 < s.length() && cur < v.get(s.charAt(i + 1))) total -= cur;
        else total += cur;
    }
    return total;                              // O(n) time, O(1) space
}
// "MCMXCIV": 1000 - 100 + 1000 - 10 + 100 - 1 + 5 = 1994

How to think: a checklist

  1. Name the alphabet and the length limit before you pick a structure. Lowercase letters and n up to 105 point to counts and O(n).
  2. Decide what matters: counts only (anagram, ransom note), order (palindrome, subsequence), or contiguous pieces (substring, window).
  3. Use one pass plus a state whenever you can: a count array, a pair of pointers, or a stack.
  4. Build results with StringBuilder or a char[], never by += in a loop.
  5. Test the edges before you submit: empty string, one character, all equal characters, leading and trailing spaces.

Edge cases and the exceptions behind them

  • Empty or null input: s.length() on null throws NullPointerException. LeetCode rarely sends null, but real code must check.
  • Leading spaces and split(" "): " a b".split(" ") gives empty strings in the array. Use trim() and split("\\s+").
  • Case: "Listen" and "Silent" are not anagrams if case matters. Read the statement; call toLowerCase() only if it says to ignore case.
  • Unicode: charAt returns a 16-bit unit, so characters outside the basic plane (many emoji) are two units. For such text, iterate over code points with s.codePoints().
  • Different lengths: return false at once in Valid Anagram. It saves work and avoids reading past the shorter string.

Mistake: comparing strings with == and re-sorting inside a loop

Wrong: == compares references

String key = new String(sortedChars);
if (key == previousKey) {                 // may be false for equal text
    group.add(word);
}

Right: equals compares text

String key = new String(sortedChars);
if (key.equals(previousKey)) {
    group.add(word);
}

With a HashMap you do not compare keys yourself; the map calls hashCode and equals for you. A related slip is using the int[] itself as a map key: arrays use identity hashCode, so two equal arrays are different keys. Convert to a String (as above) or a List first.

Interview angle

Valid Anagram is a warm-up; the follow-up "what if the strings contain Unicode?" expects a HashMap. Group Anagrams expects you to explain the key choice and its cost. For compress/reverse-words, they check that you handle empty input, multiple spaces and runs of 10 or more.

Hashing: how it works, frequency maps and the two-sum idea

A hash table trades O(n) extra space for O(1) average lookups, which turns many O(n²) "find a matching pair" searches into one O(n) pass; the model example is Two Sum.

How hashing works (just enough for DSA)

A HashMap turns a key into an integer with hashCode(), reduces it to a bucket index, and stores the entry there. Lookup computes the same index and compares keys with equals(). With a good hash function and a table that resizes (load factor 0.75), buckets stay tiny, so get, put and containsKey are O(1) on average. The full internals are in Core Java · Module 4.

Worst case: if many keys land in one bucket (collisions), operations slow down. Since Java 8 a bucket with many entries becomes a balanced tree, so the worst case is about O(log n) for comparable keys, but treat "O(1) average" as the honest statement. Two practical consequences:

  • Keys must be immutable or at least not changed after insertion; and objects used as keys need equals and hashCode overridden together. int[] as a key compares by reference — convert to a List<Integer>, a String, or encode as a long.
  • Iteration order of HashMap/HashSet is unspecified. Use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap if the order matters.

Rule: choose the structure by the question you ask

"Have I seen x?" → HashSet. "How many times have I seen x?" / "Where did I see x?" → HashMap. "Is x in a small fixed alphabet or range 0..n?" → plain array (faster, no hashing). "Give me keys in sorted order / nearest key" → TreeMap.

Template 1: frequency map

import java.util.*;

public class FrequencyMap {
    static Map<Integer, Integer> frequency(int[] a) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
        return freq;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> f = frequency(new int[]{3, 1, 3, 2, 3, 1});
        System.out.println(f);                       // {1=2, 2=1, 3=3}
        int mostFrequent = Collections.max(f.entrySet(), Map.Entry.comparingByValue()).getKey();
        System.out.println(mostFrequent);
    }
}
{1=2, 2=1, 3=3}
3

Template 2: the two-sum idea

Two Sum (1): return the indices of two numbers adding to target. Brute force tries all pairs: O(n²). The key observation: for each x you want target - x. Store every number you have already passed in a map from value → index. At each element, look up its complement before inserting itself.

import java.util.*;

public class TwoSum {
    static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();      // value -> index
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            Integer j = seen.get(target - nums[i]);
            if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i};
            seen.put(nums[i], i);                           // insert AFTER checking
        }
        return new int[]{-1, -1};
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(twoSum(new int[]{3, 2, 4}, 6)));
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(twoSum(new int[]{3, 3}, 6)));
    }
}
[1, 2]
[0, 1]

Time O(n), space O(n). Checking before inserting stops an element from pairing with itself (for [3, 2, 4] and target 6, the first 3 must not match itself) while still handling duplicates like [3, 3]. Compare with the sorted two-pointer approach (O(n log n) time, O(1) space, but indices are lost unless you sort pairs):

ApproachTimeSpaceNeeds
Brute force pairsO(n²)O(1)Nothing
Hash map one passO(n)O(n)Hashable values
Sort + two pointersO(n log n)O(1) or O(n)Values, not indices (or sorted input — Two Sum II)

Mistake: using the same element twice

If you insert nums[i] into the map first and then look up the complement, target 6 with [3, 2, 4] returns [0, 0]. Look up first, insert second.

Recognising hashing problems

  • "Find a pair/triple with a property" — the complement idea.
  • "Duplicates", "first repeated", "distinct count" — a set.
  • "Count occurrences", "most frequent", "group by something" — a map keyed by the something.
  • "Subarray with sum K" — prefix sums stored in a map (next article).
  • The brute force has an inner loop that searches for something — replace the search with a lookup.

Interview angle

"Time complexity of HashMap get?" O(1) average; worst case O(log n) in Java 8+ with treeified buckets (O(n) in older versions or with non-comparable keys). Then say what you pay: O(n) extra memory and the boxing of int into Integer. Mention the two-pointer alternative on a sorted array to show you see the trade-off.

Hashing problems: duplicates, subarray sum K, longest consecutive, intersection

The classics all follow the pattern "store what you have seen, then ask the map": a set for duplicates, a prefix-sum map for subarray sums, and a set plus run starts for consecutive sequences.

Contains Duplicate (217) and variants

import java.util.*;

public class Duplicates {
    static boolean containsDuplicate(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) {
            if (!seen.add(x)) return true;          // add returns false if already present
        }
        return false;
    }

    // Contains Duplicate II (219): equal values at most k indices apart
    static boolean containsNearbyDuplicate(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> last = new HashMap<>();   // value -> last index
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            Integer j = last.get(a[i]);
            if (j != null && i - j <= k) return true;
            last.put(a[i], i);
        }
        return false;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(containsDuplicate(new int[]{1, 2, 3, 1}) + " "
            + containsNearbyDuplicate(new int[]{1, 0, 1, 1}, 1));
    }
}
true true

O(n) time and space. Alternatives: sort and compare neighbours (O(n log n), O(1) extra), which is the right answer when memory is restricted.

Subarray Sum Equals K (560): prefix sum + map

Count contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k (values may be negative, so a sliding window fails). Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i elements. A subarray (j, i] sums to k when prefix[i] - prefix[j] = k, that is prefix[j] = prefix[i] - k. So while scanning, count how many earlier prefixes equal current - k. Seed the map with {0: 1} for the empty prefix, which handles subarrays starting at index 0.

import java.util.*;

public class SubarraySumK {
    static int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> countOfPrefix = new HashMap<>();
        countOfPrefix.put(0, 1);                       // empty prefix
        int prefix = 0, answer = 0;
        for (int x : nums) {
            prefix += x;
            answer += countOfPrefix.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0);
            countOfPrefix.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        return answer;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(subarraySum(new int[]{1, 1, 1}, 2));
        System.out.println(subarraySum(new int[]{1, 2, 3, -3, 3}, 3));
    }
}
2
5

Dry run, [1, 2, 3], k = 3. Map {0:1}. x=1: prefix 1, need −2 → 0; map {0:1, 1:1}. x=2: prefix 3, need 0 → count 1 (subarray [1,2]); answer 1; map adds 3. x=3: prefix 6, need 3 → count 1 (subarray [3]); answer 2. Result 2. Time O(n), space O(n). Use long for the prefix if sums can exceed the int range.

The same trick solves Continuous Subarray Sum (store prefix % k with first index), Subarray Sums Divisible by K (count equal remainders; normalise negatives with ((p % k) + k) % k), and Contiguous Array (turn 0 into −1 and find the longest subarray with sum 0).

Longest Consecutive Sequence (128)

Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like 4, 5, 6, 7) in an unsorted array, in O(n). Sorting gives O(n log n). The O(n) idea: put all numbers in a set; only start counting from a number that has no predecessor (x - 1 not in the set). Then walk up with x + 1, x + 2… Each number is visited once as part of a run, so the total work is O(n).

import java.util.*;

public class LongestConsecutive {
    static int longestConsecutive(int[] nums) {
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : nums) set.add(x);
        int best = 0;
        for (int x : set) {
            if (set.contains(x - 1)) continue;         // not the start of a run
            int len = 1;
            while (set.contains(x + len)) len++;
            best = Math.max(best, len);
        }
        return best;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(longestConsecutive(new int[]{100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2}));
    }
}
4

Without the "is it a start?" check the same code is O(n²) (e.g. re-walking from every element of a long run). That one continue line is the whole trick.

Intersection of Two Arrays (349, 350)

Unique intersection: put one array in a set, scan the other, collect matches (remove from the set to avoid duplicates). With multiplicities (350): count the first array in a map, then decrement while scanning the second.

import java.util.*;

public class Intersection {
    static int[] intersectUnique(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) set.add(x);
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int y : b) if (set.remove(y)) out.add(y);   // remove returns true if present
        return out.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }

    static int[] intersectWithCounts(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) cnt.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int y : b) {
            int c = cnt.getOrDefault(y, 0);
            if (c > 0) { out.add(y); cnt.put(y, c - 1); }
        }
        return out.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {1, 2, 2, 1}, b = {2, 2};
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(intersectUnique(a, b)) + " "
            + Arrays.toString(intersectWithCounts(a, b)));
    }
}
[2] [2, 2]

O(n + m) time, O(min(n, m)) space if you build the set/map from the smaller array. If both arrays are already sorted, two pointers need O(1) space.

More hashing problems to practise

  • Group Anagrams (49) — covered in the strings article; key = canonical form.
  • Top K Frequent Elements (347) — frequency map, then a heap or bucket sort (Module 2).
  • Happy Number (202) — a set to detect a cycle.
  • 4Sum II (454) — store all sums of two arrays; look up the negatives of the other two. O(n²).
  • Ransom Note (383) — counting with int[26].
  • Valid Sudoku (36) — a set per row, column and box.

Edge cases and pitfalls

Empty array; all elements equal; negative numbers (sliding window is invalid, prefix-sum map is fine); integer overflow in prefix sums; Integer equality — compare boxed values with equals or unbox, since == on two Integer objects above 127 compares references; and never modify a map while iterating over it (ConcurrentModificationException).

Tip: how to think

  1. Write the brute force. Find the inner loop that is a search.
  2. Ask "what exactly am I searching for?" — a complement, a previous prefix, a neighbour value.
  3. Decide what the key and the value of the map are, and write them in a comment.
  4. Decide the order: look up first, then insert (or the reverse); seed the map with the base case ({0: 1}).

Interview angle

For Subarray Sum Equals K, strong candidates say why the sliding window fails (negatives), define the prefix equation, and explain the {0:1} seed. For Longest Consecutive Sequence, the follow-up is "why is this O(n) with a loop inside a loop?" — answer: each element is walked only from the start of its run.

Sorting: bubble, selection and insertion sort

The three simple sorts are O(n²), easy to write and good for learning the ideas of swaps, invariants and stability; only insertion sort has a real use in practice, for small or nearly sorted data.

Why learn sorting at all?

In real code you call Arrays.sort. In interviews, you are asked to implement a sort, to explain properties (stable? in place? worst case?), or to use sorting as a tool: "sort first, then two pointers", "sort intervals by start". Sorting changes an O(n²) search into O(n log n) + O(n) in dozens of problems. Know these terms:

In place
Uses O(1) extra memory (apart from the call stack in some cases).
Stable
Equal elements keep their original relative order. If records (Rahul, 90) and (Priya, 90) are sorted by marks, a stable sort leaves Rahul before Priya if he came first.
Comparison sort
Decides order only by comparing two elements. No comparison sort can beat O(n log n) in the worst case.
Adaptive
Runs faster on nearly sorted input.

Bubble sort

Repeatedly walk through the array, swapping adjacent pairs that are out of order. After pass k, the k largest elements have "bubbled" to the end. If a whole pass makes no swap, the array is sorted and you can stop early.

import java.util.*;

public class BubbleSort {
    static void bubbleSort(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        for (int pass = 0; pass < n - 1; pass++) {
            boolean swapped = false;
            for (int i = 0; i < n - 1 - pass; i++) {      // last 'pass' elements are final
                if (a[i] > a[i + 1]) {
                    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[i + 1]; a[i + 1] = t;
                    swapped = true;
                }
            }
            if (!swapped) break;                           // already sorted: O(n) best case
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {5, 1, 4, 2, 8};
        bubbleSort(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]

Dry run: [5,1,4,2,8] → pass 1: [1,4,2,5,8] → pass 2: [1,2,4,5,8] → pass 3: no swap, stop. Time: best O(n) (with the flag), average and worst O(n²). Space O(1). Stable (it swaps only when strictly greater).

Selection sort

Find the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it to the front of that part. The sorted prefix grows by one each round.

import java.util.*;

public class SelectionSort {
    static void selectionSort(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
            int min = i;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) {
                if (a[j] < a[min]) min = j;
            }
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[min]; a[min] = t;       // at most one swap per round
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {64, 25, 12, 22, 11};
        selectionSort(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[11, 12, 22, 25, 64]

Time O(n²) in every case (it always scans the rest), space O(1), only O(n) swaps — useful when writes are expensive. Not stable: swapping the minimum to the front can jump over an equal element.

Insertion sort

Like sorting playing cards in your hand: take the next element and slide it left into its correct place among the already sorted prefix.

import java.util.*;

public class InsertionSort {
    static void insertionSort(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            int key = a[i];
            int j = i - 1;
            while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {      // shift bigger elements right
                a[j + 1] = a[j];
                j--;
            }
            a[j + 1] = key;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {12, 11, 13, 5, 6};
        insertionSort(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[5, 6, 11, 12, 13]

Dry run: [12,11,13,5,6] → insert 11: [11,12,13,5,6] → 13 stays → insert 5: [5,11,12,13,6] → insert 6: [5,6,11,12,13]. Time: best O(n) (already sorted), average and worst O(n²); space O(1); stable (it stops at an equal element); adaptive.

Where insertion sort is actually used

For tiny arrays (roughly under a few dozen elements) its low overhead beats O(n log n) algorithms. Real library sorts such as TimSort and dual-pivot quicksort switch to insertion sort for small ranges or runs. It is also the right choice when data is "almost sorted" — each element is only a few places from its final position.

Side by side

SortBestAverage / worstStableNotes
BubbleO(n) with flagO(n²)YesTeaching only
SelectionO(n²)O(n²)NoFewest swaps
InsertionO(n)O(n²)YesGreat for small / nearly sorted

Interview angle

"Which sort for nearly sorted data?" Insertion sort: O(n + number of inversions). "Which makes the fewest writes?" Selection sort. "Is bubble sort ever used?" Practically no, but the early-exit flag question is a favourite. The follow-up is always: "now do it in O(n log n)" — merge sort or quick sort, next.

Merge sort and counting inversions

Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges the two sorted halves in linear time: O(n log n) always, stable, but it needs O(n) extra space.

The idea: divide, conquer, combine

Sorting two halves is easier than sorting the whole, and merging two already sorted lists is easy: repeatedly take the smaller of the two front elements. The recursion bottoms out at arrays of size 1, which are sorted by definition.

Code

import java.util.*;

public class MergeSort {
    static void mergeSort(int[] a) {
        if (a.length < 2) return;
        int[] tmp = new int[a.length];               // allocate the buffer once
        sort(a, tmp, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static void sort(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return;                        // base case: 0 or 1 element
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        sort(a, tmp, lo, mid);
        sort(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi);
        merge(a, tmp, lo, mid, hi);
    }

    private static void merge(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int mid, int hi) {
        int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = lo;
        while (i <= mid && j <= hi) {
            if (a[i] <= a[j]) tmp[k++] = a[i++];     // <= keeps equal elements in order: stable
            else tmp[k++] = a[j++];
        }
        while (i <= mid) tmp[k++] = a[i++];
        while (j <= hi) tmp[k++] = a[j++];
        for (k = lo; k <= hi; k++) a[k] = tmp[k];    // copy back
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10};
        mergeSort(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]

Complexity. Recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). By the recursion tree there are log2 n levels with n work each → O(n log n) in best, average and worst cases (see analysing recursion). Space: O(n) for the buffer plus O(log n) for the call stack. Stable if the merge takes from the left half on ties (<=). Not in place (for arrays).

Dry run of one merge: left [3, 27, 38, 43], right [9, 10, 82]. Compare 3 vs 9 → 3; 27 vs 9 → 9; 27 vs 10 → 10; 27 vs 82 → 27; 38 vs 82 → 38; 43 vs 82 → 43; right leftover 82. Result [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

Mistakes in merge sort

Allocating a new array in every recursive call (correct but slow and memory hungry); using < instead of <= in the merge and losing stability; forgetting to copy the buffer back; computing (lo + hi) / 2 (can overflow for huge indices); and using lo == hi as the base case when lo > hi can happen for empty ranges — lo >= hi covers both.

Application: counting inversions

An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]; it measures how unsorted an array is. Brute force over all pairs is O(n²). Merge sort counts them for free: during a merge, when you take an element from the right half, it is smaller than every element still waiting in the left half — that is mid - i + 1 inversions at once.

public class Inversions {
    static long countInversions(int[] a) {
        return sort(a.clone(), new int[a.length], 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static long sort(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return 0;
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        long count = sort(a, tmp, lo, mid) + sort(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi);
        int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = lo;
        while (i <= mid && j <= hi) {
            if (a[i] <= a[j]) tmp[k++] = a[i++];
            else {
                tmp[k++] = a[j++];
                count += mid - i + 1;               // a[i..mid] are all greater than a[j]
            }
        }
        while (i <= mid) tmp[k++] = a[i++];
        while (j <= hi) tmp[k++] = a[j++];
        for (k = lo; k <= hi; k++) a[k] = tmp[k];
        return count;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(countInversions(new int[]{2, 4, 1, 3, 5}));
        System.out.println(countInversions(new int[]{5, 4, 3, 2, 1}));
    }
}
3
10

For [2,4,1,3,5] the inversions are (2,1), (4,1), (4,3) = 3. The worst case (reverse sorted, n = 5) has n(n−1)/2 = 10. Return long: for n = 105 there can be 5 × 109 inversions. The same merge-and-count idea solves Count of Smaller Numbers After Self and Reverse Pairs.

Why choose merge sort?

Strengths

  • Guaranteed O(n log n); no bad inputs.
  • Stable.
  • Works well on linked lists (O(1) extra space, no random access needed) and for external sorting of data larger than memory.
  • Parallelises naturally.

Weaknesses

  • O(n) extra space on arrays.
  • Slower constants than quick sort on arrays (copying).

Java connection

Arrays.sort(Object[]), Collections.sort and List.sort use TimSort, a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort that detects existing sorted runs — stable and O(n) on already sorted data.

Why it is correct and why it is n log n

Correctness comes from one invariant: before each merge, both halves are sorted. Merging keeps the smallest unused element of each half in front, so the output is built in sorted order, one smallest element at a time. By induction on size, every call returns a sorted range. For speed, count the work per level. At the top, one merge touches n elements. At the next level, two merges touch n/2 each, again n in total. Every level costs n, and halving n down to 1 takes log2 n levels. For n = 8 that is 3 levels, so about 8 × 3 = 24 element moves, not 8 × 8 = 64. For n = 1,000,000 the gap is about 20 million versus 1012.

Bottom-up merge sort (no recursion)

You can skip recursion: merge runs of width 1, then 2, 4, 8 and so on until one run covers the array. It has no call stack, so there is no StackOverflowError risk, and it is how many library sorts are built. Add it to the same MergeSort class, reusing merge.

static void bottomUp(int[] a) {
    int n = a.length;
    int[] tmp = new int[n];
    for (int width = 1; width < n; width *= 2) {
        for (int lo = 0; lo < n - width; lo += 2 * width) {
            int mid = lo + width - 1;                      // end of the left run
            int hi = Math.min(lo + 2 * width - 1, n - 1);  // last run may be shorter
            merge(a, tmp, lo, mid, hi);
        }
    }
}

The guard lo < n - width means a right run exists; if it does not, the left run is already sorted and is left alone.

Sort a linked list in O(n log n)

Merge sort is the natural sort for linked lists. Finding the middle needs the slow and fast pointers from fast and slow pointers; merging relinks nodes and needs no extra array, so the extra space is only the recursion stack, O(log n).

// fragment: class ListNode { int val; ListNode next; ListNode(int v) { val = v; } }
static ListNode sortList(ListNode head) {
    if (head == null || head.next == null) return head;
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head.next;    // fast starts one step ahead: left half not longer
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    ListNode right = slow.next;
    slow.next = null;                          // cut the list into two
    return mergeLists(sortList(head), sortList(right));
}

static ListNode mergeLists(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    while (a != null && b != null) {
        if (a.val <= b.val) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; }   // <= keeps it stable
        else { tail.next = b; b = b.next; }
        tail = tail.next;
    }
    tail.next = (a != null) ? a : b;           // attach the leftover run
    return dummy.next;
}

Dry run: counting inversions step by step

Take [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]. The split is [2,4,1] and [3,5]; [2,4,1] splits into [2,4] and [1].

  • Merge [2,4] with [1]: 1 < 2, so 1 is taken from the right while both 2 and 4 wait on the left. That is mid - i + 1 = 2 inversions, (2,1) and (4,1). Result [1,2,4].
  • Merge [3] and [5] (from [3,5]): no right element is smaller. Zero inversions.
  • Merge [1,2,4] with [3,5]: 1 and 2 come from the left; then 3 < 4, so 3 is taken from the right while 4 waits. One inversion, (4,3). Then 4 and 5 are copied.

The total is 2 + 0 + 1 = 3, matching the program output.

Another problem: Reverse Pairs

Count pairs i < j with nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]. It is inversions with a doubled right side, so you cannot count during the merge itself. Instead, count before merging, while both halves are sorted: for each left element, a moving pointer j finds how many right elements are less than half of it. Because the left side is sorted, j only moves forward, so the counting step is O(n) per level.

// call between the two recursive sorts and merge(...)
private static long countPairs(int[] a, int lo, int mid, int hi) {
    long count = 0;
    int j = mid + 1;
    for (int i = lo; i <= mid; i++) {
        while (j <= hi && (long) a[i] > 2L * a[j]) j++;   // long: 2 * a[j] can overflow int
        count += j - (mid + 1);                           // right elements smaller than a[i] / 2
    }
    return count;
}

Count of Smaller Numbers After Self uses the same merge-and-count idea but must carry each element's original index through the sort. The pattern to remember: a pair-counting question over i < j with a comparison between values is often merge sort in disguise.

Top-down versus bottom-up

Top-down (recursive)Bottom-up (iterative)
Extra spaceO(n) buffer + O(log n) stackO(n) buffer
Code lengthShorter, mirrors the ideaA little longer
Best forInterviews, counting problemsNo-recursion limits

Edge cases

  • Empty or one-element array: the base case lo >= hi returns at once. For the inversion counter, a.length == 0 calls sort(..., 0, -1), which returns 0.
  • Duplicates and inversions: equal elements are not inversions. The merge takes from the left on ties (<=), so the count is not touched. Using < would wrongly count equal pairs.
  • Already sorted or reverse sorted input: same O(n log n); merge sort has no bad case. Only the inversion count changes (0 or n(n−1)/2).
  • Overflow: the inversion count needs long; (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow for indices near 231.

Mistake: counting with the wrong tie rule

Wrong: strict compare on the left side

if (a[i] < a[j]) tmp[k++] = a[i++];     // ties go right
else { tmp[k++] = a[j++]; count += mid - i + 1; }
// [2, 2] reports 1 inversion

Right: ties go to the left, no count

if (a[i] <= a[j]) tmp[k++] = a[i++];
else { tmp[k++] = a[j++]; count += mid - i + 1; }
// [2, 2] reports 0 inversions

Interview angle

Write it, state T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n → O(n log n), O(n) space, stable. Common follow-ups: "sort a linked list in O(n log n)" (find the middle with slow/fast pointers, merge), "count inversions", "merge k sorted lists" (heap, Module 2), and "why does Java use a merge-based sort for objects?" — because stability matters for objects.

Quick sort, partitioning and quickselect

Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements come before it and larger ones after, then recurses on both sides: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case, in place and not stable.

The idea

Merge sort does the hard work when combining; quick sort does it when splitting. After one partition step the pivot is at its final sorted position, so the two sides can be sorted independently, with nothing to combine afterwards.

Lomuto partition (simple)

Pivot = last element. Keep an index i marking the end of the "smaller than pivot" zone; scan j from left to right and swap smaller elements into that zone. Finally swap the pivot into place.

import java.util.*;

public class QuickSort {
    private static final Random RNG = new Random();

    static void quickSort(int[] a) {
        sort(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static void sort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return;
        int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
        sort(a, lo, p - 1);
        sort(a, p + 1, hi);
    }

    // Lomuto partition with a random pivot; returns the pivot's final index
    private static int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        swap(a, lo + RNG.nextInt(hi - lo + 1), hi);      // random pivot moved to the end
        int pivot = a[hi];
        int i = lo - 1;
        for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
            if (a[j] < pivot) swap(a, ++i, j);
        }
        swap(a, i + 1, hi);
        return i + 1;
    }

    private static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {7, 2, 9, 4, 3, 8, 1};
        quickSort(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9]

Hoare partition (fewer swaps)

Two pointers start at the ends and move toward each other; swap when the left one holds a value ≥ pivot and the right one holds a value ≤ pivot. It does about three times fewer swaps than Lomuto on average, but returns a split point, not the pivot's final index, so the recursion is on [lo, p] and [p+1, hi].

import java.util.*;

public class HoareSort {
    static void sort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return;
        int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
        sort(a, lo, p);                  // note: p, not p - 1
        sort(a, p + 1, hi);
    }

    static int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        int pivot = a[lo + (hi - lo) / 2];
        int i = lo - 1, j = hi + 1;
        while (true) {
            do { i++; } while (a[i] < pivot);
            do { j--; } while (a[j] > pivot);
            if (i >= j) return j;
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2, 5};
        sort(a, 0, a.length - 1);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[1, 2, 3, 5, 5, 8, 9]

Edge case: Hoare is fragile — memorise the exact form

Small changes (using hi as pivot, recursing on p - 1, changing do/while to while) cause infinite recursion or missed elements. In an interview, Lomuto is safer unless asked for Hoare.

Complexity: why average O(n log n) and worst O(n²)

  • Good split (pivot near the middle): T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n → O(n log n). Even a 10/90 split every time gives O(n log n), because depth is log10/9 n.
  • Worst split (pivot is the smallest or largest each time): T(n) = T(n−1) + n → O(n²). It happens with a first/last-element pivot on an already sorted array, or many duplicates with a naive partition. The recursion depth also becomes n, which can cause StackOverflowError.
  • Fixes: pick a random pivot (expected O(n log n) for any input), median of three, recurse into the smaller side first, and use three-way partitioning when there are many equal keys.
  • Space: O(log n) average for the call stack; O(n) worst case. Time is typically faster than merge sort in practice thanks to cache-friendly in-place scans.

Quickselect: the k-th element in O(n) average

You do not need a full sort to find the k-th smallest element. After partitioning, the pivot is at its final index p: if p equals the target index you are done, otherwise recurse into only one side. T(n) = T(n/2) + n averages to O(n); the worst case is O(n²) (use a random pivot).

import java.util.*;

public class QuickSelect {
    private static final Random RNG = new Random();

    // Kth Largest Element in an Array (215)
    static int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
        int target = nums.length - k;            // index in ascending order
        int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;
        while (lo <= hi) {
            int p = partition(nums, lo, hi);
            if (p == target) return nums[p];
            if (p < target) lo = p + 1;
            else hi = p - 1;
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("k out of range");
    }

    private static int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        int r = lo + RNG.nextInt(hi - lo + 1);
        int t = a[r]; a[r] = a[hi]; a[hi] = t;
        int pivot = a[hi], i = lo - 1;
        for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
            if (a[j] < pivot) { i++; t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; }
        }
        t = a[i + 1]; a[i + 1] = a[hi]; a[hi] = t;
        return i + 1;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(findKthLargest(new int[]{3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4}, 2));
    }
}
5

A min-heap of size k gives O(n log k) and is safer (no bad worst case); quickselect is O(n) expected. Quickselect modifies the input array.

Counting sort (brief)

If values are integers in a small range 0..k, you do not need comparisons: count each value, then write them out in order. Time O(n + k), space O(k). It is stable in its prefix-sum form and powers radix sort. Sort Colors is counting sort with k = 3.

import java.util.*;

public class CountingSort {
    static void countingSort(int[] a, int maxValue) {
        int[] count = new int[maxValue + 1];
        for (int x : a) count[x]++;
        int idx = 0;
        for (int v = 0; v <= maxValue; v++) {
            while (count[v]-- > 0) a[idx++] = v;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1};
        countingSort(a, 8);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));
    }
}
[1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8]

Three-way partitioning for many duplicates

With Lomuto and a strict <, an array where every element is equal puts the whole array on one side every time: the pivot lands at the first index, the split is 0 and n−1, and the time becomes O(n²). The fix is the Dutch national flag partition (the same idea as Sort Colors): split into three zones — less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot — and recurse only on the first and last zone. The middle zone is already in its final place.

// add to the QuickSort class (uses RNG and swap from above)
private static void sort3(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int pivot = a[lo + RNG.nextInt(hi - lo + 1)];
    int lt = lo, i = lo, gt = hi;
    // invariant: a[lo..lt-1] < pivot, a[lt..i-1] == pivot, a[gt+1..hi] > pivot
    while (i <= gt) {
        if (a[i] < pivot) swap(a, lt++, i++);
        else if (a[i] > pivot) swap(a, i, gt--);      // do not advance i: new value unseen
        else i++;
    }
    sort3(a, lo, lt - 1);
    sort3(a, gt + 1, hi);
}

On an array of all equal values this finishes in one pass: every element goes to the middle zone. With few distinct keys the time approaches O(n).

Lomuto, Hoare and three-way compared

LomutoHoareThree-way
PivotUsually lastMiddle or firstAny (random)
ReturnsFinal pivot indexSplit point onlyTwo boundaries
SwapsMoreFewerModerate
DuplicatesSlow when all equalHandles them fairlyBest
Quickselect-friendlyYesNeeds careYes

Keeping the stack small

Recursion depth is log n only on balanced splits. A bad split gives depth n and can throw StackOverflowError for large inputs. A cheap guarantee: recurse into the smaller side and loop on the larger side. Each recursive call then handles at most half the range, so the depth is at most log2 n even in the worst case (the time can still be O(n²) without a good pivot).

private static void sort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    while (lo < hi) {
        int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
        if (p - lo < hi - p) {            // left side is smaller: recurse on it
            sort(a, lo, p - 1);
            lo = p + 1;                   // then loop on the right side
        } else {
            sort(a, p + 1, hi);
            hi = p - 1;
        }
    }
}

Dry run of quickselect

Find the 2nd largest in [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4]. The target index in ascending order is n − k = 4. Suppose the random pivot happens to be the last element, 4. Lomuto scans: 3, 2 and 1 are smaller and move to the front; 5 and 6 stay. The pivot swaps into index 3, giving [3, 2, 1, 4, 6, 5], so p = 3. Since 3 < 4, the answer is on the right: lo = 4. The range [6, 5] has pivot 5; 6 is not smaller, so the pivot swaps to index 4: [..., 5, 6], p = 4 = target. The answer is 5. Only part of the array was ever touched, which is why the average cost is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n).

Quickselect or heap?

QuickselectMin-heap of size kFull sort
TimeO(n) average, O(n²) worstO(n log k)O(n log n)
Extra spaceO(1)O(k)depends
Modifies inputYesNoYes
Works on a streamNoYesNo

Use the heap when data arrives one by one or the array must stay unchanged (see heap problems). Use quickselect when you hold the whole array and want the best average time.

What Java uses

Arrays.sort(int[]) and the other primitive overloads use a dual-pivot quicksort. Stability does not matter for primitives, because equal ints are indistinguishable. Object arrays use TimSort, which is stable (see comparators and stability).

Edge cases

  • Sorted or reverse-sorted input with a first/last pivot: O(n²) and recursion depth n. A random or median-of-three pivot avoids it.
  • All equal elements: O(n²) with Lomuto and strict comparison; fixed by three-way partition.
  • Empty array: hi = -1, so lo >= hi returns immediately. But RNG.nextInt(hi - lo + 1) would throw IllegalArgumentException if called with a bound of 0 or less, so the base case must run first.
  • k out of range in quickselect: k < 1 or k > n never meets the target index; the loop ends and the code throws an exception. Validate k up front.

Mistake: a fixed pivot on sorted input

Wrong: always the first element

int pivot = a[lo];                       // sorted input: splits 0 and n-1

Right: a random element

int r = lo + RNG.nextInt(hi - lo + 1);
swap(a, r, hi);                          // then partition with a[hi] as pivot

Interview angle

"Worst case of quick sort?" O(n²) when pivots are always extreme (sorted input with first/last pivot). "How do you avoid it?" Random pivot or median-of-three. "Is quick sort stable?" No — partition swaps jump over equal elements. "Why does Java use quicksort for int[] but a merge sort for objects?" Primitives have no identity, so stability is irrelevant and in-place speed wins; objects need stability.

Comparators, stability and choosing a sort
