A binary tree is nodes with at most two children; DFS visits depth first (preorder, inorder, postorder) using recursion or an explicit stack, and BFS visits level by level using a queue.

A tree is a hierarchy: one root node at the top, and every other node has exactly one parent. In a binary tree each node has at most two children, called left and right. Folders in your laptop, a company org chart and the HTML DOM are trees. A node with no children is a leaf.

public class TreeNode {
    int val;
    TreeNode left, right;
    TreeNode(int val) { this.val = val; }
    TreeNode(int val, TreeNode left, TreeNode right) {
        this.val = val; this.left = left; this.right = right;
    }
}

Terminology

Depth of a node
Number of edges from the root down to the node. The root has depth 0.
Height of a node
Number of edges on the longest path from the node down to a leaf. A leaf has height 0. The tree's height is the root's height. (LeetCode's "maximum depth" counts nodes, so it is height + 1.)
Level
All nodes at the same depth.
Full binary tree
Every node has 0 or 2 children.
Complete binary tree
All levels are full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. Heaps are complete trees (see Heaps).
Perfect binary tree
All internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are on the same level. It has 2h+1 − 1 nodes for height h.
Balanced tree
For every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1 (the LeetCode definition). A balanced tree has height O(log n); a skewed tree (each node one child) has height n.

Almost every tree algorithm costs O(n) time because it visits each node once, and O(h) space for the recursion stack, where h is the height: O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed.

DFS traversals, recursive

Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible before backing up. The three classic orders differ only in when you handle the current node relative to its children:

OrderSequenceTypical use
Preordernode, left, rightCopy a tree, serialize, prefix expressions
Inorderleft, node, rightSorted order of a BST
Postorderleft, right, nodeDelete a tree, compute heights, anything that needs children's results first
 
void preorder(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;
    out.add(node.val);               // visit BEFORE the children
    preorder(node.left, out);
    preorder(node.right, out);
}
void inorder(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;
    inorder(node.left, out);
    out.add(node.val);               // visit BETWEEN the children
    inorder(node.right, out);
}
void postorder(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;
    postorder(node.left, out);
    postorder(node.right, out);
    out.add(node.val);               // visit AFTER the children
}

For the tree in the diagram above, preorder gives 1 2 4 5 7 3 6, inorder gives 4 2 7 5 1 3 6, postorder gives 4 7 5 2 6 3 1, and level order gives 1 2 3 4 5 6 7. Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) stack space.

Iterative traversals with an explicit stack

Recursion uses the call stack; a tree of 100,000 nodes in a straight line can cause StackOverflowError. Interviewers also ask for iterative versions to see whether you understand what the call stack does.

Preorder. Push the root. Pop a node, record it, then push the right child and then the left child, so the left is popped first.

public List<Integer> preorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return out;
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(root);
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = stack.pop();
        out.add(node.val);
        if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right);   // right first...
        if (node.left != null)  stack.push(node.left);    // ...so left pops first
    }
    return out;
}

Inorder (the careful one). Go left as far as you can, pushing every node on the way. When you cannot go left, pop (this is the next node in order), record it, then move to its right child and repeat. The pointer cur means "the next subtree to dive into".

public List<Integer> inorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (cur != null) {          // dive left, remembering the path
            stack.push(cur);
            cur = cur.left;
        }
        cur = stack.pop();             // leftmost unvisited node
        out.add(cur.val);
        cur = cur.right;               // then its right subtree
    }
    return out;
}

Dry run on the tree 2 / (1, 3): dive pushes 2, 1; pop 1, record, cur = null (1 has no right); pop 2, record, cur = 3; dive pushes 3; pop 3, record; stack empty and cur null, stop. Output 1 2 3.

Postorder. A neat trick: postorder (left, right, node) is the reverse of "node, right, left". Do a preorder that pushes left before right, collect the result, and reverse it.

public List<Integer> postorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    LinkedList<Integer> out = new LinkedList<>();
    if (root == null) return out;
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(root);
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = stack.pop();
        out.addFirst(node.val);                  // adding at the front = reversing
        if (node.left != null)  stack.push(node.left);
        if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right);
    }
    return out;
}

All three iterative versions are O(n) time and O(h) space (O(n) for the result list).

Level-order and zigzag

Level-order BFS is in the queue article. Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal (LeetCode 103) alternates direction each level. Keep a boolean leftToRight; after building each level list, if it is false, call Collections.reverse(level) (or insert with level.add(0, val)), then flip the boolean. Same O(n) time.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the node == null base case, or checking node.left.val without a null check.
  • Using if (!stack.isEmpty()) instead of while in the iterative inorder loop.
  • Confusing height (edges) with depth/levels (nodes). Check which one the problem counts.
  • Declaring a leaf as "node with a null child". A leaf has both children null. This matters in Minimum Depth and Path Sum.

Interview angle

Know the three orders by heart, write inorder iteratively without notes, and state that recursion depth is the tree height. A frequent trick question: "which traversal of a BST gives sorted output?" (inorder). Also be ready for "reconstruct a tree from two traversals", covered in the LCA and views article.

Tree recursion: what does each node return?

Most tree problems are solved by defining one question per node, "what should this call return for its subtree?", and combining the answers from the left and right children; some also update a global best value on the way.

The trick with tree recursion is to stop tracing every call and instead trust a one-sentence contract. For example, "height(node) returns the height of the subtree rooted at node." Write the base case (usually null), assume the two recursive calls obey the contract, and combine their answers. Three shapes cover most problems.

  • Bottom-up (return a value): compute from the children, then return. Height, size, balanced, diameter, maximum path sum.
  • Top-down (pass information down): pass a parameter such as the current depth, a running sum, or allowed min/max bounds. Path sum, validate BST, count good nodes.
  • Global best (the diameter pattern): the function returns one thing to its parent (for example the height) but, while computing it, updates a separate field with the answer to the real question.
R solve(TreeNode node /*, top-down info */) {
    if (node == null) return /* identity value */;
    R left = solve(node.left /*, new info */);
    R right = solve(node.right /*, new info */);
    // combine left, right and node.val into the result for this subtree
    // optionally: update a global answer here
    return /* result */;
}

Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (LeetCode 104)

public int maxDepth(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return 0;
    return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right));
}

Contract: returns the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space. A BFS that counts levels gives the same answer.

Diameter of Binary Tree (LeetCode 543): the global-max pattern

The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes; the path need not pass through the root. For each node, the longest path that bends at that node is leftHeight + rightHeight. But the function must return only the height (a path going up to the parent can use one side). So return height, and record the best bend in a field.

private int diameter = 0;

public int diameterOfBinaryTree(TreeNode root) {
    height(root);
    return diameter;
}

private int height(TreeNode node) {           // height in NODES of this subtree
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = height(node.left);
    int right = height(node.right);
    diameter = Math.max(diameter, left + right);   // path bending at this node
    return 1 + Math.max(left, right);              // what the parent needs
}

With height counted in nodes, left + right equals the number of edges on the bent path. Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space. Remember the reset: if the method is called more than once, set diameter = 0 first.

Balanced Binary Tree (LeetCode 110)

Calling height separately at every node costs O(n²) in a skewed tree. Instead, return -1 as a sentinel meaning "unbalanced somewhere below", and bubble it up.

public boolean isBalanced(TreeNode root) {
    return check(root) != -1;
}

private int check(TreeNode node) {            // height, or -1 if unbalanced
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = check(node.left);
    if (left == -1) return -1;
    int right = check(node.right);
    if (right == -1 || Math.abs(left - right) > 1) return -1;
    return 1 + Math.max(left, right);
}

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space.

Same Tree, Symmetric Tree, Invert Tree

These three are "recurse on two trees at once" or "swap children".

// Same Tree (LeetCode 100)
public boolean isSameTree(TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (p == null || q == null) return p == q;        // both null -> true
    return p.val == q.val
        && isSameTree(p.left, q.left)
        && isSameTree(p.right, q.right);
}

// Symmetric Tree (LeetCode 101): left subtree must mirror the right one
public boolean isSymmetric(TreeNode root) {
    return root == null || mirror(root.left, root.right);
}
private boolean mirror(TreeNode a, TreeNode b) {
    if (a == null || b == null) return a == b;
    return a.val == b.val
        && mirror(a.left, b.right)                   // outer pair
        && mirror(a.right, b.left);                  // inner pair
}

// Invert Binary Tree (LeetCode 226)
public TreeNode invertTree(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    TreeNode left = invertTree(root.left);
    TreeNode right = invertTree(root.right);
    root.left = right;
    root.right = left;
    return root;
}

All three are O(n) time and O(h) space. Note the trick p == q when at least one is null: it is true only when both are null.

Path Sum I and II (LeetCode 112, 113): top-down

Does a root-to-leaf path add up to target? Pass the remaining sum down. At a leaf, check whether the remaining value equals the leaf's value.

public boolean hasPathSum(TreeNode node, int remaining) {
    if (node == null) return false;
    if (node.left == null && node.right == null) return node.val == remaining;
    return hasPathSum(node.left, remaining - node.val)
        || hasPathSum(node.right, remaining - node.val);
}

For Path Sum II you must return all such paths. Keep a shared path list, add the node on the way in, and remove it on the way out (backtracking). Copy the list when you store it.

public List<List<Integer>> pathSum(TreeNode root, int targetSum) {
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    dfs(root, targetSum, new ArrayList<>(), result);
    return result;
}

private void dfs(TreeNode node, int remaining, List<Integer> path,
                 List<List<Integer>> result) {
    if (node == null) return;
    path.add(node.val);                                  // choose
    if (node.left == null && node.right == null && node.val == remaining) {
        result.add(new ArrayList<>(path));              // COPY, path keeps changing
    } else {
        dfs(node.left, remaining - node.val, path, result);
        dfs(node.right, remaining - node.val, path, result);
    }
    path.remove(path.size() - 1);                        // un-choose
}

Complexity: O(n) time to visit; copying paths adds O(n) per stored path, so O(n²) worst case. Space O(h) plus the output.

Common mistake: storing the shared list itself

result.add(path) stores a reference to the same list that you keep modifying, so every answer ends up empty. Always new ArrayList<>(path).

Brief: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (LeetCode 124)

This is the diameter pattern with values instead of lengths. A path may start and end anywhere. The function returns the best downward path starting at the node (the node plus at most one child), ignoring negative branches with Math.max(0, …). The bent path through the node, node.val + left + right, updates the global best.

private int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

public int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) {
    gain(root);
    return best;
}

private int gain(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = Math.max(0, gain(node.left));       // drop negative branches
    int right = Math.max(0, gain(node.right));
    best = Math.max(best, node.val + left + right);     // bend at this node
    return node.val + Math.max(left, right);            // one side only
}

Start best at Integer.MIN_VALUE, not 0, because all values may be negative. Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space.

How to think about a new tree problem

  1. Write the contract: what does f(node) return?
  2. Decide the base case for null (0, true, an empty list, or null).
  3. Is the answer the return value (bottom-up), or does it need extra information from above (top-down parameters)?
  4. If the answer is a path that bends, return the one-sided value and update a global with the two-sided value.
  5. Test on a single node, a null tree, and a skewed tree.

Binary trees: LCA, views, construction and serialization

Lowest common ancestor is a bottom-up recursion that returns a node when it finds a target; side views use level-order BFS; top and bottom views add a horizontal-distance map; construction and serialization rebuild a tree from preorder data.

These problems use the ideas from traversals and tree recursion. Each one is a small change to BFS or DFS.

Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (LeetCode 236)

The lowest common ancestor (LCA) of nodes p and q is the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant). Think of two employees and the nearest manager above both.

Contract: lca(node, p, q) returns p or q if it finds one of them in this subtree, the LCA if it finds both, otherwise null. If both the left and right calls return non-null, the current node is where the two paths meet, so it is the LCA. If only one side returns non-null, pass that up.

public TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;   // found one, or fell off
    TreeNode left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
    TreeNode right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (left != null && right != null) return root;           // p and q are on both sides
    return left != null ? left : right;                        // both on one side
}

Dry run on the tree 3 / (5, 1) with p = 5, q = 1: the left call returns 5 at once, the right call returns 1 at once, both are non-null, so the answer is 3. If p = 5 and q is inside 5's subtree, the left call returns 5 (it stops at 5 without searching deeper) and the right call returns null, so the answer is 5, which is correct. Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space. This code assumes both nodes exist in the tree.

Views of a binary tree

Right side view (LeetCode 199): the nodes you see standing on the right of the tree. That is the last node of every level. Use the level-order template and keep the node at index size - 1. For the left view, keep the first node (i == 0).

public List<Integer> rightSideView(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> view = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return view;
    Queue<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(root);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int size = q.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = q.poll();
            if (i == size - 1) view.add(node.val);     // last in the level
            if (node.left != null)  q.offer(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
        }
    }
    return view;
}

A DFS version visits the right child first and records a value the first time it reaches a new depth: if (depth == view.size()) view.add(node.val). Complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space for BFS.

Top view and bottom view with horizontal distance

Draw vertical lines through the tree. Give the root horizontal distance (HD) 0, a left child HD − 1 and a right child HD + 1. Nodes with the same HD sit on the same vertical line. The top view shows the first node you meet on each line going downward (use BFS so higher nodes come first, and store a value only if the HD is new). The bottom view shows the last node on each line (BFS, overwrite the value every time). A TreeMap keeps columns sorted from left to right.

public List<Integer> topView(TreeNode root) {
    TreeMap<Integer, Integer> firstAtHd = new TreeMap<>();   // hd -> value
    if (root == null) return new ArrayList<>();
    Queue<TreeNode> nodes = new ArrayDeque<>();
    Queue<Integer> hds = new ArrayDeque<>();
    nodes.offer(root);  hds.offer(0);
    while (!nodes.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = nodes.poll();
        int hd = hds.poll();
        firstAtHd.putIfAbsent(hd, node.val);       // top view: keep the first
        // bottom view: use firstAtHd.put(hd, node.val) to keep the last
        if (node.left != null)  { nodes.offer(node.left);  hds.offer(hd - 1); }
        if (node.right != null) { nodes.offer(node.right); hds.offer(hd + 1); }
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(firstAtHd.values());       // ordered left to right
}

Do not use DFS for the top view: a deeper node could be seen before a shallower node of the same column. Complexity: O(n log n) time because of the TreeMap (O(n + c) if you track min/max HD and use an array or HashMap), O(n) space. Vertical Order Traversal (LeetCode 987) is the same idea keeping every node per column, sorted by row and then value.

Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder (LeetCode 105)

Preorder starts with the root. Find that root in the inorder array: everything to its left is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree. The size of the left part tells you how many preorder elements belong to the left subtree. Recurse. A HashMap from value to inorder index replaces the linear search (values are unique).

private int preIdx = 0;
private Map<Integer, Integer> inIndex = new HashMap<>();

public TreeNode buildTree(int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
    for (int i = 0; i < inorder.length; i++) inIndex.put(inorder[i], i);
    return build(preorder, 0, inorder.length - 1);
}

private TreeNode build(int[] preorder, int lo, int hi) {   // range in inorder
    if (lo > hi) return null;
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(preorder[preIdx++]);      // next preorder = root
    int mid = inIndex.get(root.val);
    root.left = build(preorder, lo, mid - 1);              // left FIRST (preorder)
    root.right = build(preorder, mid + 1, hi);
    return root;
}

With preorder = [3,9,20,15,7] and inorder = [9,3,15,20,7]: root 3, inorder index 1, so 9 is the left subtree and [15,20,7] the right one. Complexity: O(n) time and space. You cannot rebuild a tree from preorder and postorder alone in general, and preorder alone is not enough either; but preorder with null markers is (next section).

Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (LeetCode 297)

Turn a tree into a string and back. Preorder with an explicit marker for null children is unambiguous, because the markers show where each subtree ends.

public class Codec {
    public String serialize(TreeNode root) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        write(root, sb);
        return sb.toString();                     // e.g. "1,2,#,#,3,#,#,"
    }
    private void write(TreeNode node, StringBuilder sb) {
        if (node == null) { sb.append("#,"); return; }
        sb.append(node.val).append(',');
        write(node.left, sb);
        write(node.right, sb);
    }

    public TreeNode deserialize(String data) {
        Deque<String> tokens = new ArrayDeque<>(Arrays.asList(data.split(",")));
        return read(tokens);
    }
    private TreeNode read(Deque<String> tokens) {
        String t = tokens.poll();
        if (t.equals("#")) return null;
        TreeNode node = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t));
        node.left = read(tokens);
        node.right = read(tokens);
        return node;
    }
}

Complexity: O(n) time and space. A level-order version using a queue gives the format LeetCode shows in its examples.

Brief: Lowest Common Ancestor shortcuts and Subtree of Another Tree

  • If every node has a parent pointer, the LCA is the intersection of two lists (see Intersection of Two Linked Lists in the linked list article).
  • Subtree of Another Tree (LeetCode 572): for each node of the big tree call isSameTree against the small tree. O(m·n) simple version.
  • Count Good Nodes, Sum Root to Leaf Numbers: top-down recursion passing the max-so-far or the number built so far.

Edge cases

  • LCA when one node is an ancestor of the other: the ancestor itself is the answer (the code above handles it).
  • LCA when a target is not in the tree: this simple code returns the other node wrongly; count matches explicitly if the problem says nodes may be missing.
  • Deserializing negative numbers or multi-digit values: that is why the format uses a separator like a comma.
  • Views of a skewed tree: the view has one node per level, so the view length is n.

Interview angle

LCA is asked at nearly every company. Explain the contract in one sentence, then the "both sides non-null means this is the LCA" rule. Be ready with the BST version (next article) that is O(h) with no recursion on both sides. For views, say why BFS (not DFS) is natural for top view and what the horizontal distance map stores.

Binary search trees: search, insert, delete, validate

A BST keeps every left descendant smaller and every right descendant larger than a node, so search, insert and delete follow one path in O(h), and an inorder walk yields sorted values.

A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree with one rule at every node: all values in the left subtree are smaller, all values in the right subtree are larger (we assume no duplicates unless a problem says otherwise). This is binary search turned into a data structure (see binary search in Module 1): at each node you discard one half of what remains.

If the tree is balanced, its height is about log₂ n, so search, insert and delete are O(log n). If you insert already sorted data into a plain BST, it degenerates into a linked list of height n and everything becomes O(n). Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) fix this; Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black trees (see below).

Search and insert

// Search in a BST (LeetCode 700)
public TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
    while (root != null && root.val != val) {
        root = (val < root.val) ? root.left : root.right;
    }
    return root;                                     // null if absent
}

// Insert into a BST (LeetCode 701)
public TreeNode insertIntoBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
    if (root == null) return new TreeNode(val);      // found the empty slot
    if (val < root.val) root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val);
    else                root.right = insertIntoBST(root.right, val);
    return root;
}

The recursive insert re-assigns root.left or root.right on the way back, which is harmless for unchanged children and attaches the new leaf at the bottom. Complexity: O(h) time; O(1) space for the loop, O(h) for the recursion.

Delete a node (LeetCode 450): three cases

First find the node. Then:

  1. Leaf: return null to the parent.
  2. One child: return that child, which takes the node's place.
  3. Two children: replace the node's value with its inorder successor (the smallest value in the right subtree, found by going right once and then left as far as possible), then delete that successor from the right subtree. The inorder predecessor (largest in the left subtree) works equally well.
public TreeNode deleteNode(TreeNode root, int key) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    if (key < root.val)      root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key);
    else if (key > root.val) root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key);
    else {
        if (root.left == null)  return root.right;     // leaf or only right child
        if (root.right == null) return root.left;      // only left child
        TreeNode succ = root.right;                    // two children
        while (succ.left != null) succ = succ.left;    // smallest in right subtree
        root.val = succ.val;                           // copy its value up
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, succ.val); // remove the successor
    }
    return root;
}

Deleting 3 from the tree above: it has two children; the successor is 4 (right child 6, then left to 4). Copy 4 into the node, then delete the old 4 (a leaf). Complexity: O(h) time and space.

Validate Binary Search Tree (LeetCode 98)

The tempting solution checks only node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val. That is wrong, because the rule applies to the whole subtree, not just the direct children.

The correct approach passes an allowed range down. Each node must lie strictly between lo and hi. Going left tightens hi to the node's value; going right raises lo.

public boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
    return valid(root, null, null);
}

private boolean valid(TreeNode node, Integer lo, Integer hi) {
    if (node == null) return true;
    if (lo != null && node.val <= lo) return false;
    if (hi != null && node.val >= hi) return false;
    return valid(node.left, lo, node.val) && valid(node.right, node.val, hi);
}

Common mistake: bounds with Integer.MIN_VALUE

If you start with long lo = Integer.MIN_VALUE as the bound, a tree containing the value Integer.MIN_VALUE is wrongly rejected. Use Integer objects with null for "no bound" as above, or use Long.MIN_VALUE and Long.MAX_VALUE.

The alternative: an inorder traversal of a valid BST is strictly increasing, so keep the previously visited value and check that each value is greater than it. Both ways are O(n) time and O(h) space.

Kth Smallest Element in a BST (LeetCode 230)

Inorder visits values in sorted order, so the k-th node visited is the answer. Use the iterative inorder from traversals and stop early.

public int kthSmallest(TreeNode root, int k) {
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (cur != null) { stack.push(cur); cur = cur.left; }
        cur = stack.pop();
        if (--k == 0) return cur.val;       // the k-th smallest
        cur = cur.right;
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("k is larger than the tree size");
}

Complexity: O(h + k) time, O(h) space. If the tree is modified often and k-th queries are frequent, store the subtree size in each node to get O(h) per query (a follow-up asked in interviews).

LCA in a BST (LeetCode 235)

The BST order lets you decide the direction without exploring both sides. If both targets are smaller than the current node, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node is where they split, so it is the LCA.

public TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    while (root != null) {
        if (p.val < root.val && q.val < root.val)      root = root.left;
        else if (p.val > root.val && q.val > root.val) root = root.right;
        else return root;                                    // split point
    }
    return null;
}

Complexity: O(h) time, O(1) space.

Floor and ceiling

The floor of x is the largest value ≤ x in the tree; the ceiling is the smallest value ≥ x. Walk down as in search; whenever a node qualifies, remember it and keep going to find a better one.

// floor: largest value <= x, or null if none
public Integer floor(TreeNode root, int x) {
    Integer best = null;
    while (root != null) {
        if (root.val == x) return x;
        if (root.val < x) { best = root.val; root = root.right; }  // candidate, go bigger
        else               root = root.left;
    }
    return best;
}
// ceiling: mirror image -> if (root.val > x) { best = root.val; root = root.left; }

Complexity: O(h).

Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree (LeetCode 108)

Choose the middle element as the root so both halves have nearly equal size, then recurse on each half. The result is height-balanced.

public TreeNode sortedArrayToBST(int[] nums) {
    return build(nums, 0, nums.length - 1);
}

private TreeNode build(int[] nums, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return null;
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    TreeNode node = new TreeNode(nums[mid]);
    node.left = build(nums, lo, mid - 1);
    node.right = build(nums, mid + 1, hi);
    return node;
}

Complexity: O(n) time, O(log n) recursion depth.

Brief: BST Iterator (LeetCode 173)

Implement next() and hasNext() over inorder. Keep a stack holding the left spine. next() pops a node, then pushes the left spine of its right child. Each node is pushed and popped once, so next() is amortized O(1) and space is O(h). It is the iterative inorder loop frozen between steps.

TreeMap and TreeSet: balanced BSTs in Java

In real projects you do not write BST code; you use TreeMap or TreeSet, which are red-black trees (self-balancing BSTs), so all operations are O(log n) guaranteed and keys stay sorted.

NeedMethodCost
Insert / search / deleteput, get, removeO(log n)
Smallest / largest keyfirstKey(), lastKey()O(log n)
Floor / ceiling keyfloorKey(x), ceilingKey(x)O(log n)
Strictly lower / higherlowerKey(x), higherKey(x)O(log n)
Range viewsubMap(a, b), headMap, tailMapO(log n) to create

Use a TreeMap when you need sorted keys or nearest-value lookups (for example "the closest earlier booking time"). Use a HashMap when you only need exact lookups at O(1) average. TreeSet has the same methods: floor, ceiling, lower, higher, first, last. See Core Java · Module 4 for the collections view.

Rule: TreeMap keys need an ordering

Keys must be Comparable or you must pass a Comparator. Two keys that compare as equal are treated as the same key, even if equals() says they differ. A null key throws NullPointerException with natural ordering.

Interview angle

The classic trap is the wrong "check only children" validation; draw the counter-example above. Know the three delete cases and say "inorder successor". Mention that a plain BST can degrade to O(n) and that TreeMap is the balanced answer. "Kth smallest" = inorder; "closest value" = walk down while tracking the best.

Heaps and PriorityQueue: how a binary heap works

A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where each parent is smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children, so the best element is always at index 0 and insert and remove cost O(log n).

Sometimes you do not need everything sorted; you only need the smallest (or largest) item, again and again, while new items keep arriving. Sorting each time costs O(n log n). A heap gives you the extreme item in O(1) and lets you add or remove in O(log n). The Java class is PriorityQueue. Typical uses: the K largest values, merging sorted streams, scheduling by priority, running medians, and Dijkstra's shortest path in Module 3.

The binary heap as an array

A binary heap is a complete binary tree (every level full except maybe the last, filled left to right), with the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is ≤ its children, so the root is the minimum; a max-heap is the reverse. Because the tree is complete, no pointers are needed; store it in an array level by level.

Note the heap is not fully sorted: 5 sits left of 3, and 9 is not smaller than 3. Only the parent-child relation is guaranteed.

Sift up and sift down

Insert: put the new value at the end of the array (the next free leaf), then sift up: while it is smaller than its parent, swap them. At most height = log n swaps.

Remove the root (poll): take the root as the answer, move the last array element to index 0, shrink the array, then sift down: swap with the smaller child while that child is smaller. Again at most log n swaps.

class MinHeap {
    private int[] a = new int[16];
    private int size = 0;

    void add(int x) {
        if (size == a.length) a = Arrays.copyOf(a, size * 2);
        a[size] = x;
        int i = size++;
        while (i > 0 && a[(i - 1) / 2] > a[i]) {          // sift up
            swap(i, (i - 1) / 2);
            i = (i - 1) / 2;
        }
    }

    int poll() {
        int top = a[0];                                      // caller checks size > 0
        a[0] = a[--size];
        int i = 0;
        while (true) {                                       // sift down
            int l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2, smallest = i;
            if (l < size && a[l] < a[smallest]) smallest = l;
            if (r < size && a[r] < a[smallest]) smallest = r;
            if (smallest == i) break;
            swap(i, smallest);
            i = smallest;
        }
        return top;
    }

    int peek() { return a[0]; }

    private void swap(int i, int j) { int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; }
}

Complexity: add and poll O(log n), peek O(1), space O(n).

Building a heap in O(n)

Inserting n items one by one costs O(n log n). A faster way: put all items in the array, then sift down every non-leaf node from the last parent (index n/2 - 1) back to index 0. Most nodes are near the bottom and move very little: half of them are leaves (0 moves), a quarter move at most 1, and so on. The sum of work is O(n). This is heapify, and it is what new PriorityQueue<>(collection) does.

PriorityQueue in Java

PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();                  // smallest first
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());

minHeap.offer(5);  minHeap.offer(1);  minHeap.offer(3);
minHeap.peek();    // 1, the smallest, not removed; null if empty
minHeap.poll();    // 1, removed; null if empty
minHeap.size();

// Order by a field or a rule
PriorityQueue<int[]> byDist = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
PriorityQueue<String> byLength =
    new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));
OperationMethodCost
Addoffer(e), add(e)O(log n)
Look at the toppeek()O(1)
Remove the toppoll()O(log n)
Remove a given elementremove(Object)O(n)
Containscontains(Object)O(n)
Build from a collectionnew PriorityQueue<>(c)O(n)

Common mistakes with PriorityQueue

  • Iterating or printing it and expecting sorted order. The iterator and toString() show the internal array order, which is only heap-ordered. Poll repeatedly to get sorted output.
  • The overflow comparator. (a, b) -> b - a overflows when the numbers are far apart (for example b = Integer.MAX_VALUE, a = -5), producing the wrong sign. Use Integer.compare(b, a) or Comparator.reverseOrder().
  • Mutating an object after adding it. The heap does not re-sort. Remove and re-add it, or push a new entry and ignore stale ones when polled.
  • Assuming it is stable. Equal-priority items come out in no guaranteed order.

Rule: elements must be comparable

A PriorityQueue of your own class needs the class to implement Comparable or a Comparator passed to the constructor. Otherwise offer throws ClassCastException. It also rejects null elements (NullPointerException). It is not thread-safe; use PriorityBlockingQueue for multiple threads.

Heap sort (brief)

Build a max-heap in O(n). Then swap the root with the last element, shrink the heap by one, and sift down the new root; repeat n times. The array ends sorted ascending. Complexity: O(n log n) time in all cases, O(1) extra space, not stable. It is rarely used in practice because quicksort and merge sort are faster on real hardware, but it shows how heaps work and is asked in theory interviews.

Recognise a heap problem

  • "Top K", "K largest/smallest/most frequent/closest".
  • "Repeatedly take the best remaining item" while items are added (scheduling, merging).
  • "Median of a stream" or any need for the min and the max of a changing set.
  • Greedy choices that need "the smallest end time" or "the cheapest next step".

Interview angle

Be able to give the index formulas, explain sift up and sift down, and say why heapify is O(n) while n inserts are O(n log n). A common question: "why can't a heap give you sorted iteration, and how is it different from a BST?" (a heap orders only parent versus child, finds the min in O(1), but searching is O(n)).

Heap problems: top K, merge K lists, median of a stream

To get the K largest items keep a min-heap of size K; to merge K sorted sources keep a min-heap with one entry from each; to track a median keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half.

These problems use the PriorityQueue from the previous article. The same few ideas appear again and again.

Kth Largest Element in an Array (LeetCode 215)

Keep a min-heap of size k holding the k largest values seen so far. The top of the heap is the smallest of them, which is the k-th largest. When a new value arrives, add it; if the size exceeds k, remove the smallest. The surprise to remember: for the K largest you use a min-heap, because you want to evict the smallest.

public int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();     // min-heap
    for (int x : nums) {
        heap.offer(x);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();                   // drop the smallest
    }
    return heap.peek();
}

Dry run: nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2. Heap after each step: {3}, {2,3}, then add 1 and remove 1 gives {2,3}, add 5 and remove 2 gives {3,5}, add 6 and remove 3 gives {5,6}, add 4 and remove 4 gives {5,6}. The top is 5. Complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Alternatives: sort in O(n log n); Quickselect (partition like quicksort, recurse into one side only) gives O(n) average but O(n²) worst case.

Top K Frequent Elements (LeetCode 347)

Count with a HashMap, then keep the K highest counts. Two good solutions:

// 1. Min-heap of size k on the counts: O(n log k)
public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    for (int x : nums) freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);

    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>> heap =
        new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Map.Entry::getValue));
    for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : freq.entrySet()) {
        heap.offer(e);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();               // evict the least frequent
    }
    int[] res = new int[k];
    for (int i = k - 1; i >= 0; i--) res[i] = heap.poll().getKey();
    return res;
}

// 2. Bucket sort on frequency: O(n)
public int[] topKFrequentBuckets(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    for (int x : nums) freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);

    List<Integer>[] buckets = new List[nums.length + 1];   // index = frequency
    for (var e : freq.entrySet()) {
        int f = e.getValue();
        if (buckets[f] == null) buckets[f] = new ArrayList<>();
        buckets[f].add(e.getKey());
    }
    int[] res = new int[k];
    int idx = 0;
    for (int f = buckets.length - 1; f >= 1 && idx < k; f--) {
        if (buckets[f] == null) continue;
        for (int num : buckets[f]) {
            if (idx == k) break;
            res[idx++] = num;
        }
    }
    return res;
}

A frequency can be at most n, so n + 1 buckets are enough; scanning from the highest bucket downward collects the most frequent first. The heap version is O(n log k) time, O(n) space; the bucket version is O(n) time, O(n) space. Generic array creation (new List[...]) gives an unchecked warning in Java, which is normal here.

K Closest Points to Origin (LeetCode 973)

Distance is x² + y² (no need for the square root, and it avoids floating point). For the K closest keep a max-heap of size k, so the farthest of your candidates is on top and gets evicted.

public int[][] kClosest(int[][] points, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(
        (a, b) -> Integer.compare(dist(b), dist(a)));        // max-heap on distance
    for (int[] p : points) {
        heap.offer(p);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();                  // drop the farthest
    }
    return heap.toArray(new int[0][]);
}

private int dist(int[] p) { return p[0] * p[0] + p[1] * p[1]; }

Coordinates are limited to ±10,000 on LeetCode, so x² + y² fits in an int; use long if the limits were larger. Complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

You want the K ...Heap to keepTop of heap is
largest / most frequentmin-heap of size kthe weakest of the k winners (evicted next)
smallest / closestmax-heap of size kthe weakest of the k winners (evicted next)

Merge K Sorted Lists (LeetCode 23)

Put the head of every list in a min-heap. Repeatedly poll the smallest node, append it to the result, and push that node's next. The heap never holds more than K nodes.

public ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
    PriorityQueue<ListNode> heap =
        new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(n -> n.val));
    for (ListNode head : lists) {
        if (head != null) heap.offer(head);          // never add null nodes
    }
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
        ListNode smallest = heap.poll();
        tail.next = smallest;
        tail = tail.next;
        if (smallest.next != null) heap.offer(smallest.next);
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

Complexity: O(N log K) time where N is the total number of nodes, O(K) extra space. Another valid O(N log K) idea is divide and conquer: merge lists in pairs using mergeTwoLists from linked lists. The same heap idea merges K sorted arrays or finds the K-th smallest in a sorted matrix.

Find Median from Data Stream (LeetCode 295): two heaps

The median is the middle value of the sorted data (or the average of the two middle values). Split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half. Keep the lower half in a max-heap (its top is the largest of the small numbers) and the upper half in a min-heap (its top is the smallest of the big numbers). Keep the sizes equal, or let the lower heap have one extra. Then the median is at the tops.

class MedianFinder {
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> lower =
        new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());    // max-heap
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> upper = new PriorityQueue<>();   // min-heap

    public void addNum(int num) {
        lower.offer(num);
        upper.offer(lower.poll());                // move the largest of lower to upper
        if (upper.size() > lower.size()) {        // rebalance: lower may have +1
            lower.offer(upper.poll());
        }
    }

    public double findMedian() {
        if (lower.size() > upper.size()) return lower.peek();
        return (lower.peek() + (long) upper.peek()) / 2.0;
    }
}

Adding 5, 2, 8, 1 step by step: after 5, lower = {5}, median 5; after 2, lower = {2}, upper = {5}, median 3.5; after 8, lower = {5, 2}, upper = {8}, median 5; after 1, lower = {2, 1}, upper = {5, 8}, median 3.5. Passing the number through lower and then upper guarantees every value in lower is ≤ every value in upper. Complexity: addNum O(log n), findMedian O(1), space O(n). The cast to long avoids integer overflow when adding two large int values.

Brief: Task Scheduler (LeetCode 621)

Tasks with the same letter must be at least n intervals apart. Greedy with a max-heap: in each cycle of n + 1 slots take up to n + 1 of the most frequent tasks, decrement their counts, and push the leftovers back. A closed form also exists: max(tasks, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + countOfMaxFreq). Heap version: O(T log 26), practically O(T).

Brief: Last Stone Weight, Reorganize String

Last Stone Weight (LeetCode 1046): max-heap, smash the two heaviest, push back the difference. Reorganize String (LeetCode 767): max-heap of letter counts; each step place the most frequent letter that differs from the previously placed one.

Choosing between a heap, sorting and quickselect

  • The data is static and you need the whole order: sort.
  • You need only the k-th element once: quickselect (O(n) average) or a size-k heap.
  • Data arrives as a stream, or k is much smaller than n: a size-k heap (O(n log k), O(k) memory).
  • Frequencies are bounded by n: bucket sort (O(n)).

Interview angle

"Kth largest" has four answers (sort, heap, quickselect, counting) and the interviewer wants you to compare them. Explain "why a min-heap for the largest K" in one sentence. For the median, draw the two heaps and the balancing rule. For streaming data, mention that memory is O(k), not O(n), for top-K.

Intervals: merge, insert, meeting rooms

Sort intervals by start time, then sweep once from left to right comparing each interval with the last one you kept; meeting rooms add a min-heap of end times or a sweep line of start and end events.

An interval is a range such as a meeting from 9 to 11, stored as int[] {start, end}. Two intervals overlap when each starts before the other ends: a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end. (Whether touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] overlap depends on the problem; check the statement. In Merge Intervals they do merge; in Meeting Rooms they do not conflict.)

The big idea: sort by start. After sorting, any interval that can overlap the current one must be next to it, so one pass is enough. The sort costs O(n log n) and is the dominant cost.

Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));   // by start
// Arrays.sort(intervals, Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0]));    // same thing

Merge Intervals (LeetCode 56)

Keep a result list. For each interval in sorted order: if the result is empty or the interval starts after the last kept interval ends, append it; otherwise it overlaps, so extend the last interval's end to max(lastEnd, end). Use max because the new interval may be fully inside the last one.

public int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    List<int[]> merged = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int[] cur : intervals) {
        if (merged.isEmpty() || merged.get(merged.size() - 1)[1] < cur[0]) {
            merged.add(cur);                                  // no overlap
        } else {
            int[] last = merged.get(merged.size() - 1);
            last[1] = Math.max(last[1], cur[1]);              // extend
        }
    }
    return merged.toArray(new int[0][]);
}

Input [[1,3],[8,10],[2,6],[15,18]] sorts to [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]; 2 ≤ 3 so [1,3] becomes [1,6]; 8 > 6 starts a new one. Result [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space for the output. The code mutates the input arrays; copy them if the caller must keep them.

Common mistake: comparator with subtraction

(a, b) -> a[0] - b[0] can overflow for large or negative values. Use Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]). And do not forget to sort first; without it the one-pass logic is wrong.

Insert Interval (LeetCode 57)

The list is already sorted and non-overlapping. Do three phases in one pass: (1) copy all intervals that end before the new one starts; (2) merge all intervals that overlap the new one into it by taking min start and max end; (3) copy the rest. No sorting needed.

public int[][] insert(int[][] intervals, int[] newInterval) {
    List<int[]> result = new ArrayList<>();
    int i = 0, n = intervals.length;
    while (i < n && intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]) result.add(intervals[i++]);   // before
    while (i < n && intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]) {                          // overlap
        newInterval[0] = Math.min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0]);
        newInterval[1] = Math.max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1]);
        i++;
    }
    result.add(newInterval);
    while (i < n) result.add(intervals[i++]);                                        // after
    return result.toArray(new int[0][]);
}

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Non-overlapping Intervals (LeetCode 435): greedy

Find the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest do not overlap. Equivalent: keep the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals. The greedy rule is to sort by end and always keep the interval that finishes earliest, because it leaves the most room for the future. The proof of this exchange argument and the family of greedy problems are in Module 3.

public int eraseOverlapIntervals(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));   // by END
    int removed = 0, lastEnd = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    for (int[] cur : intervals) {
        if (cur[0] >= lastEnd) lastEnd = cur[1];     // keep it
        else removed++;                              // overlaps: remove it
    }
    return removed;
}

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

Meeting Rooms I (LeetCode 252) and II (LeetCode 253)

I: can one person attend all meetings? Sort by start and check that each meeting starts at or after the previous one ends.

public boolean canAttendMeetings(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    for (int i = 1; i < intervals.length; i++) {
        if (intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]) return false;   // overlap
    }
    return true;
}

II: the minimum number of rooms needed. Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of the end times of the rooms in use. For each meeting, if the earliest-ending room is free by now (heap.peek() <= start), reuse it (poll); then add this meeting's end. The final heap size is the number of rooms.

public int minMeetingRooms(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    PriorityQueue<Integer> endTimes = new PriorityQueue<>();
    for (int[] meeting : intervals) {
        if (!endTimes.isEmpty() && endTimes.peek() <= meeting[0]) endTimes.poll();
        endTimes.offer(meeting[1]);
    }
    return endTimes.size();
}

For [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]: [0,30] → heap {30}; [5,10]: 30 > 5 so no reuse, heap {10,30}; [15,20]: 10 ≤ 15 so reuse, heap {20,30}. Answer 2. Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

Sweep line alternative

A sweep line turns each interval into two events: +1 at its start and −1 at its end. Sort all events by time (ending before starting when times tie, so touching meetings share a room) and keep a running count. The maximum count is the number of rooms. Sorting the starts and ends separately gives a compact version.

public int minMeetingRooms(int[][] intervals) {
    int n = intervals.length;
    int[] starts = new int[n], ends = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { starts[i] = intervals[i][0]; ends[i] = intervals[i][1]; }
    Arrays.sort(starts);
    Arrays.sort(ends);
    int rooms = 0, maxRooms = 0, e = 0;
    for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) {
        if (starts[s] < ends[e]) rooms++;      // a new meeting begins before any ends
        else e++;                              // reuse: one meeting has ended
        maxRooms = Math.max(maxRooms, rooms);
    }
    return maxRooms;
}

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. The sweep line idea also solves "maximum overlap", "employee free time" and the "car pooling" problem.

Interval List Intersections (LeetCode 986)

Two sorted lists of disjoint intervals. Use two pointers: the intersection of A[i] and B[j] is [max(starts), min(ends)], valid if start ≤ end. Then advance the pointer whose interval ends first (it cannot overlap anything further in the other list).

public int[][] intervalIntersection(int[][] A, int[][] B) {
    List<int[]> res = new ArrayList<>();
    int i = 0, j = 0;
    while (i < A.length && j < B.length) {
        int lo = Math.max(A[i][0], B[j][0]);
        int hi = Math.min(A[i][1], B[j][1]);
        if (lo <= hi) res.add(new int[] {lo, hi});
        if (A[i][1] < B[j][1]) i++; else j++;        // drop the one that ends first
    }
    return res.toArray(new int[0][]);
}

Complexity: O(m + n) time. This is the "two arrays" shape of two pointers.

Recognising interval problems

  • Words: meetings, schedules, ranges, bookings, "overlap", "merge", "free time".
  • First move: sort by start (to merge or find conflicts) or by end (to pick the maximum number of non-overlapping ones).
  • "How many at the same time?" means heap of end times or sweep line.

Interview angle

Merge Intervals is among the most asked questions. State the overlap condition and the touching-interval rule before coding. For Meeting Rooms II give both the heap and the sweep line. For Non-overlapping Intervals explain why sorting by end (not start) is the greedy choice.

Matrix problems: directions, spiral, rotate, search

A matrix is an array of arrays addressed by row and column; most problems need careful boundary handling, a direction array for neighbours, and small tricks such as transpose-then-reverse or treating the grid as one sorted line.

A matrix (grid) in Java is int[][] grid with m = grid.length rows and n = grid[0].length columns. The cell grid[r][c] is row r, column c. Indexes run from 0 to m - 1 and 0 to n - 1. Always read the constraints: can the matrix be empty, one row, one column, or non-square? Most matrix bugs are off-by-one errors on boundaries.

Direction arrays and boundary checks

To visit the four neighbours (up, right, down, left) loop over a small array of row and column offsets instead of writing four copies of the code.

int[][] dirs = {{-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {1, 0}, {0, -1}};    // up, right, down, left
// for 8 directions add the diagonals: {-1,-1}, {-1,1}, {1,1}, {1,-1}

for (int[] d : dirs) {
    int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
    if (nr < 0 || nr >= m || nc < 0 || nc >= n) continue;   // out of bounds
    // use grid[nr][nc]
}

Check the bounds before reading the cell, or you get ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. A flat index id = r * n + c converts a cell to one number, and r = id / n, c = id % n converts back.

Spiral Matrix (LeetCode 54)

Return all elements in spiral order. Keep four boundaries top, bottom, left, right. Walk the top row left to right, the right column top to bottom, the bottom row right to left, the left column bottom to top, shrinking a boundary after each side. The two inner checks stop you from walking a row or column twice when one is left over.

public List<Integer> spiralOrder(int[][] matrix) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    int top = 0, bottom = matrix.length - 1;
    int left = 0, right = matrix[0].length - 1;
    while (top <= bottom && left <= right) {
        for (int c = left; c <= right; c++) out.add(matrix[top][c]);
        top++;
        for (int r = top; r <= bottom; r++) out.add(matrix[r][right]);
        right--;
        if (top <= bottom) {                       // a bottom row still exists
            for (int c = right; c >= left; c--) out.add(matrix[bottom][c]);
            bottom--;
        }
        if (left <= right) {                       // a left column still exists
            for (int r = bottom; r >= top; r--) out.add(matrix[r][left]);
            left++;
        }
    }
    return out;
}

For [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]] the output is 1 2 3 6 9 8 7 4 5. Complexity: O(m·n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output. Spiral Matrix II (LeetCode 59) fills an n×n grid with 1..n² using the same four boundaries.

Rotate Image (LeetCode 48)

Rotate an n×n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place. Two simple steps: transpose (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i], turning rows into columns), then reverse each row.

public void rotate(int[][] matrix) {
    int n = matrix.length;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {          // only above the diagonal
            int t = matrix[i][j];
            matrix[i][j] = matrix[j][i];
            matrix[j][i] = t;
        }
    }
    for (int[] row : matrix) {
        for (int l = 0, r = n - 1; l < r; l++, r--) {
            int t = row[l]; row[l] = row[r]; row[r] = t;
        }
    }
}

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(1) space. For anticlockwise rotation, reverse the rows first and then transpose (or transpose and reverse the columns). If you start the inner loop at j = 0, you swap every pair twice and end up with the original matrix.

Set Matrix Zeroes (LeetCode 73)

If a cell is 0, set its whole row and column to 0. The simple way uses two boolean arrays (O(m + n) space). For O(1) space, use the first row and first column of the matrix itself as the markers: matrix[i][0] = 0 means "row i must be zeroed", matrix[0][j] = 0 means "column j must be zeroed". Two extra booleans remember whether the first row and first column themselves contained a zero.

public void setZeroes(int[][] matrix) {
    int m = matrix.length, n = matrix[0].length;
    boolean firstRowZero = false, firstColZero = false;
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) if (matrix[0][j] == 0) firstRowZero = true;
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) if (matrix[i][0] == 0) firstColZero = true;

    for (int i = 1; i < m; i++)                 // record zeros in the markers
        for (int j = 1; j < n; j++)
            if (matrix[i][j] == 0) { matrix[i][0] = 0; matrix[0][j] = 0; }

    for (int i = 1; i < m; i++)                 // apply, skipping row 0 and col 0
        for (int j = 1; j < n; j++)
            if (matrix[i][0] == 0 || matrix[0][j] == 0) matrix[i][j] = 0;

    if (firstRowZero) for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) matrix[0][j] = 0;
    if (firstColZero) for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) matrix[i][0] = 0;
}

Complexity: O(m·n) time, O(1) space. The order matters: handle the first row and column last, or the markers get overwritten before use.

Search a 2D Matrix (LeetCode 74): one binary search

Each row is sorted and the first number of a row is greater than the last of the previous row, so the whole matrix is one sorted list in row-major order. Binary search over indexes 0 .. m*n - 1 and convert an index with row = mid / n, col = mid % n (binary search is in Module 1).

public boolean searchMatrix(int[][] matrix, int target) {
    int m = matrix.length, n = matrix[0].length;
    int lo = 0, hi = m * n - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        int v = matrix[mid / n][mid % n];
        if (v == target) return true;
        if (v < target) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return false;
}

Complexity: O(log(m·n)) time, O(1) space.

Search a 2D Matrix II (LeetCode 240): staircase

Here rows are sorted and columns are sorted, but rows do not continue from each other. Start at the top-right corner. If the value is bigger than the target, the whole column below is bigger, so move left. If it is smaller, the whole row to its left is smaller, so move down. Every step removes a row or a column.

public boolean searchMatrix(int[][] matrix, int target) {
    int r = 0, c = matrix[0].length - 1;          // top-right corner
    while (r < matrix.length && c >= 0) {
        int v = matrix[r][c];
        if (v == target) return true;
        if (v > target) c--;                      // discard this column
        else r++;                                 // discard this row
    }
    return false;
}

Complexity: O(m + n) time, O(1) space. The bottom-left corner works the same way; top-left and bottom-right do not, because both choices increase (or both decrease) the value.

Brief: diagonal traversal and flood fill

  • Diagonal Traverse (LeetCode 498): cells on one diagonal share r + c. Walk each diagonal and reverse the direction on every other one. O(m·n).
  • Flood Fill (LeetCode 733) and Number of Islands (LeetCode 200): from a start cell, visit all connected cells with the same value using DFS or BFS and the dirs array, marking visited cells (by changing the value or using a boolean grid). This is the bridge to graph search; the full treatment is in Module 3.
public int[][] floodFill(int[][] image, int sr, int sc, int color) {
    int original = image[sr][sc];
    if (original != color) fill(image, sr, sc, original, color);   // avoids infinite loop
    return image;
}

private void fill(int[][] img, int r, int c, int original, int color) {
    if (r < 0 || r >= img.length || c < 0 || c >= img[0].length) return;
    if (img[r][c] != original) return;
    img[r][c] = color;                       // doubles as the "visited" mark
    fill(img, r + 1, c, original, color);
    fill(img, r - 1, c, original, color);
    fill(img, r, c + 1, original, color);
    fill(img, r, c - 1, original, color);
}

Complexity: O(m·n) time, O(m·n) recursion depth in the worst case.

Common mistakes

  • Swapping m and n, so rows and columns are mixed up in a non-square grid.
  • Reading matrix[0].length on an empty matrix.
  • Flood fill with the new colour equal to the old one: infinite recursion.
  • Copying a matrix with clone() and expecting a deep copy; it copies only the outer array, so rows are shared.

Interview angle

Matrix questions test care more than cleverness. Say the dimensions and edge cases first (1×1, one row, one column), name your four boundaries or direction array, and test with a 3×3 and a 2×3 grid. Be ready for the in-place and O(1) space follow-ups (rotate image, set matrix zeroes).

Interview questions — Core patterns

How do you decide between two pointers and a sliding window?

Both use two indexes that only move forward. Use sliding window when the answer is a contiguous subarray or substring and you maintain a summary (sum, counts) of what is between the indexes. Use two pointers when you compare the elements at the two indexes themselves: pairs in a sorted array, palindromes, in-place read/write. See Two pointers and Sliding window.

Why is the sliding window O(n) even though it has a while loop inside a for loop?

The left pointer only moves forward and never passes the right pointer, so across the whole run it moves at most n times. Each element is added once and removed at most once. The total work is O(n), not O(n²). This is amortized analysis. The same argument proves the monotonic stack and monotonic deque are O(n).

Why does a sum-based sliding window fail with negative numbers? What do you use instead?

The window logic needs monotonicity: adding an element must not decrease the sum, and removing one must not increase it. With negatives that breaks, so "shrink while the sum is too large/valid" can stop too early and miss answers. Use prefix sums with a HashMap: the subarray sum ending at i equals k if an earlier prefix equals prefix - k. This works for any signs (Subarray Sum Equals K).

How do you find the start of a cycle in a linked list, and why does it work?

Run slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps) until they meet. Then reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle entry. Let a be the distance from head to entry and c the distance from the meeting point onward to the entry. At the meeting, slow walked a + b and fast walked twice as much, which gives a = (k − 1)(cycle length) + c. So walking a steps from the meeting point lands exactly on the entry. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Reverse a linked list iteratively. What are the three pointers?

Keep prev (head of the reversed part, starts null), cur (the node being flipped) and nxt (the saved cur.next). Loop: save nxt = cur.next, set cur.next = prev, move prev = cur, move cur = nxt. Return prev. It is O(n) time and O(1) space. The recursive version is O(n) stack space and can overflow on long lists.

What is a dummy node and when do you use it?

A fake node placed before the real head so that dummy.next is the head. You use it whenever the head can be deleted, replaced or inserted before, such as Remove Nth From End, Merge Two Lists or Remove Elements. It removes the special case for the head, and you return dummy.next.

Why prefer ArrayDeque over Stack and LinkedList in Java?

Stack extends Vector: synchronized (slow), and it exposes index-based methods that break stack semantics. LinkedList allocates a node per element and is slower and heavier. ArrayDeque is a resizable circular array: fast, compact, and it works as stack, queue and deque. Its drawbacks: no null elements and not thread-safe. Remember pop() throws NoSuchElementException on empty, while peek() and poll() return null.

Explain the monotonic stack and give its complexity.

A stack whose values stay in one order (for example decreasing). When a new element breaks the order, pop elements until the order is restored; the popped elements have just found their "next greater" element. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole scan is O(n). Use it for next greater/smaller, Daily Temperatures, Stock Span and Largest Rectangle in Histogram. Store indexes so you can compute distances.

How do you compute the maximum of every window of size k in O(n)?

Use a monotonic deque of indexes with decreasing values. For each new element pop from the back all smaller or equal values, push the new index, pop the front if it left the window (front <= i - k), and read the front as the maximum. Each index enters and leaves once, so O(n) time and O(k) space. A max-heap with lazy deletion also works in O(n log n).

What is the difference between height and depth of a tree node, and what is a balanced tree?

Depth is the number of edges from the root to the node; height is the number of edges on the longest path down to a leaf. A tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1, which keeps the height at O(log n). A skewed tree has height n, and recursion on it uses O(n) stack.

Write an iterative inorder traversal and explain how it works. 
Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
TreeNode cur = root;
while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
    while (cur != null) { stack.push(cur); cur = cur.left; }
    cur = stack.pop();
    visit(cur);
    cur = cur.right;
}

Push the whole left spine, pop the leftmost node, visit it, then repeat for its right subtree. The stack holds the ancestors still waiting. O(n) time, O(h) space.

How do you find the diameter of a binary tree in O(n)?

Write a height function that also updates a global answer. At each node the longest path bending there is leftHeight + rightHeight; record the maximum. Return 1 + max(left, right) to the parent, because a path going up can use only one child. Calling a separate height function at every node would be O(n²) in a skewed tree.

How does the recursive LCA algorithm work?

The function returns the node itself if it equals p or q, or null at a null node. Otherwise it recurses into both children. If both results are non-null, p and q are on different sides, so the current node is the LCA. If only one is non-null, return it up. In a BST you do not need both sides: go left if both values are smaller, right if both are larger, else the current node is the LCA. O(n) for a general tree, O(h) for a BST.

Why is "check left.val < node.val < right.val" not enough to validate a BST?

The BST rule covers the entire subtree, not just the children. A node deep in the right subtree can be smaller than the root even if it is correctly placed relative to its own parent. Pass down a (lo, hi) range: going left sets hi to the node's value, going right sets lo to it. Or check that an inorder traversal is strictly increasing. Use Integer bounds or long to avoid problems with Integer.MIN_VALUE.

Find the K largest elements: why a min-heap, and how does it compare with sorting and quickselect?

Keep a min-heap of size k. Its top is the smallest of the k largest, i.e. the next one to evict when a bigger value arrives. Time O(n log k), memory O(k), and it works on streams. Sorting is O(n log n). Quickselect is O(n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case and needs all the data in memory. If values are bounded or counts are involved, bucket sort gives O(n).

How do you find the minimum number of meeting rooms?

Sort meetings by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of occupied rooms. For each meeting, if the earliest end time is at or before its start, reuse that room (poll). Push the meeting's end. The heap size at the end is the answer. Alternatively sort the starts and ends separately and sweep with two pointers. Both are O(n log n).

Cheat sheet — Core patterns

  • Two pointers (opposite ends) sorted input or palindrome: move the pointer that can improve the answer; O(n).
  • Read/write pointers in-place filtering or de-duplication: read scans, write marks the kept prefix.
  • Fixed window add right, check size k, record, remove left. O(n).
  • Variable window expand right; shrink left while invalid (longest) or while valid (shortest, record before shrinking).
  • Window needs non-negative numbers for sums; otherwise use prefix sums plus a HashMap.
  • Exactly K = atMost(K) − atMost(K − 1).
  • Linked list use a dummy node when the head can change; save next before rewiring.
  • Reverse list prev, cur, nxt; iterative is O(1) space, recursive is O(n).
  • Fast/slow middle, cycle detection; reset one pointer to head to find the cycle entry; gap of n for the n-th from the end.
  • Stack in Java Deque<T> s = new ArrayDeque<>() with push, pop, peek. Never Stack.
  • Valid parentheses push the expected closer; the stack must be empty at the end.
  • Monotonic stack store indexes; pop while the top breaks the order; each index pushed and popped once; O(n).
  • Queue/Deque offer/poll/peek; offerFirst/offerLast/pollFirst/pollLast. Use ArrayDeque.
  • BFS by levels size = q.size() at the start of each round of the while loop.
  • Sliding window max deque of decreasing values; pop back while smaller; pop front when out of range.
  • Tree traversals preorder N-L-R, inorder L-N-R (sorted for a BST), postorder L-R-N; recursion uses O(h) stack.
  • Tree recursion define what each call returns; base case null; for bent paths return one side, update a global with both.
  • Height/diameter/balanced one pass, bottom-up; -1 sentinel for unbalanced.
  • LCA both sides non-null means the current node; BST version walks one path in O(h).
  • Views side views by BFS level; top/bottom view with horizontal distance and a TreeMap.
  • BST left smaller, right larger; delete with 0, 1 or 2 children (use the inorder successor); validate with (lo, hi) bounds.
  • Heap array parent (i - 1) / 2, children 2i + 1, 2i + 2; offer/poll O(log n), peek O(1), heapify O(n).
  • PriorityQueue min-heap by default; Comparator.reverseOrder() for max; use Integer.compare, not subtraction.
  • Top K K largest = min-heap of size k; K smallest = max-heap of size k; O(n log k).
  • Median of a stream max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half; keep sizes within 1.
  • Intervals sort by start to merge; sort by end to keep the most; heap of end times or sweep line for rooms.
  • Matrix dirs array and bounds checks; rotate = transpose + reverse rows; staircase from the top-right in a sorted-rows-and-columns grid.

Practice — Core patterns

Roadmap target for this module: about 100 problems over months 4 to 6. Start the weekly LeetCode contest in month 4 (one contest per week; solving even the first two problems under time pressure is a good habit). For each problem: say the pattern out loud before coding, write the solution without notes, state time and space, and test an empty and a one-element input.

  1. Month 4: two pointers, sliding window, linked lists (35 problems). Do about 12 two-pointer problems (Two Sum II, 3Sum, Container With Most Water, Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array, Valid Palindrome, Trapping Rain Water, Sort Colors), about 12 sliding-window problems (Maximum Average Subarray, Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Minimum Window Substring, Longest Repeating Character Replacement, Permutation in String, Fruit Into Baskets) and about 11 linked-list problems. Done when you can write the fixed and variable window templates from memory and explain why they are O(n).
  2. Linked list set. Implement from scratch, without looking: Reverse Linked List (both ways), Merge Two Sorted Lists, Linked List Cycle and Cycle II, Middle of the Linked List, Remove Nth Node From End, Palindrome Linked List, Add Two Numbers, Reorder List. Done when each runs correctly on empty, one-node and two-node inputs.
  3. Month 5: stacks, queues, intervals, matrix (30 problems). Stacks and monotonic stack: Valid Parentheses, Min Stack, Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, Daily Temperatures, Next Greater Element II, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Decode String. Queues: Implement Queue using Stacks, Sliding Window Maximum, a BFS on a small grid. Done when you can state the stack invariant of each problem in one sentence.
  4. Intervals and matrix set. Merge Intervals, Insert Interval, Non-overlapping Intervals, Meeting Rooms I and II (heap and sweep line), Spiral Matrix, Rotate Image, Set Matrix Zeroes, Search a 2D Matrix I and II, Flood Fill. Done when Rotate Image and Set Matrix Zeroes are in place with O(1) extra space.
  5. Month 6: binary trees, BSTs, heaps (35 problems). Trees: all three traversals recursively and iteratively, Maximum Depth, Diameter, Balanced Binary Tree, Same/Symmetric/Invert Tree, Path Sum I and II, Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum, Lowest Common Ancestor, Right Side View, Zigzag Level Order, Construct from Preorder and Inorder, Serialize and Deserialize. Done when you can solve a new tree problem by first writing the contract "what does this call return?".
  6. BST set. Validate BST (with bounds), Kth Smallest Element, Insert and Delete in a BST, LCA of a BST, Convert Sorted Array to BST, BST Iterator. Then use a TreeMap for one problem (for example My Calendar I). Done when you can explain the three delete cases and why checking only the children is wrong.
  7. Heap set. Kth Largest Element in an Array, Top K Frequent Elements (heap and bucket versions), K Closest Points to Origin, Merge K Sorted Lists, Find Median from Data Stream, Task Scheduler. Done when you can implement a min-heap with sift up and sift down on paper.
  8. Build the toolkit. Write your own MinHeap class, an LRU cache with a doubly linked list and a HashMap, and a circular queue. Done when all three pass tests you write yourself, including the full and empty cases.
  9. Weekly contest review. After each contest, re-solve the problems you missed within 48 hours and write down the pattern name and the trick you missed. Done when you keep a one-line-per-problem log of at least 8 contests.
  10. Mock interview. Pick one problem from each pattern group at random, solve it in 30 minutes on paper or a plain editor, and explain the complexity aloud. Next steps: graphs, recursion, dynamic programming and greedy in Module 3. Done when you finish three problems in a row within the time limit.
3

Module 3·Months 7–9 · about 90 problemsMust

Advanced

41 topics · about 6.5 h of reading

Stage 3 (months 7–9) is where problems stop being "one clever loop" and become search and modelling problems. You learn to try every choice and undo it (backtracking), to take the best local choice and prove that it is safe (greedy), to model things and their connections and walk through them (graphs), and to remember the answers of repeated subproblems (dynamic programming). The module ends with tries, a tree built for fast prefix search. Product companies and startups ask these topics in almost every coding round, and service companies use them for their harder rounds.

Everything here builds on Stages 1 and 2: recursion and the call stack, ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue, sorting with comparators, and trees (a tree is simply a connected graph without cycles). The same ideas appear in everyday backend work: Gradle runs tasks in an order computed from a dependency graph, Spring Boot refuses to start (by default) when beans depend on each other in a cycle, map apps compute shortest routes, and "people you may know" is a walk over a friendship graph. The first half of this module covers backtracking, greedy and graphs (targets: about 12 backtracking, 10 greedy, 15 graph-basics and 15 graph-algorithm problems). The second half covers dynamic programming and tries.

  • Write the backtracking template from memory and adapt it to subsets, permutations, combinations, N-Queens and grid word search — with pruning and duplicate handling.
  • Decide whether a greedy rule is correct, justify it with an exchange argument, and recognise when greedy fails and dynamic programming is needed.
  • Model a problem as a graph, pick a representation, and use BFS and DFS for reachability, connected components, shortest paths in unweighted graphs, cycle detection and bipartite checks.
  • Apply topological sort, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, 0-1 BFS, union-find, Kruskal and Prim — and choose the right one from the problem statement.
  • Solve dynamic programming problems and use tries for prefix and word problems (second half of the module).
  • State and justify the time and space complexity of every solution in an interview.

Backtracking: choose, explore, un-choose

Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time, explores each choice with recursion and undoes it before trying the next one — a depth-first walk over the tree of all possible choices that cuts off branches which cannot lead to an answer.

Think of walking through a maze. At every junction you pick a corridor. If it ends in a wall, you walk back to the last junction and try the next corridor. You never need a map of the whole maze; you only remember the path you are standing on. Backtracking is exactly this idea written as recursion: make a choice, recurse, and when the recursion returns, undo the choice so that the next choice starts from a clean state.

You use backtracking when a problem asks for all arrangements ("return all subsets", "list every permutation", "all valid boards"), or for any one arrangement that satisfies hard rules ("solve this sudoku", "does this word exist in the grid?"). The number of possible answers grows exponentially, so the input in these problems is always small — and that small input size is itself a strong hint.

Key terms

State (partial solution)
What you have built so far — for example the list [1, 3] while generating subsets, or the queens already placed in the first three rows.
Choice
One option you can add to the current state — the next number, the next letter, the column for the next queen.
Constraint
A rule every valid state must obey — "no two queens attack each other", "the sum must not exceed the target".
Goal (base case)
The test that says the state is a complete answer — the path has k elements, every row has a queen, every letter of the word matched.
State-space tree
