With the amount outer, every coin can be the last coin of every amount, so different orders are counted separately — that gives permutations." Then give the 1+2 / 2+1 example. Also be ready for "why not greedy?" with the [1, 3, 4], amount 6 counter-example.

More 1D DP: word break and maximum product subarray

Word Break is a 1D DP over string prefixes ("can the first i characters be split into dictionary words?"), and Maximum Product Subarray is a Kadane-style DP that tracks both the largest and the smallest product ending at each index.

These two look unrelated, but both teach an important 1D lesson. Word Break shows a transition that looks back over many earlier states, not just one or two. Maximum Product Subarray shows that sometimes one value per state is not enough — you need two.

Word Break (LeetCode 139)

Problem: given a string s and a dictionary of words, return true if s can be split into a sequence of dictionary words (words may be reused). "leetcode" with ["leet", "code"] → true. "applepenapple" with ["apple", "pen"] → true. "catsandog" with ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"] → false.

Why brute force is too slow: trying every split point is exponential. For s = "aaaa…ab" with words ["a", "aa", "aaa"], every split of the a's is tried, and each one fails only at the final 'b'. The failing work for "the suffix starting at index 7" is repeated over and over — overlapping subproblems.

  • State: dp[i] = true if the prefix s[0..i) can be split into words.
  • Transition: the last word is s[j..i) for some j < i: dp[i] = OR over j of (dp[j] && dict contains s[j..i)).
  • Base case: dp[0] = true (the empty prefix needs no words).
  • Answer: dp[n].
import java.util.*;

public class WordBreak {
    public boolean wordBreak(String s, List<String> wordDict) {
        Set<String> dict = new HashSet<>(wordDict);   // O(1) average lookups
        int maxLen = 0;
        for (String w : wordDict) maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, w.length());

        int n = s.length();
        boolean[] dp = new boolean[n + 1];        // dp[i] = s[0..i) can be split
        dp[0] = true;                             // empty prefix
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            // the last word is s[j..i), and no word is longer than maxLen
            for (int j = Math.max(0, i - maxLen); j < i; j++) {
                if (dp[j] && dict.contains(s.substring(j, i))) {
                    dp[i] = true;
                    break;                        // one valid split is enough
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[n];
    }
}

Complexity: n end positions × at most maxLen start positions × O(maxLen) to build and hash each substring = O(n · maxLen²) time; without the maxLen limit it is O(n³). Space O(n) plus the dictionary.

The same idea top-down — memoize on the start index. Boolean[] gives you a third value, null, for "not computed":

private Boolean[] memo;                           // memo[start]: can s[start..] be split?

private boolean canBreak(String s, int start, Set<String> dict) {
    if (start == s.length()) return true;
    if (memo[start] != null) return memo[start];
    for (int end = start + 1; end <= s.length(); end++) {
        if (dict.contains(s.substring(start, end)) && canBreak(s, end, dict)) {
            memo[start] = true;
            return true;
        }
    }
    memo[start] = false;
    return false;
}
// call: memo = new Boolean[s.length()]; return canBreak(s, 0, dict);

Note: Word Break II and the trie speed-up

Word Break II (LeetCode 140) asks for every sentence. The output itself can be exponential, so it is backtracking with memoization of "all sentences from index i". For large dictionaries, a trie lets you walk forward from j character by character and stop as soon as no word continues, instead of hashing every substring.

Maximum Product Subarray (LeetCode 152), briefly

Problem: find the contiguous subarray with the largest product. [2, 3, -2, 4] → 6 ([2, 3]); [-2, 0, -1] → 0.

Kadane's algorithm for sums keeps "the best sum ending here". For products that is not enough: a very negative product can become the largest one after one more negative number. So keep two values per index: the largest and the smallest product of a subarray ending here.

  • State: maxHere, minHere = largest and smallest product of a subarray ending at i.
  • Transition: either start fresh at x, or extend the old max or the old min: maxHere = max(x, oldMax·x, oldMin·x) and minHere = min(x, oldMax·x, oldMin·x).
  • Answer: the largest maxHere seen at any index.
public int maxProduct(int[] nums) {
    int maxHere = nums[0], minHere = nums[0], best = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int x = nums[i];
        int a = maxHere * x, b = minHere * x;     // use the OLD values for both
        maxHere = Math.max(x, Math.max(a, b));
        minHere = Math.min(x, Math.min(a, b));
        best = Math.max(best, maxHere);
    }
    return best;
}

A zero resets both values to 0, and the next element starts fresh because x itself is one of the three options. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. LeetCode promises that every subarray product fits in an int; in your own code consider long.

Mistake: plain Kadane on products

Wrong: forgets that min × negative becomes max

int cur = nums[0], best = nums[0];
for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
    cur = Math.max(nums[i], cur * nums[i]);
    best = Math.max(best, cur);
}
// [-2, 3, -4] returns 3, the answer is 24

Right: track max and min together

int a = maxHere * x, b = minHere * x;
maxHere = Math.max(x, Math.max(a, b));
minHere = Math.min(x, Math.min(a, b));
best = Math.max(best, maxHere);

Rule: when two variables update together, compute both from the old values

If you update maxHere first and then use it to compute minHere, the min is built from the new max — a silent bug. Save the old values (a, b above) or swap max and min when x is negative.

Edge cases

  • All negative or a single element: [-3] → -3. Starting best at 0 is wrong; start it at nums[0].
  • Word Break with a word longer than s: harmless, it is never matched.
  • Word Break dictionaries are case-sensitive strings; "Apple" does not match "apple".

Interview angle

For Word Break, start with the recursion "can s[start..] be split?", point at the repeated start values, then memoize — that story shows you understand why DP applies. For Maximum Product Subarray, the key sentence is "a negative number swaps the roles of the largest and smallest product, so I track both".

Longest increasing subsequence: O(n²) DP and O(n log n)

LIS asks for the longest strictly increasing subsequence; the DP "best sequence ending at i" costs O(n²), and keeping a sorted "tails" array with binary search brings it down to O(n log n).

A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements (it is not the same as a subarray, which must be contiguous). For [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18] the LIS length is 4, for example 2, 3, 7, 18. LIS (LeetCode "Longest Increasing Subsequence") is one of the most asked DP problems because it has two good solutions, and interviewers like to ask for the second after you give the first.

Method 1: dp[i] = LIS that ends at index i

The trick is the state. "Best LIS in the first i elements" is not enough, because to extend it you must know its last value. So fix the last element: dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at nums[i].

  • State: dp[i], ending at index i.
  • Transition: look at every earlier j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]; you can append nums[i] to the best sequence ending at j. So dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over those j.
  • Base case: every dp[i] starts at 1 (the element alone).
  • Answer: the maximum over all dp[i], not dp[n-1], because the best sequence may end anywhere.
public int lengthOfLIS(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    java.util.Arrays.fill(dp, 1);              // each element alone is a sequence of 1
    int best = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (nums[j] < nums[i]) {           // strictly increasing
                dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
            }
        }
        best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
    }
    return best;                               // empty input is not allowed by the problem
}

Dry run on [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7]: dp = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]. For 7 (index 5) the smaller earlier values are 2, 5 and 3 with dp 1, 2, 2, so dp[5] = 3. Complexity: O(n²) time, O(n) space. Fine for n up to about 2,500; too slow for n = 105.

Method 2: tails array and binary search

Keep an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. The array is always sorted, which is why binary search works. For each number x:

  1. Find the first position pos in tails with tails[pos] >= x (a lower bound).
  2. If no such position exists, x is bigger than every tail: append it, the LIS grows by one.
  3. Otherwise overwrite tails[pos] = x. A smaller tail for the same length is strictly better for future extensions.
public int lengthOfLIS(int[] nums) {
    int[] tails = new int[nums.length];
    int size = 0;                              // tails[0..size-1] is in use and sorted
    for (int x : nums) {
        int lo = 0, hi = size;                 // lower bound: first index with tails[idx] >= x
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            if (tails[mid] < x) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid;
        }
        tails[lo] = x;
        if (lo == size) size++;                // x extended the longest sequence
    }
    return size;
}

Complexity: O(n log n) time (one binary search per element), O(n) space.

The tails array is not a valid subsequence

After the run above tails = [2, 3, 7, 18] happens to be real, but in general it is a mix of different candidate sequences (for example [2, 3] was built after 5 was replaced). Only its length is guaranteed correct. To print the actual LIS, store for each element its parent index and the index sitting in each tails slot, then walk back from the last slot; or use the O(n²) DP with a parent[] array.

Strict vs non-strict

For a strictly increasing sequence use lower bound (first tails[idx] >= x), so equal values replace instead of append. For a non-decreasing sequence use upper bound (first tails[idx] > x). Using the wrong one is the classic bug: [2, 2, 2] must give 1 for strict LIS.

Where LIS hides

  • Russian Doll Envelopes: sort by width ascending, and for equal widths by height descending, then run LIS on heights. The descending tie-break stops two envelopes of equal width from chaining.
  • Number of LIS (count of optimal sequences): keep a second array count[i] in the O(n²) DP.
  • Largest divisible subset and longest chain of pairs: sort, then the same "best chain ending at i" DP.
  • Minimum deletions to make an array sorted = n - LIS.

Maximum Product Subarray (brief)

A neighbour of Kadane's algorithm, but a negative number flips the biggest into the smallest. So track both the maximum and the minimum product ending at the current index.

public int maxProduct(int[] nums) {
    int curMax = nums[0], curMin = nums[0], best = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int x = nums[i];
        int a = curMax * x, b = curMin * x;    // a negative x swaps the roles
        curMax = Math.max(x, Math.max(a, b));  // restart at x, or extend
        curMin = Math.min(x, Math.min(a, b));
        best = Math.max(best, curMax);
    }
    return best;                               // O(n) time, O(1) space
}

Dry run on [2, 3, -2, 4]: (max, min) goes (2,2), (6,3), (-2,-12), (4,-48); best is 6.

Interview angle

Give the O(n²) DP first and say why the state is "ending at i". When asked to improve, describe the tails array: "the smallest tail for each length, kept sorted, so I binary search". Mention strict vs non-strict and that tails is not the sequence itself.

Grid DP: unique paths, min path sum, triangle, maximal square

In grid DP the state is a cell (row, col), and each cell is computed from the cells above and to the left, so a double loop in reading order fills the table in O(rows × cols).

When a robot moves only right and down, the way to reach a cell depends only on the cell above and the cell to the left. That is optimal substructure in its cleanest form. The state is dp[r][c]; the iteration order is row by row, left to right, so that both neighbours are ready; and because each row reads only the previous row, you can usually shrink the table to one row.

The grid template

int[][] dp = new int[m][n];
dp[0][0] = /* start value */ 0;
// first row and first column have only one source each: fill them first
for (int c = 1; c < n; c++) dp[0][c] = /* from dp[0][c-1] */ 0;
for (int r = 1; r < m; r++) dp[r][0] = /* from dp[r-1][0] */ 0;
for (int r = 1; r < m; r++) {
    for (int c = 1; c < n; c++) {
        dp[r][c] = /* combine(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]) */ 0;
    }
}
return dp[m - 1][n - 1];

Unique Paths (LeetCode 62)

A robot starts at the top-left of an m × n grid and moves only right or down. How many paths reach the bottom-right? State: dp[r][c] = number of paths to that cell. Transition: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]. Base: the whole first row and first column are 1 (only one way: straight).

public int uniquePaths(int m, int n) {
    int[] row = new int[n];                    // one row is enough
    java.util.Arrays.fill(row, 1);             // first row: 1 way to each cell
    for (int r = 1; r < m; r++) {
        for (int c = 1; c < n; c++) {
            row[c] += row[c - 1];              // row[c] (above) + row[c-1] (left)
        }
    }
    return row[n - 1];
}

For a 3 × 3 grid the rows become [1,1,1], [1,2,3], [1,3,6], so the answer is 6. Complexity: O(m·n) time, O(n) space. A maths shortcut is C(m+n-2, m-1), but it overflows easily; the DP is safer.

Unique Paths II: with obstacles (LeetCode 63)

Same problem, but cells marked 1 are blocked. An obstacle cell has zero paths. The first row and column are no longer all 1: once a blocked cell appears, everything after it in that row (or column) is unreachable.

public int uniquePathsWithObstacles(int[][] g) {
    int m = g.length, n = g[0].length;
    int[] row = new int[n];
    row[0] = g[0][0] == 1 ? 0 : 1;             // start blocked means 0 paths
    for (int r = 0; r < m; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (g[r][c] == 1) {
                row[c] = 0;                    // blocked: no way to be here
            } else if (c > 0) {
                row[c] += row[c - 1];          // above (old row[c]) + left
            }
        }
    }
    return row[n - 1];
}

The code handles row 0 naturally: row[c] starts at 0 for c > 0 and receives the left value. Complexity: O(m·n) time, O(n) space.

Minimum Path Sum (LeetCode 64)

Each cell has a cost; find the cheapest right/down path. Transition: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]). In the first row and column only one neighbour exists.

public int minPathSum(int[][] grid) {
    int m = grid.length, n = grid[0].length;
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    for (int r = 0; r < m; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (r == 0 && c == 0) dp[c] = grid[0][0];
            else if (r == 0) dp[c] = dp[c - 1] + grid[r][c];       // only from the left
            else if (c == 0) dp[c] = dp[c] + grid[r][c];           // only from above
            else dp[c] = Math.min(dp[c], dp[c - 1]) + grid[r][c];
        }
    }
    return dp[n - 1];
}

For [[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]] the answer is 7 (1→3→1→1→1). Complexity: O(m·n) time, O(n) space. If you must not change the input, the 1D array is the clean choice; if you may, reusing grid as the table gives O(1) extra space.

Triangle (LeetCode 120)

Find the minimum path from the top of a triangle to the bottom, moving to an adjacent number on the row below (index j or j+1). Going bottom-up is neat: start with the last row as the base and fold upward, so the answer ends in dp[0] and you need no edge checks.

public int minimumTotal(java.util.List<java.util.List<Integer>> triangle) {
    int n = triangle.size();
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) dp[j] = triangle.get(n - 1).get(j);   // last row
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
        for (int j = 0; j <= i; j++) {
            dp[j] = triangle.get(i).get(j) + Math.min(dp[j], dp[j + 1]);
        }
    }
    return dp[0];                              // O(n^2) time, O(n) space
}

Maximal Square (LeetCode 221)

Given a 0/1 matrix, find the area of the largest square of 1s. State: dp[r][c] = side length of the largest square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c). If the cell is 0, it is 0. Otherwise the square is limited by the weakest of its three neighbours: dp[r][c] = 1 + min(up, left, up-left).

public int maximalSquare(char[][] matrix) {
    int m = matrix.length, n = matrix[0].length;
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];        // extra row and column of zeros: no edge checks
    int side = 0;
    for (int r = 1; r <= m; r++) {
        for (int c = 1; c <= n; c++) {
            if (matrix[r - 1][c - 1] == '1') {
                dp[r][c] = 1 + Math.min(dp[r - 1][c],
                                Math.min(dp[r][c - 1], dp[r - 1][c - 1]));
                side = Math.max(side, dp[r][c]);
            }
        }
    }
    return side * side;                        // area, O(m*n) time and space
}

Why the min of three? A square of side k at the corner needs squares of side k-1 above, to the left and diagonally. Any smaller neighbour is the bottleneck.

Dungeon Game (brief)

A knight moves right/down from top-left to bottom-right; cells add or subtract health; health must stay at least 1. Going forward fails because "best so far" is not enough: you need to know the minimum health required. So run the DP backwards: need[r][c] = minimum health needed when entering the cell. need[r][c] = max(1, min(need[r+1][c], need[r][c+1]) - dungeon[r][c]), with the princess cell using max(1, 1 - dungeon). Lesson: when a forward state is not enough, define it backwards.

Common grid DP mistakes

  • Forgetting to initialise the first row and column (or the padding row) so index -1 is read.
  • Mixing up m (rows) and n (columns) when allocating new int[m][n].
  • In the 1D version, updating in the wrong direction; for right/down grids a left-to-right sweep is correct.

0/1 knapsack: 2D table, then 1D with reverse iteration

0/1 knapsack picks each item at most once to maximise value within a weight limit; the 2D table is dp[i][w], and the 1D version works only if the capacity loop runs from high to low.

You have n items, each with a weight and a value, and a bag that holds weight W. Each item is taken 0 or 1 times (that is the "0/1"). Maximise the total value. Greedy by value-per-weight fails here (it works only for the fractional version). Brute force tries 2n subsets. The DP solves it in O(n·W) — a pseudo-polynomial time, because it depends on the number W, not on its bit length.

The 2D table

  • State: dp[i][w] = best value using only the first i items with capacity w.
  • Transition: for item i either skip it, dp[i-1][w], or take it (if wt[i-1] <= w), dp[i-1][w - wt[i-1]] + val[i-1]. Take the max.
  • Base cases: row 0 (no items) and column 0 (no capacity) are all 0.
  • Order: row by row; each row reads only the previous row.
  • Answer: dp[n][W].
public static int knapsack(int[] wt, int[] val, int W) {
    int n = wt.length;
    int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][W + 1];        // zeros are the base cases
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        for (int w = 0; w <= W; w++) {
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w];                           // skip item i-1
            if (wt[i - 1] <= w) {
                dp[i][w] = Math.max(dp[i][w],
                        dp[i - 1][w - wt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1]); // take it
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[n][W];
}

Example: weights [1, 3, 4, 5], values [1, 4, 5, 7], W = 7. The best is items of weight 3 and 4 for value 9. Complexity: O(n·W) time and space.

The 1D version and why you iterate backwards

Row i uses only row i-1, so one array can hold "the previous row" and be updated in place. The catch: dp[w] must use the old dp[w - wt] (from row i-1). If you loop w upward, dp[w - wt] has already been updated for item i, so the same item can be counted again and again — you have turned the problem into the unbounded knapsack by accident. Looping w from W down to wt guarantees that smaller indexes are still untouched when you read them.

public static int knapsack1D(int[] wt, int[] val, int W) {
    int[] dp = new int[W + 1];                 // dp[w] = best value with capacity w
    for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++) {
        for (int w = W; w >= wt[i]; w--) {     // REVERSE: each item used at most once
            dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]);
        }
    }
    return dp[W];                              // O(n*W) time, O(W) space
}

Wrong: forward loop reuses the item

for (int w = wt[i]; w <= W; w++) {
    dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]);
}
// weights [3], values [4], W = 9 gives 12 (three copies)

Right: backward loop uses it once

for (int w = W; w >= wt[i]; w--) {
    dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]);
}
// same input gives 4 (one copy)

Which items were chosen?

The 1D array loses the history. To recover the chosen items, keep the 2D table and walk back from dp[n][W]: if dp[i][w] != dp[i-1][w], item i-1 was taken, so record it and set w -= wt[i-1]; then move to i-1.

int w = W;
java.util.List<Integer> chosen = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
for (int i = n; i >= 1; i--) {
    if (dp[i][w] != dp[i - 1][w]) {            // value changed, so item i-1 was taken
        chosen.add(i - 1);
        w -= wt[i - 1];
    }
}

Recognising a 0/1 knapsack in disguise

Look for "choose a subset, each element at most once, with a limit or a target": subset sum, partition, target sum, last stone weight II, ones and zeroes (a 2D capacity). The next article turns these into small variations of the same loop. The unbounded sibling is in Unbounded knapsack and rod cutting.

Pseudo-polynomial time

O(n·W) looks polynomial, but with W = 109 the table cannot be built. Knapsack is NP-hard in general; the DP only helps when W is small. If the constraints give W up to 109 but values are small, swap the roles: let the DP index be total value and store the minimum weight.

Why greedy fails and why the DP is correct

A greedy idea is to sort by value per weight and take items until the bag is full. On the example above the ratios are 1, 1.33, 1.25 and 1.4, so greedy takes the weight-5 item (value 7) first, then only the weight-1 item fits in the remaining 2 units: total 8. The true best is 9 (weights 3 and 4). Greedy fails because items are indivisible: a good-looking item can waste space that two other items would use better. The DP never commits early; for every capacity it keeps the best answer over both choices for the current item.

Correctness follows from the "take or skip" split. Any best selection for the first i items either does not contain item i (then it is a best selection for the first i-1 items at the same capacity) or contains it (then the rest is a best selection for the first i-1 items at capacity w - wt). Those two cases cover every possibility, and the table stores the best of each.

The same recurrence top-down

In an interview you can start from the recursion and then convert it. The state is (index of the item, remaining capacity). The memo table has n × W cells, which is why the time is O(n·W).

static int solve(int i, int w, int[] wt, int[] val, int[][] memo) {
    if (i == wt.length || w == 0) return 0;           // no items or no room left
    if (memo[i][w] != -1) return memo[i][w];
    int best = solve(i + 1, w, wt, val, memo);        // skip item i
    if (wt[i] <= w) {                                 // take item i if it fits
        best = Math.max(best, val[i] + solve(i + 1, w - wt[i], wt, val, memo));
    }
    return memo[i][w] = best;
}
// call: fill every row of memo with -1, then solve(0, W, wt, val, memo)

Recursion depth is n, so for n in the thousands prefer the iterative table. Without the memo the same code is O(2n).

Dry run of the 1D array

Weights [1, 3, 4, 5], values [1, 4, 5, 7], W = 7. The array dp starts as eight zeros (index 0 to 7). The inner loop runs from 7 down.

After itemdp[0..7]What changed
(wt 1, val 1)0 1 1 1 1 1 1 1every w ≥ 1 gets 1
(wt 3, val 4)0 1 1 4 5 5 5 5dp[7] = max(1, dp[4] + 4) = 5, dp[3] = max(1, dp[0] + 4) = 4
(wt 4, val 5)0 1 1 4 5 6 6 9dp[7] = max(5, dp[3] + 5) = 9
(wt 5, val 7)0 1 1 4 5 7 8 9dp[5] = 7, dp[6] = dp[1] + 7 = 8

These rows are the same rows as the 2D diagram. Because the loop runs downward, when dp[7] is computed in the second step, dp[4] still holds the value from before this item (1), not a value that already includes it.

At most W versus exactly W

The code above fills the bag up to W: all cells start at 0, so unused space is allowed. Some problems demand that the weight equals the target exactly (subset sum with value, "can you fill the bag exactly"). Then initialise dp[0] = 0 and every other cell to negative infinity (a large negative number, or a separate boolean array), so that unreachable capacities are never extended. The recurrence does not change; only the starting values do.

QuestionStart of dpAnswer
Best value, bag need not be fullall 0dp[W]
Best value, weight exactly Wdp[0] = 0, others −∞dp[W] (if still −∞, impossible)
Can I reach exactly W?dp[0] = truedp[W]

When W is huge but n is small

If W is around 109 and n is at most about 40, the table is impossible, but 2n is also too big. A meet in the middle approach splits the items into two halves, lists all subset (weight, value) pairs of each half (220 each), sorts one list, and combines with binary search. It runs in about O(2n/2 · n). It is rarely required, but it shows you know where the DP stops working.

Edge cases

  • An item heavier than W: the inner loop w >= wt[i] never runs, so the item is skipped. No exception, no special case.
  • W = 0 or no items: the answer is 0 from the initial array.
  • Weight 0 with positive value: the reverse loop adds that value exactly once (it reads the old dp[w]), which is correct for 0/1. In an unbounded problem such an item would give an infinite answer.
  • Negative weight or value: the recurrence assumes non-negative numbers. A negative weight makes w - wt[i] exceed W and read outside the array.
  • Large values: total value can exceed int; use long when values are large.

Mistake: a 1D array with a forward loop

Wrong: forward loop reuses the item

for (int w = wt[i]; w <= W; w++)
    dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]);   // 1D array, forward

Right: read the previous row (2D) or go backward (1D)

dp2[i][w] = Math.max(dp2[i - 1][w], dp2[i - 1][w - wt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1]);
// or, with one array: for (int w = W; w >= wt[i]; w--) ...

Interview angle

Two questions are common: "optimise the space" (answer: 1D array, reverse loop) and "why reverse?" (answer: forward lets the same item be used twice because dp[w - wt] already includes it).

Subset sum, partition, target sum and counting subsets

These four problems are the 0/1 knapsack with a boolean or count in place of a value: iterate items, loop the sum downwards, and either OR, or add, the "without this item" answer.

Once you can write the 1D 0/1 loop, the next problems are mostly a change of what dp[s] stores. The structure never changes: for each item, for s from target down to item.

Subset sum (can we reach exactly T?)

State: dp[s] = true if some subset of the items seen so far sums to s. Base: dp[0] = true (the empty subset). Transition: dp[s] |= dp[s - x].

public static boolean subsetSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1];
    dp[0] = true;                              // the empty subset makes 0
    for (int x : nums) {
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) {    // reverse: use each number once
            dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - x];
        }
    }
    return dp[target];                         // O(n * target) time, O(target) space
}

Partition Equal Subset Sum (LeetCode 416)

Can the array be split into two subsets with equal sums? Let total be the sum. If it is odd, the answer is no. Otherwise ask for a subset summing to total / 2; the rest then also sums to total / 2.

public boolean canPartition(int[] nums) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int x : nums) total += x;
    if (total % 2 != 0) return false;          // odd sums cannot split evenly
    int target = total / 2;
    boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1];
    dp[0] = true;
    for (int x : nums) {
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) dp[s] |= dp[s - x];
        if (dp[target]) return true;           // early exit
    }
    return dp[target];
}

For [1, 5, 11, 5], total 22, target 11: 11 alone works, so true. Complexity: O(n · total/2) time, O(total/2) space. A bitset (java.util.BitSet or a long shift trick) is a faster constant but not needed in interviews.

Count of subsets with a given sum

Now count rather than decide. State: dp[s] = number of subsets giving sum s. Base: dp[0] = 1. Transition: dp[s] += dp[s - x] (the subsets without x are already in dp[s]; those with x come from dp[s - x]). Reverse loop again.

public static int countSubsets(int[] nums, int target) {
    int[] dp = new int[target + 1];
    dp[0] = 1;                                 // one way to make 0: take nothing
    for (int x : nums) {
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) {
            dp[s] += dp[s - x];
        }
    }
    return dp[target];                         // use long if the count can be huge
}

Zeros change the count

If nums may contain 0, then a zero can be in or out of any subset, so the answer doubles per zero. The loop above handles it correctly only when x = 0 is allowed to run: the inner loop s >= 0 then does dp[s] += dp[s] in reverse order, which doubles every entry — correct. Always test with a zero in the input.

Target Sum (LeetCode 494)

Put a + or - before every number; how many ways reach target? Let P be the sum of numbers with + and N the sum with -. Then P - N = target and P + N = total, so P = (total + target) / 2. The problem becomes "count subsets with sum P". Guard the impossible cases: total + target odd, or |target| > total.

public int findTargetSumWays(int[] nums, int target) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int x : nums) total += x;
    if (Math.abs(target) > total || (total + target) % 2 != 0) return 0;
    int p = (total + target) / 2;              // the sum of the numbers that get '+'
    int[] dp = new int[p + 1];
    dp[0] = 1;
    for (int x : nums) {
        for (int s = p; s >= x; s--) dp[s] += dp[s - x];
    }
    return dp[p];                              // O(n * p) time, O(p) space
}

For [1,1,1,1,1] with target 3: total 5, P = 4; subsets of four 1s: C(5,4) = 5. Answer 5.

Last Stone Weight II (idea)

Smashing stones is the same as splitting them into two groups and minimising the difference of the sums. Find the largest subset sum s <= total/2 that is reachable; the answer is total - 2 * s. It is subset sum with a "closest to half" read at the end.

The pattern across the four problems

Problemdp[s] meansUpdateBase
Subset sumreachable?dp[s] |= dp[s-x]dp[0] = true
Partitionreachable total/2?same as abovedp[0] = true
Count subsetsnumber of subsetsdp[s] += dp[s-x]dp[0] = 1
Target sumsubsets with sum Psame as countdp[0] = 1

Mistakes to avoid

  • Looping s upward: numbers get reused (this becomes combination counting with unlimited copies).
  • Forgetting the odd-total check in partition, or the sign/parity check in target sum.
  • Negative array values in subset sum: the array index would be negative. These problems assume non-negative numbers.

Dry runs: what the array holds

Decide (partition). For [1, 5, 11, 5] the target is 11. Think of dp as the set of reachable sums. It starts as {0}. Item 1 adds 1: {0, 1}. Item 5 adds 5 to each existing sum: {0, 1, 5, 6}. Item 11 adds 11: {0, 1, 5, 6, 11, ...}, and 11 is the target, so the answer is true. The reverse loop is what prevents "5 + 5 + 1" from being built out of one 5: while processing the first 5 the loop reads only sums that existed before it.

Count. For [1, 2, 3] and target 3, dp starts as [1, 0, 0, 0].

After itemdp[0..3]Meaning
11 1 0 0sum 1 is made by {1}
21 1 1 1sum 2 by {2}; sum 3 by {1,2}
31 1 1 2sum 3 also by {3}

The answer is 2: the subsets {3} and {1, 2}.

Minimum subset sum difference and Last Stone Weight II

Split the array into two groups so that the difference of their sums is as small as possible. If one group has sum s, the other has total - s, and the difference is total - 2s. To make this small, make s as close to total/2 from below as possible. So run subset sum up to total/2 and take the largest reachable s.

public static int minDifference(int[] nums) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int x : nums) total += x;
    int half = total / 2;
    boolean[] dp = new boolean[half + 1];
    dp[0] = true;
    for (int x : nums) {
        for (int s = half; s >= x; s--) dp[s] |= dp[s - x];
    }
    for (int s = half; s >= 0; s--) {          // largest reachable sum not above half
        if (dp[s]) return total - 2 * s;
    }
    return total;                              // not reached: dp[0] is always true
}
// [2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 1]: total 23, half 11, s = 11 (2+7+1+1) -> 23 - 22 = 1

Last Stone Weight II is this exact code: smashing stones equals choosing signs, which equals splitting into two groups.

Which subset? Reconstruction

A 1D boolean array cannot tell you which numbers were used. Keep the 2D table reach[i][s] = "can the first i numbers make sum s", then walk back from reach[n][target]: if reach[i-1][s] is true, item i-1 was not needed; otherwise it was used, so record it and subtract its value from s. The cost is O(n · target) memory, so do it only when the question asks for the set itself.

Choosing between the problems

The question asksdp typeTypical problems
Is it possible?boolean, ORSubset sum, partition
How many ways?int or long, plusCount subsets, target sum
Best value or fewest items?int, max or minKnapsack, minimum difference
Which items?2D table, walk backPrint the subset

Edge cases

  • Target 0: always true (the empty subset), and the count includes that empty subset. With zeros in the array the count of subsets for target 0 is 2 raised to the number of zeros.
  • Target larger than the total: the answer is false or 0. Check this first; otherwise you allocate a huge array for nothing.
  • Target Sum with target negative: the sign split is symmetric, so use Math.abs(target). The code above already rejects |target| > total and a wrong parity.
  • Counts overflow: a count of subsets can reach 2n. If the problem does not promise it fits in int, use long or a modulo such as 109 + 7.
  • Negative numbers: not supported by these loops; you would need an offset or a map from sum to count.

Mistake: using a forward loop for counting

Wrong: each number can be used many times

for (int x : nums)
    for (int s = x; s <= target; s++) dp[s] += dp[s - x];
// [1,2,3], target 3 gives 3 (adds 1+1+1), not 2

Right: backward loop, each number once

for (int x : nums)
    for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) dp[s] += dp[s - x];
// [1,2,3], target 3 gives 2

Interview angle

Partition Equal Subset Sum is the usual first question. A strong answer says four things: the odd-total shortcut, the reduction to "subset with sum total/2", the 1D boolean array with a reverse loop, and the time O(n · total/2). Then expect two follow-ups: "count the ways" (change OR to plus and the base to 1) and "what if the numbers are large?" (the DP is pseudo-polynomial; with a big sum you need another idea, such as meet in the middle for small n). For Target Sum, show the algebra: P − N = target and P + N = total, so P = (total + target) / 2.

Unbounded knapsack, rod cutting, and the knapsack variants table

In unbounded knapsack each item can be used any number of times, so the capacity loop runs forward (low to high); rod cutting and coin change are the same recurrence.

"Unbounded" means unlimited copies of every item. The recurrence is dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val) — identical to 0/1 — but you want the item to be reusable, so dp[w - wt] should already include the current item. That is exactly what a forward loop gives. The whole difference between the two knapsacks is the loop direction.

Unbounded knapsack

public static int unbounded(int[] wt, int[] val, int W) {
    int[] dp = new int[W + 1];                 // dp[w] = best value with capacity w
    for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++) {
        for (int w = wt[i]; w <= W; w++) {     // FORWARD: item i may be reused
            dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]);
        }
    }
    return dp[W];                              // O(n*W) time, O(W) space
}

With weights [2, 3], values [3, 5], W = 7: two items of weight 2 and one of weight 3 give 3 + 3 + 5 = 11; three items of weight 2 give only 9. The best is 11.

Rod cutting

A rod of length n can be cut into integer pieces; price[k] is the price of a piece of length k+1. Maximise the total price. Each piece length is an "item" with weight = length and value = price, unlimited copies, and the rod length is the capacity — an unbounded knapsack where you must fill the capacity exactly (it always can, using pieces of length 1).

public static int rodCutting(int[] price, int n) {
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];                 // dp[len] = best revenue for a rod of length len
    for (int len = 1; len <= n; len++) {
        for (int cut = 1; cut <= len && cut <= price.length; cut++) {
            dp[len] = Math.max(dp[len], price[cut - 1] + dp[len - cut]);
        }
    }
    return dp[n];                              // O(n^2) time, O(n) space
}

For prices [1, 5, 8, 9, 10, 17, 17, 20] and n = 8 the answer is 22 (cut into 2 and 6: 5 + 17).

Coin change as unbounded knapsack

Coin change is the same shape: coins are items of unlimited supply. For the minimum number of coins, dp[w] = min(dp[w], dp[w - c] + 1) with dp[0] = 0 and "infinity" elsewhere. For the number of ways, dp[w] += dp[w - c] with the coin loop on the outside — that outer-coin order counts combinations, not permutations, as shown in that article.

Ones and Zeroes (2D capacity, brief)

Choose the largest subset of binary strings using at most m zeros and n ones. Each string is an item with two weights. Use dp[z][o] and loop both downwards for each string: it is 0/1 knapsack with a two-dimensional bag.

Variants at a glance

ProblemItem useCapacity loopUpdate
0/1 knapsackat most oncehigh to lowmax(dp[w], dp[w-wt]+val)
Subset sum / partitionat most oncehigh to lowdp[s] |= dp[s-x]
Count subsets / target sumat most oncehigh to lowdp[s] += dp[s-x]
Unbounded knapsack, rod cuttingunlimitedlow to highmax(dp[w], dp[w-wt]+val)
Coin change (min coins)unlimitedlow to highmin(dp[w], dp[w-c]+1)
Coin change II (ways)unlimitedlow to high, coins outsidedp[w] += dp[w-c]

One question decides the loop direction

Ask: "may the same item be used again for this capacity?" If yes, go forward (low to high) so the updated cell is visible. If no, go backward (high to low) so only the old cells are visible.

Dry run of the forward loop

Weights [2, 3], values [3, 5], W = 7. The array dp starts as zeros.

After itemdp[0..7]Notice
(wt 2, val 3)0 0 3 3 6 6 9 9dp[4] = dp[2] + 3 uses the item twice
(wt 3, val 5)0 0 3 5 6 8 10 11dp[7] = dp[4] + 5 = 11

The first row shows the difference from 0/1: dp[4] is 6, because by the time the loop reaches w = 4, dp[2] already contains one copy of the item. A backward loop would have left dp[4] at 3.

Loop order: when it matters

For maximum or minimum answers, the order of the two loops does not change the result: both "items outside, capacity inside" and "capacity outside, items inside" explore all multisets. It matters when you count:

  • Items outside, capacity inside: each combination is counted once, in the order of the items. This is Coin Change II (combinations).
  • Capacity outside, items inside: the same coins in a different order count again, so you get permutations. This is Combination Sum IV.

For rod cutting above we used capacity outside and cuts inside; it is fine because we only take a maximum.

Another problem: Perfect Squares

The fewest perfect squares that sum to n. The "items" are 1, 4, 9, 16, ... with unlimited copies, the "capacity" is n, and each item has cost 1. That is unbounded knapsack with a minimum. For n = 12 the answer is 3 (4 + 4 + 4).

public int numSquares(int n) {
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];                 // dp[i] = fewest squares summing to i
    java.util.Arrays.fill(dp, n + 1);          // n + 1 acts as infinity (1+1+...+1 needs only i)
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j * j <= i; j++) {
            dp[i] = Math.min(dp[i], dp[i - j * j] + 1);
        }
    }
    return dp[n];                              // O(n * sqrt(n)) time, O(n) space
}

Ones and Zeroes in code (2D capacity)

Each binary string costs some zeros and some ones, and each string can be used once, so both capacity loops run downwards.

public int findMaxForm(String[] strs, int m, int n) {
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];        // dp[z][o] = most strings using at most z zeros, o ones
    for (String s : strs) {
        int zeros = 0, ones = 0;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (c == '0') zeros++; else ones++;
        }
        for (int z = m; z >= zeros; z--) {
            for (int o = n; o >= ones; o--) {
                dp[z][o] = Math.max(dp[z][o], dp[z - zeros][o - ones] + 1);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];                           // O(len * m * n) time, O(m * n) space
}

Bounded knapsack: each item has a limit

Between 0/1 (one copy) and unbounded (infinite copies) is the bounded version: item i has cnt[i] copies. The simplest method is to treat every copy as a separate 0/1 item, which costs O(W · total copies). A faster method splits cnt into pieces of size 1, 2, 4, ... plus a remainder, and treats each piece as one 0/1 item of weight and value multiplied by the piece size. Any number of copies from 0 to cnt can be formed from these pieces.

for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++) {
    int left = cnt[i];
    for (int k = 1; left > 0; k <<= 1) {
        int take = Math.min(k, left);
        left -= take;
        int w = take * wt[i], v = take * val[i];       // a bundle of 'take' copies
        for (int c = W; c >= w; c--) {                 // 0/1 loop: backward
            dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v);
        }
    }
}

The table with bounded added

Copies per itemNameCapacity loop
Exactly 0 or 10/1 knapsackhigh to low
0 up to cBounded knapsackhigh to low, with binary splitting
Any numberUnbounded knapsacklow to high

Edge cases

  • Weight 0 and positive value: the forward loop would grow forever in theory (an unlimited gain). Problems rule this out; check the constraints.
  • No exact fit: in "fill exactly W" versions (coin change) use a large sentinel and test it at the end; return −1 if W cannot be made.
  • Rod longer than the price list: in rod cutting, cap the cut length by price.length (the loop above does) or price[cut - 1] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  • Overflow with sentinel: Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 becomes negative. Use a smaller sentinel such as W + 1 or guard the addition.

Mistake: the wrong direction for the question

Wrong: backward loop for unlimited coins

for (int w = W; w >= wt[i]; w--)       // item used at most once
    dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]);
// weights [2], values [3], W = 7 gives 3 instead of 9

Right: forward loop

for (int w = wt[i]; w <= W; w++)
    dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]);
// same input gives 9 (three copies of weight 2)

Interview angle

A favourite follow-up is "what changes between 0/1 and unbounded?" Answer in one line: the direction of the inner loop. Be ready to prove it with a one-item example (weight 3, value 4, W = 9).

Longest common subsequence and longest common substring

LCS fills a table dp[i][j] over prefixes of two strings: equal last characters extend the diagonal, otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either string; walk the table backwards to rebuild the answer.

String DP almost always uses two indexes, one per string (or two ends of one string). The state is "the answer for the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b". A subsequence may skip characters, a substring may not. LCS (LeetCode "Longest Common Subsequence") is the base of edit distance, palindromic subsequence, shortest common supersequence and many diff tools.

LCS: state and transition

  • State: dp[i][j] = length of the LCS of a[0..i) and b[0..j).
  • Transition: if a[i-1] == b[j-1], that character is in the LCS: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. Otherwise one of the two characters is not used: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
  • Base cases: dp[0][j] = dp[i][0] = 0 (an empty string has no common subsequence). A new int[m+1][n+1] gives this for free.
  • Order: row by row, left to right (each cell reads up, left and up-left).
  • Answer: dp[m][n].
public static int lcsLength(String a, String b) {
    int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;
            } else {
                dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];                           // O(m*n) time and space
}

Reconstructing the string

Start at dp[m][n] and walk back. If the characters match, that character belongs to the LCS: record it and move diagonally. Otherwise move toward the neighbour with the larger value (up or left). The characters come out in reverse, so reverse them at the end.

public static String lcsString(String a, String b, int[][] dp) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    int i = a.length(), j = b.length();
    while (i > 0 && j > 0) {
        if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
            sb.append(a.charAt(i - 1));        // part of the LCS
            i--; j--;
        } else if (dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]) {
            i--;                               // the value came from above
        } else {
            j--;                               // the value came from the left
        }
    }
    return sb.reverse().toString();
}

Several different LCS strings can exist with the same length; this code returns one of them. Reconstruction needs the full table, so the space-saving version (two rows) gives only the length.

Space optimisation

Only the previous row is needed, so keep two arrays of size n+1 and swap them. Time stays O(m·n), space drops to O(n). Pick the shorter string as the column dimension.

Longest common substring

Here the characters must be contiguous, so a mismatch breaks the run. Redefine the state: dp[i][j] = length of the common substring that ends exactly at a[i-1] and b[j-1]. If they match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; if not, dp[i][j] = 0. The answer is the maximum anywhere in the table, not the last cell.

public static int longestCommonSubstring(String a, String b) {
    int m = a.length(), n = b.length(), best = 0;
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;
                best = Math.max(best, dp[i][j]);   // track the max cell
            }                                      // else stays 0: run is broken
        }
    }
    return best;                               // O(m*n) time; O(n) with one rolling row
}
SubsequenceSubstring
Contiguous?NoYes
On mismatchmax(up, left)reset to 0
Answerdp[m][n]max over all cells

Problems that are LCS in disguise

  • Shortest common supersequence length = m + n - LCS.
  • Minimum deletions/insertions to turn a into b: deletions m - LCS, insertions n - LCS (this is "delete operation for two strings").
  • Longest palindromic subsequence = LCS of a string and its reverse (see the palindromes article).
  • Uncrossed lines: the same as LCS on two integer arrays.

Off-by-one with the padded table

With a table of size (m+1) × (n+1), row i stands for the first i characters, so the character is a.charAt(i - 1). Writing a.charAt(i) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on the last row.

Why the recurrence is correct

Look only at the last characters of the two prefixes. If they are equal, some best common subsequence can always use them as its final pair: matching them costs nothing, and it leaves the best problem for the shorter prefixes, so the answer is one more than the diagonal cell. If they differ, they cannot both be the last character of the common subsequence, so at least one of them is unused. Dropping the last character of a gives dp[i-1][j]; dropping the last character of b gives dp[i][j-1]; the answer is the larger. Because both cases only look at smaller prefixes, filling the table row by row is a valid order.

Recognise LCS by these signs: two sequences, the words "common", "align", "delete or insert to make equal", and elements that must keep their order but may skip. When the question is about one sequence (palindrome, increasing), try an interval or single-index DP instead.

Dry run: walking back for "abcde" and "ace"

Start at (i, j) = (5, 3), the bottom-right cell with value 3.

  1. a[4] = 'e' equals b[2] = 'e': record e, move to (4, 2).
  2. 'd' versus 'c' differ. Compare dp[3][2] = 2 (above) with dp[4][1] = 1 (left): above is not smaller, so move up to (3, 2).
  3. 'c' equals 'c': record c, move to (2, 1).
  4. 'b' versus 'a' differ. dp[1][1] = 1 is at least dp[2][0] = 0: move up to (1, 1).
  5. 'a' equals 'a': record a, move to (0, 0) and stop.

The recorded characters are e, c, a; reversed, they give ace.

The same idea top-down

If the table order feels hard, write the recursion first: f(i, j) is the LCS of the first i and j characters. Cache the results in an int[m+1][n+1] filled with −1.

static int f(String a, String b, int i, int j, int[][] memo) {
    if (i == 0 || j == 0) return 0;                       // an empty prefix
    if (memo[i][j] != -1) return memo[i][j];
    int res;
    if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
        res = 1 + f(a, b, i - 1, j - 1, memo);
    } else {
        res = Math.max(f(a, b, i - 1, j, memo), f(a, b, i, j - 1, memo));
    }
    return memo[i][j] = res;                              // recursion depth up to m + n
}

For strings of length 1,000 the depth reaches about 2,000 frames, which Java's default stack usually handles; for much longer strings prefer the bottom-up table.

Two-row version in code

public static int lcsTwoRows(String a, String b) {
    if (b.length() > a.length()) { String t = a; a = b; b = t; }   // columns = shorter string
    int n = b.length();
    int[] prev = new int[n + 1], cur = new int[n + 1];
    for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) cur[j] = prev[j - 1] + 1;
            else cur[j] = Math.max(prev[j], cur[j - 1]);
        }
        int[] t = prev; prev = cur; cur = t;            // the finished row becomes "previous"
    }
    return prev[n];                                     // O(m*n) time, O(min(m, n)) space
}

If you need the string and cannot afford the full table, Hirschberg's algorithm recovers it in linear space by divide and conquer; it is a name worth knowing, but rarely coded.

One more classic: Delete Operation for Two Strings

Make two strings equal by deleting characters from either one; minimise the deletions. What remains must be a common subsequence, and the longest one keeps the most characters, so the answer is m + n - 2 * LCS. There is no new DP, only the formula.

public int minDistance(String a, String b) {
    int lcs = lcsLength(a, b);                 // from the code above
    return a.length() + b.length() - 2 * lcs;
}
// "sea" and "eat": LCS "ea" has length 2 -> 3 + 3 - 4 = 2 deletions

LCS and its neighbours

ProblemMismatch ruleAnswer
LCSmax(up, left)last cell
Longest common substring0max cell
Edit distance1 + min(three neighbours)last cell (next article)
Longest increasing subsequenceone sequencesee LIS; LCS with the sorted array also works

Edge cases

  • An empty string: row 0 and column 0 are zeros, so the answer is 0 with no special case.
  • Identical strings: the LCS is the string itself, and the table has the diagonal 1, 2, 3, ...
  • No common character: the table stays all zeros.
  • Memory: two strings of 5,000 characters need a 25-million-cell int table (about 100 MB). Use the two-row version when you only need the length.

Mistake: using the subsequence answer for a substring

Wrong: returns the last cell

// longest common substring of "abcdef" and "xabcy"
return dp[m][n];            // 0, because f and y differ and the run resets

Right: track the maximum while filling

best = Math.max(best, dp[i][j]);
return best;                // 3 ("abc")

Interview angle

State the recurrence in words ("if the last characters match, extend the diagonal; else drop one"), fill a small table on the whiteboard, and offer reconstruction without being asked. Mention the rolling-row optimisation and that it loses the ability to rebuild the string.

Edit distance, distinct subsequences, wildcard and regex matching

Edit distance uses the same two-prefix table as LCS but each cell takes the cheapest of insert, delete and replace; distinct subsequences and wildcard matching are variations on the same table.

Edit Distance (LeetCode 72)

Problem: the minimum number of operations (insert, delete, replace one character) to turn word1 into word2. This is the Levenshtein distance, used in spell checkers and fuzzy search.

  • State: dp[i][j] = edits to turn the first i characters of word1 into the first j of word2.
  • Transition: if the last characters are equal, no work: dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise 1 + min(dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — replace, delete from word1, or insert into word1.
  • Base cases: dp[i][0] = i (delete all), dp[0][j] = j (insert all).
  • Answer: dp[m][n].
public int minDistance(String w1, String w2) {
    int m = w1.length(), n = w2.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;     // delete i characters
    for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;     // insert j characters
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (w1.charAt(i - 1) == w2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1];
            } else {
                dp[i][j] = 1 + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j - 1],        // replace
                                Math.min(dp[i - 1][j],           // delete
                                         dp[i][j - 1]));         // insert
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];                           // O(m*n) time; O(n) with two rows
}

Reading the three neighbours

Diagonal = replace (or match), up = delete a character of word1, left = insert a character. Walking back from the corner and noting which neighbour gave the minimum prints the actual edit script.

Distinct Subsequences (LeetCode 115, brief)

Count how many subsequences of s equal t. State: dp[i][j] = number of ways the first i characters of s contain the first j of t. Base: dp[i][0] = 1 (the empty target is made one way). If s[i-1] == t[j-1] you can use it or skip it: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + dp[i-1][j]; otherwise only skip: dp[i-1][j].

public int numDistinct(String s, String t) {
    int n = t.length();
    long[] dp = new long[n + 1];               // dp[j] for the current prefix of s
    dp[0] = 1;                                 // empty t: exactly one way
    for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++) {
        for (int j = n; j >= 1; j--) {         // reverse: dp[j-1] must still be the old row
            if (s.charAt(i - 1) == t.charAt(j - 1)) {
                dp[j] += dp[j - 1];
            }
        }
    }
    return (int) dp[n];                        // the problem guarantees the answer fits in int
}

For s = "rabbbit", t = "rabbit" the answer is 3 (choose which of the three b's to skip). Notice the reverse loop, the same rule as 0/1 knapsack. Complexity: O(m·n) time, O(n) space. Intermediate counts can exceed int, hence long.

Wildcard Matching (LeetCode 44, brief)

Pattern p may contain ? (any one character) and * (any sequence, including empty). State: dp[i][j] = does s[0..i) match p[0..j).

  • If p[j-1] is ? or equals s[i-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1].
  • If p[j-1] is *: it matches empty (dp[i][j-1]) or swallows one more character (dp[i-1][j]).
  • Base: dp[0][0] = true; dp[0][j] is true only while the pattern so far is all stars.
public boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
    int m = s.length(), n = p.length();
    boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1];
    dp[0][0] = true;
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
        if (p.charAt(j - 1) == '*') dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 1];
    }
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            char pc = p.charAt(j - 1);
            if (pc == '*') {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i][j - 1] || dp[i - 1][j];
            } else if (pc == '?' || pc == s.charAt(i - 1)) {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1];
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];                           // O(m*n) time and space
}

Regular Expression Matching (LeetCode 10, idea)

Here . matches any one character and * means "zero or more of the previous element", so a star always pairs with the character before it. Same table, different star rule: when p[j-1] == '*', either use the star zero times (dp[i][j-2]) or, if s[i-1] matches p[j-2] (equal or .), use it once more (dp[i-1][j]). The first row needs care: a*b* can match the empty string, so dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-2] when p[j-1] is a star.

Wildcard star vs regex star

In wildcard matching * stands alone and matches any sequence. In regex * modifies the previous character. Mixing the two rules up is the most common bug in these problems.

Why the three neighbours are the three operations

Think of turning the first i characters of word1 into the first j characters of word2. Look at the last characters.

  • Equal: keep both, no cost. The problem becomes (i−1, j−1).
  • Replace the last character of word1 by the last character of word2: one operation, then solve (i−1, j−1).
  • Delete the last character of word1: one operation, then solve (i−1, j): now the shorter word1 must still become the whole word2 prefix.
  • Insert the last character of word2 at the end of word1: one operation, and that new character now matches, so solve (i, j−1).

Take the cheapest option. When the characters are equal you may skip the other options: matching is never worse than any edit, so the diagonal is safe. The base cases are intuitive: turning an empty string into j characters needs j inserts, and turning i characters into an empty string needs i deletes.

Dry run: a few cells of the "horse" to "ros" table

CellCharactersComputationValue
(1,1)h vs r1 + min(dp[0][0], dp[0][1], dp[1][0]) = 1 + min(0, 1, 1)1
(2,2)o vs oequal, so dp[1][1]1
(3,3)r vs s1 + min(dp[2][2], dp[2][3], dp[3][2]) = 1 + min(1, 2, 2)2
(5,3)e vs s1 + min(dp[4][2], dp[4][3], dp[5][2]) = 1 + min(3, 2, 4)3

The corner (5, 3) is the answer, 3.

Space optimisation: one row and a saved diagonal

Each cell needs its up, left and up-left neighbours. With one array, dp[j] before the update is the "up" value, dp[j-1] is the "left" value (already updated), and the up-left value would be overwritten, so save it in a variable before you overwrite it.

public int minDistance1D(String a, String b) {
    int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
    for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[j] = j;              // row 0
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        int diag = dp[0];                                  // dp[i-1][0]
        dp[0] = i;                                         // dp[i][0]
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            int up = dp[j];                                // dp[i-1][j], before the overwrite
            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) dp[j] = diag;
            else dp[j] = 1 + Math.min(diag, Math.min(up, dp[j - 1]));
            diag = up;                                     // becomes dp[i-1][j-1] next time
        }
    }
    return dp[n];                                          // O(m*n) time, O(n) space
}

Printing the edit script

Walk back from the corner with the full table. At each cell, equal characters mean "keep" (move diagonally); otherwise see which neighbour plus one produced the value. The operations come out in reverse order.

int i = m, j = n;
while (i > 0 || j > 0) {
    if (i > 0 && j > 0 && w1.charAt(i - 1) == w2.charAt(j - 1)) {
        i--; j--;                                           // keep
    } else if (i > 0 && j > 0 && dp[i][j] == dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1) {
        System.out.println("replace " + w1.charAt(i - 1) + " with " + w2.charAt(j - 1));
        i--; j--;
    } else if (i > 0 && dp[i][j] == dp[i - 1][j] + 1) {
        System.out.println("delete " + w1.charAt(i - 1));
        i--;
    } else {
        System.out.println("insert " + w2.charAt(j - 1));
        j--;
    }
}

Regular expression matching in code

The idea above becomes the following. The star is read together with the character before it, so when p[j-1] is a star the previous pattern character is p[j-2]. (LeetCode guarantees that a star never starts the pattern, so j - 2 is valid.)

public boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
    int m = s.length(), n = p.length();
    boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1];
    dp[0][0] = true;
    for (int j = 2; j <= n; j++) {                        // patterns like a*b* match ""
        if (p.charAt(j - 1) == '*') dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 2];
    }
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            char pc = p.charAt(j - 1);
            if (pc == '*') {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i][j - 2];                   // use the star zero times
                char prev = p.charAt(j - 2);
                if (prev == '.' || prev == s.charAt(i - 1)) {
                    dp[i][j] |= dp[i - 1][j];              // or one more copy
                }
            } else if (pc == '.' || pc == s.charAt(i - 1)) {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1];
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];                                       // O(m*n) time and space
}

Check with s = "aab" and p = "c*a*b": the first row becomes true at the stars (c* and then c*a* both match the empty string), the stars absorb the two a's, and b matches b. The result is true.

The four problems in one table

ProblemStateBaseMatch rule
Edit distancemin editsdp[i][0] = i, dp[0][j] = jequal: diagonal; else 1 + min of three
Distinct subsequencesnumber of waysdp[i][0] = 1equal: diagonal + up; else up
Wildcard matchingbooleandp[0][0] = true*: left or up
Regex matchingbooleanstars can match empty*: two columns back, or up

Edge cases

  • One string empty: the answer is the length of the other (all inserts or all deletes). The base cases give it without a special branch.
  • Equal strings: the answer is 0; the diagonal copies zeros.
  • Pattern of only stars in wildcard matching matches every string, including the empty one.
  • Distinct subsequences when t is longer than s: the answer is 0.

Mistake: forgetting the base row and column

Wrong: first row and column left at 0

int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
// "" to "abc" would report 0 edits

Right: fill them first

for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;
for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;

Interview angle

Edit distance is asked often. Explain why the three neighbours mean replace, delete and insert, give the base cases, and mention O(n) space. Distinct subsequences and the matching problems usually appear as "hard" follow-ups; naming the state and the star rule is already most of the answer.

Palindromic subsequence, longest palindromic substring, counting substrings

A substring palindrome grows from a centre, so expanding around each of the 2n-1 centres is O(n²) with O(1) space; a palindromic subsequence is an LCS with the reversed string or a DP over the two ends of an interval.

"Palindrome" problems split into two families. For substrings (contiguous), the palindrome property is local: s[i..j] is a palindrome if s[i] == s[j] and s[i+1..j-1] is a palindrome. For subsequences (skipping allowed), the table runs over the two ends of an interval.

Longest Palindromic Substring: expand around the centre

Every palindrome has a centre: one character (odd length) or the gap between two characters (even length). Try all 2n - 1 centres and expand outwards while both ends match.

public String longestPalindrome(String s) {
    int start = 0, maxLen = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < s.length(); c++) {
        int odd = expand(s, c, c);             // centre on one character
        int even = expand(s, c, c + 1);        // centre between two characters
        int len = Math.max(odd, even);
        if (len > maxLen) {
            maxLen = len;
            start = c - (len - 1) / 2;         // works for both odd and even lengths
        }
    }
    return s.substring(start, start + maxLen);
}

private int expand(String s, int left, int right) {
    while (left >= 0 && right < s.length() && s.charAt(left) == s.charAt(right)) {
        left--;
        right++;
    }
    return right - left - 1;                   // length after the last successful step
}

Complexity: O(n²) time (each expansion is up to O(n), there are 2n-1 centres), O(1) space. For "babad" it returns "bab" ("aba" is also valid). Manacher's algorithm does it in O(n), but it is rarely required.

The DP alternative for substrings

State: isPal[i][j] = is s[i..j] a palindrome. Transition: s[i] == s[j] && (j - i < 3 || isPal[i+1][j-1]) (lengths 1 to 3 need no inner check). The order matters: row i depends on row i+1, so loop i from n-1 down to 0 and j from i up.

boolean[][] isPal = new boolean[n][n];
for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {              // i goes down: row i+1 is already done
    for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
        isPal[i][j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)
                && (j - i < 3 || isPal[i + 1][j - 1]);
    }
}
// isPal[i][j] now answers "is s[i..j] a palindrome?" in O(1). Time and space O(n^2).

Use the table when you need many palindrome queries (for example Palindrome Partitioning); use expand-around-centre when you need one answer, because it uses O(1) space.

Palindromic Substrings: count them (LeetCode 647)

Count every substring that is a palindrome, counting equal substrings at different positions separately. With the expand idea, each successful step of the loop is one more palindrome, so count them directly.

public int countSubstrings(String s) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < s.length(); c++) {
        count += countAround(s, c, c);         // odd-length palindromes
        count += countAround(s, c, c + 1);     // even-length palindromes
    }
    return count;
}

private int countAround(String s, int l, int r) {
    int found = 0;
    while (l >= 0 && r < s.length() && s.charAt(l) == s.charAt(r)) {
        found++;                               // s[l..r] is a palindrome: count it
        l--;
        r++;
    }
    return found;
}

For "aaa" the answer is 6 (three of length 1, two of length 2, one of length 3). Complexity: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

Longest Palindromic Subsequence (LeetCode 516)

Now characters may be skipped. Two equivalent solutions:

  1. LCS with the reverse. A palindrome reads the same both ways, so the longest palindromic subsequence of s is the LCS of s and reverse(s). Reuse the LCS code.
  2. Interval DP. dp[i][j] = length of the longest palindromic subsequence inside s[i..j]. If s[i] == s[j], both ends join: 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]. Otherwise drop one end: max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base: dp[i][i] = 1.
public int longestPalindromeSubseq(String s) {
    int n = s.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[n][n];
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        dp[i][i] = 1;                          // a single character
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)) {
                dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i + 1][j - 1];   // when j = i+1 this reads dp[i+1][i] = 0
            } else {
                dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[0][n - 1];                       // O(n^2) time and space
}

For "bbbab" the answer is 4 ("bbbb"). A related result: the minimum insertions to make a string a palindrome is n - longestPalindromeSubseq.

ProblemMethodTimeSpace
Longest palindromic substringExpand around centreO(n²)O(1)
Count palindromic substringsExpand around centreO(n²)O(1)
Many palindrome queriesisPal[i][j] tableO(n²)O(n²)
Longest palindromic subsequenceInterval DP or LCS with reverseO(n²)O(n²)

Forgetting the even-length centres

Expanding only from (c, c) misses "abba" and "aa". Always run both (c, c) and (c, c + 1).

Iteration order in interval DP

The cell dp[i][j] reads dp[i+1][...], so i must go from n-1 down to 0. A normal top-down row loop reads cells that are still zero and gives wrong answers without any exception.

How to recognise and choose

Ask two questions. First: contiguous or not? A substring palindrome is checked from the inside out, so expanding from a centre fits. A subsequence palindrome uses both ends of an interval, so use a table with the interval [i, j] as the state. Second: one answer or many queries? For one answer, the O(1)-space expansion is enough. When a later step asks "is s[i..j] a palindrome?" many times (Palindrome Partitioning), build the boolean table once.

Dry run of expand-around-centre

"babad". At centre c = 1 (a), the odd expansion starts with left = right = 1. The characters match, so left = 0 and right = 2: b equals b, so left = −1 and right = 3, and the loop stops because left is out of range. The length is right - left - 1 = 3 - (-1) - 1 = 3. The start is c - (len - 1) / 2 = 1 - 1 = 0, so the substring is "bab".

"cbbd". At c = 1 the even expansion starts with (1, 2): b equals b, so left = 0, right = 3: c versus d differ, stop. The length is 3 - 0 - 1 = 2 and the start is 1 - (2 - 1) / 2 = 1 - 0 = 1 (integer division), so the substring is "bb". The same start formula works for odd and even lengths.

Palindrome Partitioning II: minimum cuts

Cut a string so that every piece is a palindrome and use as few cuts as possible. State: cuts[j] = fewest cuts for s[0..j]. If s[i..j] is a palindrome, the prefix s[0..i-1] plus this last piece costs cuts[i-1] + 1 (or 0 when the whole prefix is one palindrome). The palindrome table is built in the same loops.

public int minCut(String s) {
    int n = s.length();
    boolean[][] pal = new boolean[n][n];
    int[] cuts = new int[n];                       // cuts[j] = min cuts for s[0..j]
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        cuts[j] = j;                               // worst case: a cut before every character
        for (int i = 0; i <= j; i++) {
            if (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j) && (j - i < 2 || pal[i + 1][j - 1])) {
                pal[i][j] = true;
                cuts[j] = (i == 0) ? 0 : Math.min(cuts[j], cuts[i - 1] + 1);
            }
        }
    }
    return cuts[n - 1];                            // O(n^2) time and space
}
// "aab": cuts = [0, 0, 1] -> one cut gives "aa" | "b"

The version that lists all partitions (Palindrome Partitioning) uses backtracking from the backtracking template, with the table giving the palindrome check in O(1).

Valid Palindrome II: one deletion allowed

Two pointers from the ends move inward. At the first mismatch you may delete either the left or the right character and check that the rest is a palindrome. This is O(n) and needs no table.

static boolean validPalindrome(String s) {
    int l = 0, r = s.length() - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        if (s.charAt(l) != s.charAt(r)) {
            return isPal(s, l + 1, r) || isPal(s, l, r - 1);   // skip one side
        }
        l++; r--;
    }
    return true;
}

static boolean isPal(String s, int l, int r) {
    while (l < r) {
        if (s.charAt(l++) != s.charAt(r--)) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Beyond O(n²): Manacher's algorithm

Manacher's algorithm finds the longest palindromic substring in O(n) time by reusing the palindrome radii already found inside a bigger palindrome (mirror positions). It is a known result and worth naming in an interview when asked "can you do better than O(n²)?". Coding it is rarely expected. The expand-around-centre solution is the answer to give and write.

Palindromes and LCS: what carries over and what does not

The longest palindromic subsequence equals the LCS of a string and its reverse. This does not carry over to substrings. The longest common substring of s and its reverse can be a string that is not a palindrome, because it may come from two different places in s. For example, s = "aacabdkacaa" has the reverse "aacakdbacaa", and the common substring "aaca" has length 4, but the longest palindromic substring of s has length 3 ("aca"). A fix exists (check that the indices line up), but expansion is simpler.

Edge cases

  • Empty string: longestPalindrome("") returns an empty string; the loop does not run. Check the problem for whether it can happen.
  • One character: the answer is that character, and countSubstrings is 1.
  • All characters equal ("aaaa"): the whole string is a palindrome, and the count is n(n+1)/2. This is the worst case for expansion (O(n²) real work).
  • Several answers of the same length: the code keeps the first found because of the strict len > maxLen. State which one you return if asked.
  • Case and non-letters: "Valid Palindrome" (125) filters to letters and digits and ignores case; the substring problems here do not.

Mistake: the base case of the interval table

Wrong: j starts at i, so dp[i][i] is overwritten

for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)
    for (int j = i; j < n; j++)
        dp[i][j] = (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)) ? 2 + dp[i + 1][j - 1]
                 : Math.max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);   // i==j gives 2, reads i+1

Right: set dp[i][i] = 1, then start j at i + 1

for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    dp[i][i] = 1;
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) { /* transition as before */ }
}

Interview angle

Longest Palindromic Substring is a top-ten question. Give the O(n²), O(1)-space expansion first and say why it has 2n − 1 centres. Mention the table version for repeated queries and Manacher as the O(n) option. For subsequences, explain the two ways (LCS with the reverse, or the interval DP) and the iteration order (i going down). A follow-up like "minimum insertions to make a palindrome" is just n - longestPalindromeSubseq.

Other DP shapes to recognise: stocks, intervals, trees, bitmasks

Four shapes appear often enough to know by sight: DP with a small set of states (stocks), interval DP (try the last or first action in a range), DP on trees (return a pair from DFS), and bitmask DP (a set of up to about 20 items as an integer).

You will not meet these every day, but a good interview answer starts with naming the shape. This article shows one compact example each. The aim is recognition and the core recurrence, not every variant.

1. DP with states: stock buy and sell

Sometimes the position in the array is not enough; you also need a small piece of extra information, such as "do I hold a share right now". Keep one variable per state and update them together. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown (after selling you must wait one day) has three states:

  • hold = best profit if I own a share at the end of today.
  • sold = best profit if I sold today.
  • rest = best profit if I own nothing and did not sell today.
public int maxProfit(int[] prices) {
    int hold = Integer.MIN_VALUE / 2;          // cannot own a share before buying
    int sold = 0, rest = 0;
    for (int p : prices) {
        int prevSold = sold;
        sold = hold + p;                       // sell the share I held
        hold = Math.max(hold, rest - p);       // keep holding, or buy (only from rest)
        rest = Math.max(rest, prevSold);       // do nothing, or finish the cooldown
    }
    return Math.max(sold, rest);               // never end holding a share
}

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. The family also includes "at most k transactions" (add a transaction-count dimension: dp[k][hold?]) and "with a fee". The method is always: list the states, write how each can be reached from yesterday's states.

2. Interval DP: burst balloons, matrix chain

State is a range dp[l][r]; the transition tries every split point k inside the range; and you fill ranges by increasing length. The key idea in Burst Balloons is to choose the last balloon burst in a range, because then its neighbours are fixed (the range borders), which makes the two halves independent.

public int maxCoins(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] a = new int[n + 2];                  // pad both ends with 1
    a[0] = 1; a[n + 1] = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i + 1] = nums[i];
    int[][] dp = new int[n + 2][n + 2];        // dp[l][r]: best for balloons strictly between l and r
    for (int len = 2; len <= n + 1; len++) {
        for (int l = 0; l + len <= n + 1; l++) {
            int r = l + len;
            for (int k = l + 1; k < r; k++) {  // k is the LAST balloon burst between l and r
                dp[l][r] = Math.max(dp[l][r],
                        dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l] * a[k] * a[r]);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[0][n + 1];                       // O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space
}

Other interval DPs: Matrix Chain Multiplication (dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost), minimum cost to cut a stick, palindrome partitioning II, and the longest palindromic subsequence from the previous article. Typical complexity is O(n³).

3. DP on trees: House Robber III

The state belongs to a tree node. Run a post-order DFS and let each call return a small array of answers for its subtree. In House Robber III you cannot rob a parent and its child; each node returns {best if robbed, best if not robbed}.

public int rob(TreeNode root) {
    int[] r = dfs(root);
    return Math.max(r[0], r[1]);
}

// returns {robThisNode, skipThisNode}
private int[] dfs(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return new int[]{0, 0};
    int[] left = dfs(node.left);
    int[] right = dfs(node.right);
    int rob = node.val + left[1] + right[1];                       // children must be skipped
    int skip = Math.max(left[0], left[1]) + Math.max(right[0], right[1]);
    return new int[]{rob, skip};               // O(n) time, O(h) recursion space
}

Same shape: diameter of a binary tree, maximum path sum, and binary tree cameras (three states per node). Remember that TreeNode is the LeetCode class; define it yourself when running locally.

4. Bitmask DP (idea)

When you must remember which of up to about 20 items have been used, encode the set as an int mask: bit i set means item i is used. The state is dp[mask][last].
