Choosing between two close patterns

  • Sliding window vs prefix sum: all numbers positive and you want the shortest/longest window: sliding window. Negatives present, or "sum equals k": prefix sum with a HashMap.
  • BFS vs Dijkstra: all edges cost the same: BFS. Different non-negative weights: Dijkstra.
  • Greedy vs DP: if a choice can be undone later by a better combination (coin change with odd coins), you need DP. If sorting plus a local rule is provably safe (activity selection), greedy works.
  • Backtracking vs DP: asked for all solutions: backtracking. Asked for the best value or the count: DP, if subproblems repeat.
  • DSU vs DFS for components: a static graph: either. Edges arriving over time ("after each union"): DSU.

When no clue fits

Write the brute force, then ask "what work is repeated?". Repeated lookups: hash map. Repeated range sums: prefix sums. Repeated subproblems: DP. Repeated scans over a sorted order: two pointers or binary search. Repeated min/max of a moving set: heap or deque.

Interview angle

Say the clue aloud: "the array is sorted and I need a pair, so two pointers or binary search". Naming the clue shows pattern skill, which interviewers value more than a lucky final answer.

Write from memory (1): binary search, lower bound, merge sort, partition

Four short routines appear inside dozens of problems; learn each one until you can type it without thinking, with the loop bounds and the update rules correct.

A template is not for copy-pasting; it is a small program you can write in two minutes while explaining it. Bugs in these routines are almost always off-by-one errors in the bounds, so each template below states its invariant (the sentence that is true at every loop step). If you remember the invariant, the code follows.

Binary search (exact match)

Invariant: if the target exists, it is inside [lo, hi] (both ends included).

static int binarySearch(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;          // never (lo + hi) / 2: it can overflow
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;                                 // O(log n) time, O(1) space
}

Lower bound and upper bound

Lower bound = the first index with a[i] >= target. Upper bound = the first index with a[i] > target. Both return n if no such index exists. Invariant: the answer is inside [lo, hi], where hi = n is allowed, and the loop uses lo < hi. This one routine solves "first occurrence", "last occurrence" (upper bound minus 1), "count of x" (upper minus lower), "insert position" and, with a predicate, "binary search on the answer".

static int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {    // first i with a[i] >= target
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length;                  // hi = n: "not found" is a valid answer
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;      // mid is too small: answer is to the right
        else hi = mid;                          // mid might be the answer: keep it
    }
    return lo;
}

static int upperBound(int[] a, int target) {    // first i with a[i] > target
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] <= target) lo = mid + 1;    // the only change: <= instead of <
        else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}
// count of target = upperBound(a, t) - lowerBound(a, t)
// smallest x in [lo, hi] for which feasible(x) is true (feasible is false...true)
static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, java.util.function.IntPredicate feasible) {
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (feasible.test(mid)) hi = mid;      // mid works: try smaller
        else lo = mid + 1;                     // mid fails: need bigger
    }
    return lo;                                 // assumes the answer exists in [lo, hi]
}

Merge sort

Split in half, sort each half, merge two sorted halves. Invariant: after sort(lo, hi), the range [lo, hi) is sorted. Use <= when taking from the left half to keep the sort stable.

static void mergeSort(int[] a) {
    mergeSort(a, new int[a.length], 0, a.length);
}

private static void mergeSort(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {   // sorts [lo, hi)
    if (hi - lo < 2) return;                   // 0 or 1 element is already sorted
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, tmp, lo, mid);
    mergeSort(a, tmp, mid, hi);
    int i = lo, j = mid, k = lo;
    while (i < mid && j < hi) {
        tmp[k++] = (a[i] <= a[j]) ? a[i++] : a[j++];   // <= keeps equal items in order
    }
    while (i < mid) tmp[k++] = a[i++];
    while (j < hi)  tmp[k++] = a[j++];
    System.arraycopy(tmp, lo, a, lo, hi - lo);
}
// O(n log n) time in every case, O(n) extra space, stable

The same split-and-merge skeleton counts inversions (count pairs while merging) and solves "count of smaller numbers after self" and "reverse pairs".

Quick sort partition and quickselect

Lomuto partition: pick the last element as pivot; i marks the end of the "smaller than pivot" zone. Invariant: a[lo..i-1] < pivot, a[i..j-1] >= pivot.

static void quickSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {         // sorts [lo, hi] inclusive
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
    quickSort(a, lo, p - 1);
    quickSort(a, p + 1, hi);
}

static int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    int r = lo + (int) (Math.random() * (hi - lo + 1));  // random pivot avoids O(n^2) on sorted input
    swap(a, r, hi);
    int pivot = a[hi], i = lo;
    for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
        if (a[j] < pivot) swap(a, i++, j);               // grow the "smaller" zone
    }
    swap(a, i, hi);                                      // pivot goes to its final place
    return i;
}

static void swap(int[] a, int x, int y) { int t = a[x]; a[x] = a[y]; a[y] = t; }

// Quickselect: k-th smallest (0-based k) in average O(n)
static int quickSelect(int[] a, int k) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
        if (p == k) return a[p];
        if (p < k) lo = p + 1; else hi = p - 1;
    }
    return -1;                                 // not reached when 0 <= k < n
}

Complexity: quick sort is O(n log n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case (made unlikely by a random pivot), O(log n) expected stack, not stable. Quickselect is O(n) average, O(n²) worst. With many equal values Lomuto degrades; the three-way partition (Dutch national flag) fixes that.

Bugs I see most often

  • Mixing the two loop styles: lo <= hi with hi = mid never ends.
  • Computing (lo + hi) / 2 for large arrays: overflow gives a negative index.
  • Using lower bound's hi = n - 1 and then missing the "greater than all" answer.
  • Merge sort that allocates a new array in every call (correct but slow; pass one temp array).

Practice drill

On a blank sheet, write all four routines and test each with an empty array, one element, all equal, and the target smaller than everything and larger than everything.

Write from memory (2): BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, union-find, topological sort, a DP

These six templates cover most graph and DP problems; each is about ten to twenty lines, and the details to remember are the visited marking, the queue discipline and the loop order.

All graph templates use an adjacency list List<List<Integer>> g (or List<int[]> for weighted edges) with nodes numbered 0..n-1. Imports: java.util.*.

BFS (shortest path in an unweighted graph)

Mark a node when you add it to the queue, not when you remove it; otherwise a node can be queued many times.

static int[] bfs(List<List<Integer>> g, int src) {
    int[] dist = new int[g.size()];
    Arrays.fill(dist, -1);                     // -1 = not visited
    Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    dist[src] = 0;
    q.add(src);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll();
        for (int v : g.get(u)) {
            if (dist[v] == -1) {               // first time we see v: this is the shortest way
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
                q.add(v);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;                               // O(V + E)
}
// Grid version: replace g.get(u) by the 4 neighbours (r+dr[k], c+dc[k]) inside the bounds.

DFS (recursive and iterative)

static void dfs(List<List<Integer>> g, int u, boolean[] seen) {
    seen[u] = true;
    for (int v : g.get(u)) {
        if (!seen[v]) dfs(g, v, seen);
    }
}

static void dfsIterative(List<List<Integer>> g, int src) {
    boolean[] seen = new boolean[g.size()];
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(src);
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        int u = stack.pop();
        if (seen[u]) continue;                 // a node can be pushed twice; skip repeats
        seen[u] = true;
        for (int v : g.get(u)) {
            if (!seen[v]) stack.push(v);
        }
    }
}
// O(V + E). Use the iterative form when the depth can reach about 10^5.

Dijkstra

Edges are int[]{to, weight} with non-negative weights. The priority queue holds {node, distance}; when a stale entry is polled (its distance is worse than the best known), skip it. This is called lazy deletion.

static long[] dijkstra(List<List<int[]>> g, int src) {
    long[] dist = new long[g.size()];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Long.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[src] = 0;
    PriorityQueue<long[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Long.compare(x[1], y[1]));
    pq.add(new long[]{src, 0});
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        long[] top = pq.poll();
        int u = (int) top[0];
        if (top[1] > dist[u]) continue;        // stale entry: a shorter path was already found
        for (int[] e : g.get(u)) {
            int v = e[0];
            long nd = dist[u] + e[1];
            if (nd < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = nd;
                pq.add(new long[]{v, nd});
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;                               // O((V + E) log V); unreachable stays Long.MAX_VALUE
}

The comparator uses Long.compare, not subtraction, to avoid overflow.

Union-find (DSU)

Path compression plus union by size gives almost constant time per operation (inverse Ackermann). union returns false when the two nodes are already connected, which is exactly the "cycle detected" signal.

static class UnionFind {
    int[] parent, size;
    int components;

    UnionFind(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        size = new int[n];
        components = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }
    }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];     // path halving: flatten as we climb
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    boolean union(int a, int b) {
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;            // already in the same set
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
        parent[rb] = ra;                       // attach the smaller tree under the larger
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        components--;
        return true;
    }
}

Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm)

Count incoming edges (in-degree). Start with all nodes of in-degree 0; removing a node lowers its neighbours' in-degree. If fewer than n nodes come out, the graph has a cycle.

static int[] topoSort(int n, List<List<Integer>> g) {
    int[] indeg = new int[n];
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++) for (int v : g.get(u)) indeg[v]++;
    Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.add(i);
    int[] order = new int[n];
    int count = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll();
        order[count++] = u;
        for (int v : g.get(u)) {
            if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.add(v);     // all prerequisites of v are done
        }
    }
    return count == n ? order : new int[0];    // empty array means a cycle; O(V + E)
}

A basic DP (coin change, minimum coins)

One DP you can write blind is enough to start any other: state, base, transition, order, answer.

static int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
    int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];            // dp[a] = fewest coins to make amount a
    Arrays.fill(dp, amount + 1);               // amount + 1 acts as infinity (no overflow when +1)
    dp[0] = 0;                                 // zero coins make amount 0
    for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++) {
        for (int c : coins) {
            if (c <= a) dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
        }
    }
    return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];   // O(amount * coins) time, O(amount) space
}

A self-test

  1. Close this page. On paper, write the ten templates of the two articles: binary search, lower bound, merge sort, partition, BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, union-find, topological sort, coin change.
  2. Time yourself; the target is under 30 minutes for all ten.
  3. Type each into an editor and run one tiny test. Fix, then mark the ones you missed in your log for the 3-day review.

Template bugs to watch

  • BFS: marking visited when polling instead of when adding. It still gives answers, but the queue can grow to O(E) duplicates.
  • Dijkstra: using it with negative edges (wrong answers) or skipping the stale-entry check (slow).
  • Topological sort: forgetting the cycle check count == n.
  • Union-find: forgetting that find must be called on both inputs before comparing roots.

Interview angle

Interviewers often ask for one of these "from scratch" as a warm-up, and then ask you to adapt it (BFS with a state, Dijkstra with a stop limit). A clean template means all your time goes into the adaptation.

Interview technique: the first five minutes and the whole 45

A coding interview scores how you think as much as what you write: clarify, give the brute force, improve it, code cleanly, test with examples, and state the complexity, speaking throughout.

Many people who can solve a problem alone fail the interview because they go silent, jump into code, or never test. The interviewer cannot read your mind; they grade what they can hear and see. A fixed routine removes the panic, because you always know the next step.

The 45-minute shape

MinutesPhaseWhat you do
0-5UnderstandRepeat the problem, ask questions, work one example
5-12PlanBrute force, its complexity, then the better idea and why
12-30CodeWrite clean code, narrating the key lines
30-40TestDry run the example, then edge cases; fix bugs calmly
40-45Wrap upState time and space complexity; discuss improvements and questions

A script for the first five minutes

  1. Restate in your own words: "So we get an array of integers and must return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Right?"
  2. Ask clarifying questions (see below).
  3. Work a small example by hand and say what you see. This often reveals the pattern.
  4. Say the constraint-driven target: "With n up to 105 I need about O(n log n)."
  5. Offer the brute force first: "The simple approach checks all pairs in O(n²). It is correct but too slow. Let me find a better way."

Clarifying questions worth asking

  • Input size and value ranges (overflow? negatives? zero?).
  • Can the input be empty or null? Duplicates? Is it sorted?
  • What should I return for no answer: -1, empty list, exception?
  • Can I modify the input? Is extra memory allowed?
  • For strings: only lowercase letters, or Unicode? Case sensitive?
  • For graphs: directed or not, weighted, connected, can there be cycles or self-loops?

Brute force first, then optimise

Always state the brute force, even when you see the optimal solution at once. It proves you understand the problem, gives a fallback if you get stuck, and lets you point to the exact waste you remove ("this inner loop recomputes the same sum, so a prefix sum removes it"). Moving from O(n²) to O(n) through a named idea (hash map, two pointers, sort, heap) is the story interviewers want to hear.

Writing clean code without an IDE

  • Use descriptive names (left, right, minCost), not a, b, x1.
  • Write the function signature first, then the edge-case guard (if (nums == null || nums.length == 0) return 0;), then the main loop.
  • Split out a helper for a repeated step (isValid, expand) instead of one long method.
  • Keep to one style; do not rush with unreadable one-liners.
  • You cannot compile, so slow down on generics, imports and semicolons; say "I will import java.util" and move on.

Test like a reviewer

When the code is written, do not say "done". Walk through it with the example from the start, line by line, with real values in a small table of variables. Then run the edge cases: empty input, one element, all equal, duplicates, negatives, the maximum size, and a case where the answer does not exist. Finding your own bug is a strong positive; hiding it is not.

nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]   (Jump Game)
i=0  reach=0 -> reach = max(0, 0+2) = 2
i=1  reach=2 -> reach = max(2, 1+3) = 4
i=2  reach=4 -> reach = max(4, 2+1) = 4
...  reach >= last index (4)  =>  true

State the complexity clearly

End with: "Time O(n log n) because of the sort, space O(n) for the map." Name what n is when there are two inputs (m and n). Mention recursion stack space. If you can improve it, say how, even if you do not code it.

Handling hints

A hint is not a failure; interviewers give hints to see how you react. Listen, restate it ("so you suggest I think about sorting first"), and use it. Do not argue, and do not ignore it. Candidates who take a hint well and finish often score better than candidates who needed none but explained nothing.

When you are stuck

  1. Say so calmly: "I am thinking about whether this is a window or a DP problem."
  2. Return to a small example and solve it by hand; write the steps you take.
  3. Walk the clue table in your head: sorted? contiguous? all solutions? dependencies?
  4. Simplify: solve a smaller version (no duplicates, no negatives, k = 1).
  5. Fall back to the brute force and code it. A correct slow solution beats a half-written fast one.
  6. Ask for a hint after a few minutes of real effort, not after thirty seconds.

Behaviours that cost offers

  • Coding in silence for fifteen minutes.
  • Starting to code before agreeing on the approach.
  • Saying "it works" without a test.
  • Defensiveness when the interviewer points out a bug.

Practise out loud

Solve one problem a week while recording yourself or talking to a friend. The first recordings sound awkward; after six weeks the routine becomes automatic. Pair mock interviews on free platforms or with college friends are even better.

Online assessments and the Java gotchas that cost marks

An online assessment (OA) is a timed, silent test with hidden test cases: scan all questions first, secure the easy marks, watch the time, and avoid the Java traps (overflow, Integer comparison, concurrent modification, string concatenation in loops).

An OA is the first filter at most companies: a timed test on a platform (HackerRank, CodeSignal, HackerEarth and similar) with two to four coding problems, sometimes plus MCQs. No one watches you think, so only passing test cases counts. Time management is a skill by itself.

OA strategy

  1. Read all problems first (2 to 4 minutes). Rank them by how sure you are.
  2. Take the easiest first and finish it fully; points are usually per test case, so partial credit exists but a full solve is worth more per minute.
  3. Set a time box for each problem (for example, in a 60-minute test with two problems, plan about 20 minutes for the easy one and 35 for the hard one, and keep 5 as a buffer).
  4. Write the brute force when stuck. It often passes the small tests, which gives partial marks. Then try to optimise if time remains.
  5. Read the input format exactly: how many lines, spaces or newlines, what to print. Many wrong answers are format mistakes.
  6. Test with the sample, then your own edge cases before the last submit. Remember that hidden tests include the maximum size.
  7. Keep ten minutes at the end to re-read, not to start something new.

Fast input and output in Java

On platforms that read from standard input, Scanner is slow for 105 numbers or more. Use BufferedReader and StringTokenizer, and StringBuilder or PrintWriter for output.

import java.io.*;
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));
        int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine().trim());
        StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer(br.readLine());
        int[] a = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = Integer.parseInt(st.nextToken());
        long sum = 0;
        for (int x : a) sum += x;              // long accumulator: the sum may exceed int
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        out.append(sum).append('\n');
        System.out.print(out);                 // one print call, not one per line
    }
}

Java gotchas in interviews and OAs

1. Integer overflow

int holds up to 2,147,483,647. Sums, products and mid-point calculations can overflow silently. Use long for sums and products, and lo + (hi - lo) / 2 for the midpoint. Use Math.addExact or Math.multiplyExact if you want an ArithmeticException instead of a silent wrap. Also remember Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.

int a = 2_000_000_000;
long wrong = a + a;                            // int + int overflows BEFORE widening: -294967296
long right = (long) a + a;                     // cast first: 4000000000
int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
// big + 1 == Integer.MIN_VALUE   (no exception)
2. == on Integer (and other wrappers)

Java caches Integer objects for values from -128 to 127, so == works for small values and fails for larger ones. This bites when you compare map values or list elements.

Wrong: compares references

List<Integer> list = List.of(1000, 1000);
if (list.get(0) == list.get(1)) { /* false! */ }

Right: compares values

if (list.get(0).equals(list.get(1))) { /* true */ }
// or unbox: (int) list.get(0) == (int) list.get(1)

Likewise compare Strings with equals, never ==.

3. Modifying a collection while iterating

Removing from an ArrayList or HashMap inside a for-each loop throws ConcurrentModificationException (fail-fast iterators). Use an Iterator with it.remove(), removeIf, iterate over a copy, or collect items to remove and remove them after the loop.

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6));
nums.removeIf(x -> x % 2 == 0);                // safe: [1, 3, 5]
// for (int x : nums) if (x % 2 == 0) nums.remove((Integer) x);
// ...the for-each version above throws ConcurrentModificationException

Also remember list.remove(int index) versus list.remove(Object o): for a List<Integer>, list.remove(3) removes the element at index 3, not the value 3. Use list.remove(Integer.valueOf(3)) for the value.

4. String concatenation in loops

Strings are immutable, so s += c in a loop copies the string every time: O(n²) for n characters. Use StringBuilder (append, reverse, insert, setCharAt) and call toString() once.

5. Other traps
  • Arrays.sort on int[] with a comparator does not compile: use Integer[], or sort a list. For int[][] use Arrays.sort(a, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(x[0], y[0])), not subtraction (x[0] - y[0] can overflow).
  • Arrays.asList(int[]) gives a list with one element (the array). Use boxed types or streams.
  • PriorityQueue is a min-heap; for a max-heap pass Collections.reverseOrder(). Its iterator order is not sorted order.
  • Integer division and modulo: -7 / 2 == -3 and -7 % 2 == -1 in Java. Use Math.floorMod for a non-negative remainder.
  • char arithmetic: 'a' + 1 is an int; cast to (char) when appending.
  • Shallow copies: new ArrayList<>(path) when saving a backtracking path; adding path itself stores a reference that keeps changing.
  • Default values: new int[n] is all zeros; new boolean[n] all false; new Integer[n] all null (unboxing a null throws NullPointerException).
  • Deep recursion (about 104 to 105 frames) risks StackOverflowError; use an explicit stack.

Partial credit and plagiarism rules

Most platforms score by test cases, so a correct brute force still earns points. Many also run plagiarism and tab-switch checks; solve on your own and follow the stated rules.

Interview angle

These gotchas appear as short "what does this print" questions and as silent bugs in your solution. Mention overflow and null/empty input when you list edge cases.

Company-tagged preparation: service companies and product companies

Use company tags to find the style and difficulty of questions, not to memorise a list; service companies lean on arrays, strings and basics, product companies on mediums across all patterns plus design.

LeetCode lets you filter problems by company tag (some filters need a paid plan), and many candidates post their interview experiences in discussion forums and on sites like GeeksforGeeks. These are useful for knowing what kind of problems to expect. They are not a guarantee.

How to use company tags responsibly

  1. Cover the patterns first. Company lists are only worth doing once your pattern base is solid, which is the point of this stage.
  2. Pick two to five target companies and look at their tagged problems, sorted by frequency, from the last six to twelve months.
  3. Solve for the pattern. A tag helps you see which patterns repeat; the exact problem will often be a variation. Write the pattern in your log.
  4. Read recent discussion posts for the round structure (how many rounds, OA first or not, whether system design appears) rather than for "leaked" questions.
  5. Treat everything as unverified. Tags and posts can be old, wrong or one person's single experience. Never rely on a fixed question bank, and never present memorised answers as your own thinking; interviewers change problems and probe follow-ups.
  6. Be honest. If you have seen a problem before, tell the interviewer.

What different companies tend to ask (patterns, not promises)

TypeUsually testsTypical emphasis
Large service companies (mass hiring)Aptitude, basic coding, SQL, OOP and core JavaEasy problems: arrays, strings, patterns, simple maths, sorting; MCQs on Java and DBMS
Service companies with a stronger track (digital / ninja roles)Easy to medium DSAHashing, two pointers, basic DP, linked lists, trees; time-boxed OA
Mid-size product companies and startupsMedium DSA, projects, one design roundArrays, hashing, trees, graphs, heaps; practical Java and Spring questions
Top product companies / big techMedium to hard DSA, 3 to 5 roundsAll patterns incl. DP, graphs, tries; HLD and LLD; behavioural round
Fintech and trading firmsHard problems, speed, mathsDP, greedy, bit tricks, probability; strong complexity analysis

This is a general picture; every company, role and year differs. Check the job description and recent posts for the actual process.

A study plan for the target list

  • Service-focused: solve all easy and basic medium problems for arrays, strings, hashing and sorting; polish one project; practise aptitude and SQL; learn to explain your Java basics.
  • Product-focused: after the pattern base, do 40 to 60 company-tagged mediums, 5 to 10 hards, timed mocks, and begin system design (see System Design).
  • For all: a one-minute self-introduction, two or three project stories you can tell clearly, and a few questions to ask the interviewer.

Common mistakes

  • Starting company lists in month 4 with weak basics; you memorise solutions and cannot adapt.
  • Believing a poster's claim that "this will definitely be asked".
  • Ignoring the non-DSA parts: core Java, SQL, Spring Boot and projects are asked at nearly every Indian full-stack interview.

For a Java full-stack role

Expect a mixed loop: one or two DSA rounds at easy-medium level, then Java/Spring/SQL questions, then a project discussion. DSA is the gate; the other topics on these pages (Collections, SQL, Spring) decide the offer.

Contests: weekly LeetCode, Codeforces and CodeChef

Contests train speed and calm under a clock; do the weekly LeetCode contest, upsolve every unsolved problem afterwards, and treat the rating as a side effect, not the goal.

Why do contests

  • They simulate the pressure of an OA: a timer, no hints, hidden tests, a penalty for wrong submissions.
  • They give you problems you have not seen, which tests real pattern recognition instead of memory.
  • They force fast, correct implementation, which makes your templates automatic.
  • Regular practice shows weak patterns clearly: the problem you could not solve is the next topic to study.

LeetCode weekly and biweekly contests

LeetCode runs a weekly contest (usually on Sunday morning in India) and a biweekly contest on Saturday nights, each with four problems and about 90 minutes. Check the exact timing on the site. Problems go from easy to hard. As a rough target: solve the first two reliably, then the third, and read the fourth for an idea. Reaching problem 3 regularly is a strong sign for interviews at good product companies.

A contest-day routine

  1. Before: be at the desk 10 minutes early, with an editor ready, water, and a plain sheet of paper. Do not warm up with a new topic.
  2. Read all four problems quickly, then start with the easiest. Do not stay on a hard one while an easy one waits.
  3. For each problem: think for 3 to 5 minutes, write the idea in a comment, code it, test the sample, and submit. A wrong answer costs a time penalty, so test small edge cases first.
  4. If stuck for 15 minutes, move on and return later.
  5. After: note which problems you solved, how long each took and which topic blocked you.

Upsolving: where the learning happens

Upsolving means solving the problems you could not finish during the contest, afterwards. This is worth more than the contest itself.

  1. Spend 30 to 60 minutes trying again without the editorial.
  2. Read the editorial or a top solution and understand the idea, not just the code.
  3. Re-implement it from scratch the next day, and add it to your log with the pattern and the "key idea" line.
  4. Add the topic to your weak-pattern list and practise three or four similar problems.

Rating is not the goal

The rating is noisy: it goes up and down with the difficulty of one set of problems, your sleep and luck. Companies do not hire by LeetCode rating. Judge progress by the number of problems you can solve cleanly in the time, and by problems you could not solve three months ago and can now. Do not skip a contest because you fear a rating drop; the practice is the point. Never use unfair means (shared solutions, bots); platforms ban accounts, and it defeats the training.

Codeforces and CodeChef (in brief)

CodeforcesCodeChef
StyleShort, tricky problems, strong maths and constructive ideasLonger contests (Starters, Cook-Off), more beginner-friendly ladders
DifficultyHigher; div 2 problems A to EWide range; star-based ranking
Helps interviews?Yes for top product and trading firmsYes for speed and basics
Java tipsUse fast I/O; most solutions are in C++, but Java is acceptedSame

These are optional. If you enjoy them, try Codeforces Div 3 and Div 4 contests, which are closer to interview difficulty, and CodeChef Starters. If you do not enjoy them, LeetCode contests plus your revision are enough.

Time budget

A contest plus its upsolve takes about 3 hours per week. If your time is limited, do one contest every week and skip the biweekly one.

Common mistakes

  • Checking the rank list during the contest instead of solving.
  • Never upsolving: the contest then becomes entertainment, not practice.
  • Submitting without testing and collecting penalties.

Segment tree: range queries with updates in O(log n)

A segment tree stores the answer for every power-of-two-style segment of an array in a binary tree, so a range query and a point update each touch only O(log n) nodes.

Optional This topic is for top product companies and contests. If your targets are service companies, skip it and come back later.

The problem it solves

You have an array and two kinds of operations that arrive in any order: query "the sum (or min, or max) of a[l..r]" and update "set a[i] to a new value". The two simple answers are both slow when there are many operations.

ApproachQueryUpdate
Loop over the rangeO(n)O(1)
Prefix sumsO(1)O(n) (rebuild)
Segment treeO(log n)O(log n)

With n and the number of operations both near 105, O(n) per operation is about 1010 steps, far too slow. The segment tree makes both O(log n).

How it works

The root represents the whole array [0, n-1]. Each node splits its range into two halves, left child and right child. A leaf is one element. Each node stores the combined answer (here the sum) of its range. In the array form, the children of node i are 2i and 2i+1 (the root is node 1), the same layout as a heap.

  • Build: recurse to the leaves, then fill each parent from its two children. O(n).
  • Point update: walk from the root to the leaf of index i (one child per level), set the leaf, then recompute the parents on the way back. O(log n).
  • Range query: for a node whose range is outside the query, return the identity (0 for sum); fully inside, return its stored value; partly overlapping, ask both children and combine. At most about four nodes per level are visited, so O(log n).

Complete Java implementation (range sum)

public class SegmentTree {
    private final int n;
    private final long[] tree;                 // tree[1] is the root; size 4n is always enough

    public SegmentTree(int[] a) {              // requires a.length >= 1
        n = a.length;
        tree = new long[4 * n];
        build(a, 1, 0, n - 1);
    }

    private void build(int[] a, int node, int l, int r) {
        if (l == r) {                          // leaf
            tree[node] = a[l];
            return;
        }
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        build(a, 2 * node, l, mid);
        build(a, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r);
        tree[node] = tree[2 * node] + tree[2 * node + 1];   // combine
    }

    /** Sets a[idx] = value. O(log n). */
    public void update(int idx, int value) {
        update(1, 0, n - 1, idx, value);
    }

    private void update(int node, int l, int r, int idx, int value) {
        if (l == r) {
            tree[node] = value;
            return;
        }
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (idx <= mid) update(2 * node, l, mid, idx, value);
        else update(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, idx, value);
        tree[node] = tree[2 * node] + tree[2 * node + 1];   // recompute on the way back
    }

    /** Sum of a[ql..qr], both ends included. O(log n). */
    public long query(int ql, int qr) {
        return query(1, 0, n - 1, ql, qr);
    }

    private long query(int node, int l, int r, int ql, int qr) {
        if (qr < l || r < ql) return 0;        // no overlap: identity for sum
        if (ql <= l && r <= qr) return tree[node];   // fully inside
        int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
        return query(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr)
             + query(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SegmentTree st = new SegmentTree(new int[]{2, 5, 1, 4, 9, 3});
        System.out.println(st.query(1, 4));    // 5 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 19
        st.update(2, 10);                      // a[2] = 10
        System.out.println(st.query(1, 4));    // 5 + 10 + 4 + 9 = 28
    }
}
19
28

Complexity: build O(n), update O(log n), query O(log n); space O(4n) = O(n). The size 4 * n is a safe upper bound for any n with this recursive layout.

Changing it to min or max

Only two things change: the combine function and the identity returned for a non-overlapping range.

QueryCombineIdentity (no overlap)
Sumleft + right0
MinimumMath.min(left, right)Long.MAX_VALUE
MaximumMath.max(left, right)Long.MIN_VALUE
GCDgcd(left, right)0
 
// in build and update:
tree[node] = Math.min(tree[2 * node], tree[2 * node + 1]);
// in query:
if (qr < l || r < ql) return Long.MAX_VALUE;     // identity for min
if (ql <= l && r <= qr) return tree[node];
int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
return Math.min(query(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr),
                query(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr));

Lazy propagation (idea only)

What if updates apply to a range, such as "add 5 to every element in a[l..r]", and queries ask for a range sum? Updating every leaf is O(n). Lazy propagation stores a pending update on a node ("add 5 to my whole range") and does not push it to the children until a later query or update needs to go below that node. A node with a pending value can answer a fully-covered query by itself: new sum = old sum + 5 × (number of elements). Each operation stays O(log n). The cost is extra bookkeeping: a second array lazy[] and a push-down step before descending. It appears in hard problems ("range add, range sum"), rarely in standard interviews.

Problems that use it

  • Range Sum Query - Mutable (point update, range sum).
  • Range minimum with updates; counting elements in a range with a value condition.
  • The Skyline Problem, Count of Range Sum, Falling Squares (often with coordinate compression).

Common mistakes

  • Allocating 2 * n nodes in the recursive layout. That crashes with ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for many sizes; use 4 * n.
  • Returning 0 as the "no overlap" value for a min tree, which makes every min wrong.
  • Using int for sums of up to 105 values of up to 109; use long.
  • Building a tree on an empty array (n - 1 = -1). Guard it.

Interview angle

You will usually be asked "how do you answer range queries with updates?" The short answer: segment tree or Fenwick tree, O(log n) each. Explain the three node cases (outside, inside, partial) and the build/update/query costs. Coding it fully is expected only for top-tier product roles.

Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) and the i & -i trick

A Fenwick tree keeps prefix sums with point updates in a single array and about ten lines of code; each index covers a block whose size is its lowest set bit, found with i & -i.

Optional A Fenwick tree (also called a binary indexed tree, BIT) supports the same "prefix sum with updates" job as a segment tree, but it is smaller and faster to write. It works for operations that can be undone (sum, XOR, counts); it is not suitable for min/max directly.

The idea: each index owns a block

Use 1-based indexes. Index i stores the sum of a block that ends at i and has length equal to the lowest set bit of i. The lowest set bit is i & -i because -i in two's complement is ~i + 1, which flips every bit above the lowest set bit and keeps that bit.

  • Prefix sum of 1..i: add tree[i], then set i -= i & -i (remove the lowest set bit), until i == 0. At most log n steps, one per set bit.
  • Point update at i: add the change to tree[i], then set i += i & -i (move to the next block that contains this index), until i > n. At most log n steps.
  • Range sum l..r: prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1).

Complete Java implementation

public class FenwickTree {
    private final int n;
    private final long[] tree;                 // 1-based; tree[0] is unused

    public FenwickTree(int n) {
        this.n = n;
        this.tree = new long[n + 1];
    }

    /** Builds from a 0-based array in O(n). */
    public FenwickTree(int[] a) {
        this(a.length);
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            tree[i] += a[i - 1];
            int parent = i + (i & -i);         // the next block that includes this one
            if (parent <= n) tree[parent] += tree[i];
        }
    }

    /** Adds delta to element at 1-based index i. O(log n). */
    public void add(int i, long delta) {
        for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) {
            tree[i] += delta;
        }
    }

    /** Sum of elements 1..i (prefix). O(log n). */
    public long prefix(int i) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) {
            sum += tree[i];
        }
        return sum;
    }

    /** Sum of elements l..r, 1-based, both ends included. */
    public long range(int l, int r) {
        return prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FenwickTree ft = new FenwickTree(new int[]{2, 5, 1, 4, 9, 3});
        System.out.println(ft.range(2, 5));    // 5 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 19
        ft.add(3, 9);                          // element 3 changes from 1 to 10
        System.out.println(ft.range(2, 5));    // 28
    }
}
19
28

To set a value instead of adding, keep a separate plain array a[] and call add(i, newValue - a[i]). Complexity: build O(n), update O(log n), query O(log n), space O(n).

A classic use: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

Process the array from right to left. Map each value to a rank 1..m (coordinate compression: sort the distinct values). For each element, the number of smaller values already seen is prefix(rank - 1); then add(rank, 1). Total O(n log n). The same trick counts inversions.

public java.util.List<Integer> countSmaller(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] sorted = java.util.Arrays.stream(nums).distinct().sorted().toArray();
    FenwickTree ft = new FenwickTree(sorted.length);
    Integer[] result = new Integer[n];
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        int rank = java.util.Arrays.binarySearch(sorted, nums[i]) + 1;   // 1-based rank
        result[i] = (int) ft.prefix(rank - 1);     // how many smaller values are to the right
        ft.add(rank, 1);
    }
    return java.util.Arrays.asList(result);
}

Segment tree vs Fenwick tree vs prefix sums

Prefix sumsFenwick treeSegment tree
Range sum queryO(1)O(log n)O(log n)
Point updateO(n)O(log n)O(log n)
Range min / maxNot with prefix sumsNot directlyYes
Range update (lazy)NoPossible with tricksYes, with lazy propagation
Code sizeVery smallSmallLarger
Use whenArray never changesSum / count with updatesMin, max, or range updates

Rule: Fenwick indexes start at 1

With index 0 the loops never move: 0 & -0 == 0, so i += i & -i loops forever in add. Convert 0-based input to 1-based before calling.

Common mistakes

  • Calling add(0, x) (infinite loop) or prefix(-1) for l = 0 in a 0-based range.
  • Using int[] and overflowing on large sums; use long[].
  • Mixing the roles: query goes down with -=, update goes up with +=.

Interview angle

Say: "Prefix sums are O(1) per query but O(n) per update. A Fenwick tree balances both at O(log n) with very little code; I would use a segment tree if I needed min or max, or range updates." Explain i & -i as "the lowest set bit".

Interview questions — Polish: patterns, technique and range queries

How do you decide which pattern to use on a new problem?

I look at three things: the input (sorted array, string, tree, graph, intervals), what is asked (min/max, count, yes/no, all solutions, an order) and the constraints on n. Sorted input suggests binary search or two pointers; a contiguous subarray suggests a sliding window or prefix sums; "all combinations" suggests backtracking; an optimum over choices with repeated subproblems suggests DP; dependencies suggest topological sort; weighted shortest path suggests Dijkstra. I say the clue aloud, then confirm with a small example.

What do you do in the first five minutes of a coding interview?

Restate the problem, ask clarifying questions (size, duplicates, empty input, what to return when no answer exists), work a small example by hand, state the target complexity from the constraints, and describe the brute force with its complexity. Only then I move to the better idea, and I agree on it with the interviewer before writing code.

Why state the brute force when you already see the optimal solution?

It shows that you understand the problem, gives a correct fallback, and lets you explain the optimisation as a clear step ("this repeated sum becomes a prefix sum"). It also gives the interviewer a chance to guide you. Skipping it makes a good solution look like a memorised one.

How does spaced repetition work for DSA practice?

Every problem that needed a hint or help goes in a log with a "next review" date. I re-solve it from a blank editor, timed, after 3 days, then 2 weeks, then 1 month. A clean solve moves it to the next gap; a failure resets it. Problems I solved quickly alone need no review. The log also shows which patterns are weak, and those decide what new problems I pick.

Write the lower-bound binary search. What is its loop invariant?

The answer (first index with a[i] >= target) always lies in [lo, hi] where hi starts at n.

int lo = 0, hi = a.length;
while (lo < hi) {
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid;
}
return lo;

The midpoint is computed as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid overflow.

What is the difference between BFS and Dijkstra, and when does BFS give shortest paths?

BFS finds shortest paths when every edge has the same cost, because it explores nodes in order of the number of edges. Dijkstra handles different non-negative weights using a priority queue of the best known distances. With negative edges Dijkstra fails and you need Bellman-Ford. Complexities: BFS O(V + E), Dijkstra O((V + E) log V).

Give three Java gotchas that commonly cause wrong answers in interviews.

(1) Integer overflow: int + int wraps silently, so use long or cast before the operation. (2) == on Integer objects compares references and works only for the cached range -128 to 127; use equals. (3) Removing from a collection inside a for-each loop throws ConcurrentModificationException; use an iterator or removeIf. Also: s += c in a loop is O(n²); use StringBuilder.

What does this print? Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; System.out.println(a == b);

It prints false. Autoboxing uses Integer.valueOf, which caches only -128 to 127, so 1000 creates two separate objects and == compares their references. With 1 instead of 1000 it would print true. Use a.equals(b).

How would you handle being stuck during an interview?

Say what I am thinking, go back to a small example and solve it by hand, walk through the patterns (sorted? contiguous? all solutions? dependencies?), try a simpler version of the problem, and if time is passing, code the brute force so that I have a correct answer. I ask for a hint after real effort, and I use the hint openly.

How do you manage time in an online assessment?

Read all questions first and start with the one I am most sure about. Give each question a time box. When stuck, submit a brute force for partial test cases, then return. Check the input and output format carefully, test the sample and a few edge cases before submitting, and keep a few minutes at the end for re-reading. I use fast input (BufferedReader) when n is large.

How should you use company-tagged questions?

After the patterns are solid, to learn the typical difficulty and style for the companies I target, and to see which patterns repeat. I do not treat them as a guaranteed question list: tags can be old, and interviewers change problems and ask follow-ups. I solve for the pattern, log it, and read recent posts mostly for the round structure.

What problem does a segment tree solve, and what are its complexities?

It supports range queries (sum, min, max, gcd) together with point updates on an array. Build is O(n); each query and update is O(log n); memory is O(n) (about 4n entries in the recursive layout). A node stores the combined answer for its range; a query uses nodes fully inside the range and splits at partial overlaps. With lazy propagation it also supports range updates in O(log n).

How does a Fenwick tree work, and why does i & -i matter?

It is a 1-indexed array where tree[i] holds the sum of the block ending at i whose length is the lowest set bit of i. That bit is i & -i. Prefix sum: add tree[i] and subtract the lowest bit until 0. Update: add the delta and add the lowest bit until past n. Both are O(log n) with very little code.

When would you choose prefix sums, a Fenwick tree or a segment tree?

Prefix sums when the array never changes (O(1) query, O(n) build). A Fenwick tree for sums or counts with point updates (O(log n) both, tiny code). A segment tree when you need min or max, or range updates with lazy propagation, or a custom combine function. For most interviews prefix sums or a Fenwick tree are enough.

What do you say at the end of a solution?

I dry run the code on the example, check the edge cases (empty, single element, duplicates, negatives, the largest input), and then state time and space complexity with names for each variable, including recursion stack space. If there is a better trade-off (more memory for less time, or the reverse), I mention it.

Cheat sheet — Polish: patterns, technique and range queries

  • Log row problem, date, pattern, result, minutes, one-line key idea, next review date.
  • Spaced repetition re-solve needed-help problems at 3 days, 2 weeks, 1 month; blank editor, timed, out loud.
  • Checklists NeetCode 150 / Striver sheet are maps for gaps, not goals; tick only what you can redo cold.
  • Constraints to complexity n ≤ 20 exponential; ≤ 500 O(n³); ≤ 5,000 O(n²); ≤ 105 O(n log n); ≤ 106 O(n); 109 O(log n).
  • Sorted + search / pair binary search, two pointers.
  • Contiguous + condition sliding window (positive) or prefix sum + HashMap (negatives).
  • All solutions backtracking; best or count with repeats DP; local choice safe greedy.
  • Graph shortest path unweighted BFS; weighted Dijkstra; negative edges Bellman-Ford.
  • Order with dependencies topological sort; cycle means count < n.
  • Connectivity over time union-find; prefix queries trie; top K heap of size K; next greater monotonic stack.
  • Binary search mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; lower bound uses lo < hi, hi = n, hi = mid.
  • Merge sort stable, O(n log n), O(n) extra; quick sort average O(n log n), random pivot; quickselect average O(n).
  • BFS mark visited when you enqueue; Dijkstra skip stale queue entries; DSU path compression + union by size.
  • Interview flow clarify, example, brute force, optimise, code, test, complexity.
  • When stuck small example, simpler version, pattern table, brute force; ask for a hint after real effort.
  • OA read all problems, easiest first, time-box, brute force for partial marks, check I/O format, fast input.
  • Java traps int overflow, Integer ==, ConcurrentModificationException, remove(int) vs remove(Object), string += in loops, subtraction in comparators.
  • Company prep patterns first; tags show style and difficulty, not a guaranteed list; be honest about problems seen before.
  • Contests read all problems, easiest first; upsolve every unsolved problem; rating is noise.
  • Segment tree build O(n), query/update O(log n), array size 4n; identity: 0 for sum, Long.MAX_VALUE for min.
  • Lazy propagation pending range updates stored on nodes; pushed down only when needed.
  • Fenwick tree 1-indexed; query i -= i & -i; update i += i & -i; range = prefix(r) − prefix(l−1).
  • Choose static array: prefix sums; sum with updates: Fenwick; min/max or range update: segment tree.

Practice — Polish: patterns, technique and range queries

Months 10 to 12 target: re-solve all your "needed help" problems, fill the gaps found by NeetCode 150 or the Striver sheet, solve company-tagged problems for your targets, and do the weekly contests, with at least 15 new problems and about 300 problems in the log by the end.

  1. Set up the log. Create the spreadsheet or file with the columns from the revision system, add every problem you remember with its result, and schedule the first reviews. Done when every "needed help" problem has a review date.
  2. Re-solve the help list. Work through all problems marked "needed help", from a blank editor, 30 to 40 minutes each, out loud. Done when you re-solve most cleanly; send the rest back to the 3-day step.
  3. Templates from memory. On paper, then in an editor, write binary search, lower bound, merge sort, partition, BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, union-find, topological sort and coin change, as in the templates. Done when all ten take under 30 minutes in total and pass small tests.
  4. Pattern sorting drill. Take 30 problem titles from the NeetCode 150 list, cover the solutions, and write the pattern and first idea for each in under two minutes. Check against the clue table. Done when you name the pattern correctly for about 25 of them.
  5. Timed mocks. Once a week solve two mediums in 70 minutes while speaking aloud, using the first-five-minutes script. Ask a friend to listen, or record yourself. Done when you finish most mediums in 30 to 40 minutes and state time and space complexity every time.
  6. OA simulation. Do three full practice assessments (three problems in 90 minutes) on a coding platform's practice mode, including fast input and the input format. Done when you submit correct solutions to at least two of three in time.
  7. Company-tagged set. For two to five target companies, solve 15 or more recent tagged problems you have not done, and log the pattern of each. Done when you can say which patterns repeat for each company.
  8. Contest cycle. Take part in four weekly LeetCode contests and upsolve every unsolved problem within two days. Done when you reach the third problem in at least one contest and have new rows in the log for each upsolve.
  9. Range-query structures (optional). Implement a segment tree and a Fenwick tree from scratch; solve Range Sum Query - Mutable with both, then Count of Smaller Numbers After Self with the Fenwick tree. Done when both pass and you can explain i & -i and the three segment-tree cases.
  10. The "done when" check. You are ready when you can spot the pattern of a new medium problem in 5 to 10 minutes, solve most mediums in 30 to 40 minutes while explaining out loud, state time and space complexity every time, have about 300 problems in the log, and write binary search, merge sort, BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, union-find and a basic DP from memory.
